levels.title: Orientation
levels.purpose: Set expectations, set your clocks, and learn the way of thinking that runs through the whole program.
objectives: Understand how the program works.
Read and accept what the program does not promise.
Set your time zone and read market time against your own.
Use the eight questions of the Analyst's Frame.

levels.title: Introduction To Trading
levels.purpose: Build the right mental model before any terminology: trading is decision-making under uncertainty, with an edge that can be measured or may not exist.
objectives: Define trading and tell it apart from investing and from gambling.
Explain why markets exist and who takes part in them.
Explain price movement as buying and selling pressure, and say honestly that the cause of one move is usually unknowable in real time.
Define an edge as a measured advantage per trade after costs, and tell it apart from a belief.
Work out simple probabilities and expected values.
Show with a simulation why losing streaks are normal.
Judge a decision by its quality, not only by its result.

levels.title: Instruments And The Forex Market
levels.purpose: Know what can be traded and exactly what a currency quote means.
objectives: Describe each asset class by what you own or are exposed to, how it trades and its main risks.
Compare instruments on ownership, hours, leverage, costs, custody and who is on the other side.
Say honestly why this program teaches with Forex, and what that does not mean.
Read a currency quote and say exactly what it means.
Group pairs as major, minor or exotic, and say the groups are a convention.
Work out a reverse quote and a cross rate.

levels.title: Forex Mechanics And Calculators
levels.purpose: Master the words and arithmetic of a single trade until they are automatic.
objectives: Read a two-way quote and work out the spread, in pips and in money.
Count pips between two prices on 5-digit, 3-digit (yen) and cross pairs without a tool.
Work out pip value for any listed pair in your account currency.
Convert lots to units, and work out profit and loss for long and short trades.
Explain leverage and margin, and work out margin, equity, free margin and margin level.
Work out swap, commission and the total cost of a trade, as a share of your risk.
From an account size, a risk percent, an entry and a stop: work out the stop distance, the position size, the dollar risk, the reward, the reward-to-risk and the result in R.

levels.title: Orders And Execution
levels.purpose: Know what each order does and why real fills differ from a chart.
objectives: Tell market, limit, stop, stop-loss, take-profit and stop-limit orders apart by their trigger and price logic.
Given an idea and a level, choose a valid order type on the correct side of the current price.
Explain liquidity, volatility, spread expansion and news as conditions that change your fills.
Explain why chart prices and broker prices can differ.
Explain why a backtest fill can be better than a live fill, and list the assumptions that cause it.

levels.title: Trading Mathematics
levels.purpose: Own the arithmetic of edge and risk: R, expectancy, drawdown.
objectives: Convert between percentages, ratios and decimals, and measure a percent change against the correct starting value.
Express any trade result in R, including partial exits, breakeven stops and costs.
Use independence and compound probability, and state the gambler's fallacy precisely.
Work out the mean, median, standard deviation and standard error of a set of results, and say what sample size does to them.
Calculate expectancy, break-even win rate, the payoff a win rate needs, and profit factor.
Calculate a drawdown in R and in percent, and the gain needed to recover from it.
Explain compounding, fixed-fractional sizing and risk of ruin, and the limits of a simulated number.

levels.title: Reading Charts
levels.purpose: A chart records what price did. Learn candles as summaries, not signals.
objectives: Explain what a candle records and what it cannot say about the path inside it.
Read the open, high, low and close, and work out the body, wicks, range and their ratios.
Combine lower-timeframe candles into a higher-timeframe candle by hand.
Find swing highs and lows under a stated size, and tell a confirmed swing from a provisional one.
Label HH, HL, LH and LL sequences and classify a chart as bullish, bearish, range or unclear.
Define consolidation, expansion, impulse, correction, breakout and pullback with stated thresholds, and see that different definitions give different counts.
Treat candlestick names as descriptions of shape, not predictions.

levels.title: Market Structure
levels.purpose: Describe any chart in a way two people would agree on.
objectives: State market structure in terms of confirmed swing points only.
Tell a swing point from a structural point, and explain that the scale (the order) is a convention.
Tell a confirmed swing from a provisional one, and explain how ignoring the difference creates look-ahead bias.
Classify structure as bullish, bearish, range or unclear, and cite the swings that support the classification.
Define a break of structure (by close or by wick) and name the level that invalidates the current structure.
Describe structure on two timeframes without predicting.
Analyse a chart at the live edge with the future hidden.

levels.title: Price Behavior, Sessions And Levels
levels.purpose: Describe and test price behavior using price, time and levels.
objectives: Classify any market statement as an observation, an interpretation, a hypothesis or evidence.
Turn a belief into a testable hypothesis and describe the test that would confirm or refute it.
Define liquidity, volatility, momentum, compression, expansion, breakout, failed breakout, continuation and reversal in measurable terms, and say which parts are debated.
Identify and mark reaction zones, previous highs and lows, and session highs and lows.
Explain how activity varies across the Asian, Frankfurt, London and New York sessions, and that this is a tested regularity that can change, not a law.
Convert between market or session time and your own time, including daylight-saving traps.

levels.title: Fundamentals And News
levels.purpose: Understand what moves currencies and why news changes trading conditions.
objectives: Explain how interest rates, inflation, employment, growth and central-bank policy relate to currencies, and label each link as an expectation, not a certainty.
Say what the US inflation report, the employment report, the FOMC, the ECB, the Bank of England and GDP releases are.
Read an economic calendar (forecast, previous, actual, revision, impact) and convert the release time correctly.
Explain why price responds to the surprise relative to expectation, and why the reaction can be erratic.
Explain how news affects spread, slippage and stops, and write a rule for trading around events.

levels.title: Risk Management
levels.purpose: Size positions, cap losses, and see what different risk settings do to an account.
objectives: Compute risk per trade and position size correctly for any listed pair, including yen pairs and non-dollar accounts.
Place a stop from invalidation, then size the position to fit it, never the reverse.
Define and apply maximum daily loss, maximum weekly loss and maximum drawdown rules.
Compute open risk and currency exposure across several positions, and identify correlated exposure.
Explain concentration and leverage risk.
Use simulation to show how risk per trade and losing streaks affect an account, and read risk-of-ruin output correctly.
Tell planned risk from realized risk (spread, slippage, gaps).
Write a personal Risk Plan that the journal will later enforce.

levels.title: Behavior And Process Quality
levels.purpose: Name the behaviors that damage results and measure them in your own data.
objectives: Judge a decision by whether the plan was followed, separately from how the trade turned out.
Grade a trade blind to its result, then reveal it, and explain outcome bias.
Recognize FOMO, revenge trading, raising risk after losses, overtrading, moving stops, and cutting winners or holding losers, each by its signature in the journal.
Recognize loss aversion, recency bias, the gambler's fallacy and confirmation bias, and the check that shows each one.
Write pre-commitment rules and a pre-trade checklist, and add behavior rules to the Risk Plan.
Name the behavior and the rule in a mixed set of scenarios.
Review a trade in the right order: process, outcome, then the evidence it adds.

levels.title: Strategy Design
levels.purpose: Move from "I think price will go up" to rules that anyone could apply.
objectives: State the ten components of a strategy and what each must specify.
Convert a belief into an unambiguous, testable rule.
Tell a setup (context) from an entry trigger (event).
Write a stop and a target as conditions, and compare target rules by expectancy.
Write a trading window with a named time zone.
Write management rules and at least three testable no-trade conditions.
Write a hypothesis before testing: the win rate range, the average R, the smallest sample and what counts as failure.
Critique a strategy for missing components, ambiguity, discretionary management and overfitting warning signs.

levels.title: Backtesting, Journaling And Evidence
levels.purpose: Gather evidence honestly and see how it goes wrong.
objectives: Explain what backtesting can and cannot establish.
Explain sample size and randomness: the standard error, why the interval shrinks only with the square root of the trades, and why a small sample can show an edge that is not there.
Recognize hindsight, look-ahead, cherry-picking, survivorship, data-snooping, overfitting and contaminated out-of-sample tests in a supplied test.
Split data into in-sample and out-of-sample before looking, and explain why the out-of-sample data can be used once.
Show what costs and conservative fills do to a result.
Run a manual backtest by a protocol: pre-registered hypothesis, fixed window and split, every valid setup logged, a calibrated conclusion.
Keep a complete, accurate journal, and compute its statistics with their uncertainty.
Describe the ladder of evidence, and why this curriculum does not encourage early live trading or funded accounts.

levels.title: Track P: Platforms, Brokers And The Path To Live
levels.purpose: Learn to operate the tools, and to evaluate providers without being told which to choose. A practical track, separate from the trading education.
objectives: Describe what a charting platform, a trading platform and a broker each do, and what an alert is.
Set up a chart honestly, and find the server time and its offset from UTC.
Open a demo account; place, modify and close a trade with a stop and target; read balance, equity, margin and free margin; export trade history.
Evaluate a provider on regulation, costs, execution, funds and restrictions by verifying at the source or measuring, rather than believing.
Read funded-account rules and compute the expected value of the fee from honest inputs.
Write a Path-To-Live Plan with readiness in numbers, a capital rule and scaling last.

concepts.name: What This Program Is Not
concepts.definition: Finishing the program shows you understand the material. It does not mean you have a profitable strategy.

concepts.name: Market Time And Your Time
concepts.definition: Markets keep the clock of the place they are in. Your clock may differ, and the difference can change during the year.

concepts.name: The Analyst's Frame
concepts.definition: Eight questions that turn a hunch into a reasoned decision.

concepts.name: Decimals
concepts.definition: Reading and subtracting decimal numbers.

concepts.name: Percentages
concepts.definition: Finding a percent of a number and a percent change.

concepts.name: Ratios
concepts.definition: Reading a ratio such as 1:3.

concepts.name: Negative Numbers
concepts.definition: Adding and multiplying with gains and losses.

concepts.name: What Trading Is
concepts.definition: Buying or selling something to profit from a change in its price, over a short or medium time.

concepts.name: The Parts Of A Trade
concepts.definition: Every trade has a market, a direction, a size, an entry, an exit and a risk limit.

concepts.name: Trading Versus Investing
concepts.definition: Investors hold for growth and income over years. Traders aim to profit from price moves over a shorter time. Both can lose money.

concepts.name: Trading Versus Gambling
concepts.definition: Both involve uncertainty. In trading you choose and cap your risk, and a measured edge is possible. Acting on a hunch with no plan is gambling in any market.

concepts.name: Costs Work Against You
concepts.definition: Every trade has a cost. Your average trade must beat it before it earns anything.

concepts.name: Why Markets Exist
concepts.definition: Markets let people exchange, discover prices, raise money and pass on risk.

concepts.name: Who Trades
concepts.definition: Central banks, banks, companies, funds, individuals and automated firms trade for different reasons. Most are not trying to profit from short price moves.

concepts.name: What Moves A Price
concepts.definition: A price is where a buyer and a seller last agreed. More buying than selling pushes it up, and the reverse pushes it down.

concepts.name: Stories After The Fact
concepts.definition: A neat explanation of a move that already happened is not a prediction of the next one.

concepts.name: What An Edge Is
concepts.definition: An edge is an average gain per trade, after costs, that is supported by evidence.

concepts.name: Expected Value
concepts.definition: The average result of a bet if it were repeated many times: multiply each outcome by its chance, then add.

concepts.name: Edge Versus Belief
concepts.definition: A belief is a feeling that something will happen. An edge is a measured average over many recorded trades.

concepts.name: Probability As Frequency
concepts.definition: A 60% chance means about 6 in 10 over many tries. It says nothing certain about the next one.

concepts.name: One Result Versus Many
concepts.definition: One result cannot be predicted. The spread of many results can.

concepts.name: Independent Results
concepts.definition: When results are independent, the last result does not change the chance of the next.

concepts.name: Losing Streaks
concepts.definition: Runs of losses happen in any random sequence, including inside a strategy that wins on average.

concepts.name: Luck Makes Results Differ
concepts.definition: Traders with identical rules and identical odds still get very different results because of luck.

concepts.name: Process Versus Outcome
concepts.definition: A decision is judged by the plan and information behind it. The result is a separate question.

concepts.name: A Good Trade Versus A Profitable One
concepts.definition: A good trade follows a tested plan at acceptable risk. It can still lose. A poor trade can win by luck.

concepts.name: The Pip
concepts.definition: The standard step in which a currency price is measured: 0.0001 on most pairs, 0.01 on yen pairs.

concepts.name: Lots
concepts.definition: A standard lot is 100,000 units of the first currency in the pair.

concepts.name: Pip Value
concepts.definition: What one pip is worth in your account currency for your position size.

concepts.name: Base And Quote Currency
concepts.definition: In a pair such as EUR/USD, the first currency is the base and the second is the quote. The price is how many units of the quote currency buy one unit of the base.

concepts.name: Major, Minor And Exotic Pairs
concepts.definition: Pairs are grouped by how heavily they trade and whether they include the US dollar. The boundaries are a convention and differ by source.

concepts.name: Reading A Rate Move
concepts.definition: If the price of a pair rises, the first currency has strengthened against the second, and the second has weakened against the first.

concepts.name: Reverse Quotes And Cross Rates
concepts.definition: A reverse quote is 1 divided by the price. A cross rate is worked out from two prices that share a currency.

concepts.name: Currency Strength Is Relative
concepts.definition: A currency has no price of its own, only a price against another currency. "The dollar rose" needs a counterpart.

concepts.name: Asset Classes
concepts.definition: An asset class is a group of similar assets. Some you own outright. Others are contracts whose value follows a price.

concepts.name: Underlying Versus Instrument
concepts.definition: The underlying is the thing whose price matters. The instrument is what you actually trade to get exposure to it.

concepts.name: Stocks
concepts.definition: A share is a piece of ownership in a company. Shares trade on exchanges with set hours, and some pay dividends.

concepts.name: ETFs
concepts.definition: An ETF is a basket of assets that trades like one share. It has running fees and may not match its index exactly.

concepts.name: Indices
concepts.definition: An index measures a basket. It is a calculation, so you trade it through an ETF, a futures contract or a CFD.

concepts.name: Commodities
concepts.definition: Physical goods in standard grades. Their prices are pushed by supply and demand shocks, and most traders use futures, funds or CFDs.

concepts.name: Bonds
concepts.definition: A bond is a loan that pays a coupon and is repaid at a set date.

concepts.name: Price And Yield Move Oppositely
concepts.definition: Yield is the yearly income divided by the price. When a bond's price rises, its yield falls, and the reverse.

concepts.name: Futures
concepts.definition: A futures contract is a standard agreement to buy or sell at a set price on a set date. It is traded on an exchange, needs a margin deposit, and expires.

concepts.name: CFDs And Leveraged Products
concepts.definition: A CFD pays the change in price. You do not own the underlying, the provider is usually the other side, leverage magnifies gains and losses, and rules vary by country.

concepts.name: Crypto Assets
concepts.definition: Digital assets that trade around the clock. Custody, platform failure and changing regulation are major risks.

concepts.name: Comparing Instruments
concepts.definition: Instruments differ in ownership, hours, leverage, costs, custody and who the counterparty is. Choose by the job, not by habit.

concepts.name: Why This Course Starts With Forex
concepts.definition: Forex is a good teaching market for practical reasons. It is not easier, safer or more profitable than any other.

concepts.name: Bid, Ask And The Spread
concepts.definition: A quote has two prices. You buy at the higher ask and sell at the lower bid. The gap is the spread, which you pay when you enter.

concepts.name: Counting Pips
concepts.definition: A pip is the fourth decimal place (the second on yen pairs). A pipette is a tenth of a pip. Count the distance between two prices in pips by dividing by the pip size.

concepts.name: Position Value
concepts.definition: The value of a position is units times price. It is far larger than the money you need to open it.

concepts.name: Long And Short
concepts.definition: A long trade buys first and gains when the price rises. A short trade sells first and gains when the price falls. A long trade opens at the ask and closes at the bid. A short trade opens at the bid and closes at the ask.

concepts.name: Profit And Loss In Money
concepts.definition: Profit or loss in money is the result in pips, times the pip value, times the number of lots. The spread is already in the prices you traded at.

concepts.name: Leverage And Margin
concepts.definition: Margin is the position value divided by the leverage. Leverage does not change what a pip is worth. It changes how big a position the account can hold, and so how far the account swings.

concepts.name: Balance, Equity, Free Margin And Margin Level
concepts.definition: Equity is balance plus floating profit or loss. Free margin is equity minus used margin. Margin level is equity divided by used margin. Brokers close positions if it falls too low.

concepts.name: Swap And Commission
concepts.definition: Holding a position overnight earns or costs swap. Some brokers also charge commission per lot, usually counted for the round trip.

concepts.name: Slippage And The Total Cost Of A Trade
concepts.definition: Total cost is spread plus commission plus swap plus slippage. Compare it with the money you risk to see how much of 1R it takes.

concepts.name: Dollar Risk And Percentage Risk
concepts.definition: Dollar risk is the account balance times the risk percent, divided by 100. Percentage risk is the money at risk divided by the account balance, times 100.

concepts.name: Stop Distance And Position Size
concepts.definition: Choose the stop first from where you would be wrong, then size the position to fit: lots = risk amount ÷ (stop distance in pips × pip value), rounded DOWN to the lot step.

concepts.name: Reward, Reward-To-Risk And R
concepts.definition: Reward-to-risk is reward divided by risk. R is a result divided by the risk taken, so risking $25 and making $75 is +3R.

concepts.name: Market Orders
concepts.definition: A market order trades at once at the best available price. You get a fill, but not necessarily the price you saw, because of slippage.

concepts.name: Limit Versus Stop
concepts.definition: A limit waits for a BETTER price than now. A stop waits for the price to move THROUGH a level. A buy limit and a sell stop sit below the price. A buy stop and a sell limit sit above it.

concepts.name: Buy Limit And Sell Limit
concepts.definition: A limit order fills at your price or better, and may never fill if the price does not come back.

concepts.name: Buy Stop And Sell Stop
concepts.definition: A stop order becomes a market order when triggered, so it fills at your price or worse, especially in a gap. A stop-loss is a stop order.

concepts.name: Stop-Loss And Take-Profit
concepts.definition: A stop-loss caps a loss and a take-profit closes at a target. Neither is guaranteed to fill at its level. If both are inside one candle, chart data cannot say which came first.

concepts.name: Stop-Limit Orders
concepts.definition: A stop-limit has a trigger and a limit. It protects you from a bad price, but it may not fill at all.

concepts.name: Choosing The Order Type
concepts.definition: Choose from your plan: now (market), a pullback (limit), a breakout (stop), a breakout with a price limit (stop-limit), protection and a target (stop-loss and take-profit).

concepts.name: Liquidity And Volatility
concepts.definition: Liquidity is how easily you can trade without moving the price. Volatility is how far and fast the price moves. Both change through the day, and both change the fills you get.

concepts.name: Spread Expansion, News And Slippage
concepts.definition: Spreads widen around news and rollover, which raises costs and can trigger stops. A short stop-loss is a buy order, so it triggers on the ask.

concepts.name: Broker Execution Models
concepts.definition: Brokers fill orders in different ways: market, instant or request execution. A label such as "no dealing desk" describes a model, not a guarantee. Test rather than trust.

concepts.name: Chart Prices Against Broker Prices
concepts.definition: A chart and a broker can show different prices: different feeds, bid or ask or middle, the spread not drawn, and candles stamped in different time zones. A level touched on one may not be touched on the other.

concepts.name: Why Backtest Fills Differ From Live Fills
concepts.definition: Touched is not filled. Chart data omits the spread, slippage and delay, and cannot order events inside a candle. A test should state its fill assumptions and be conservative.

concepts.name: Percentages, Ratios And Decimals
concepts.definition: A percent change is measured against the starting value. A ratio compares parts of a whole. A rise and an equal fall in percent do not cancel out.

concepts.name: R-Multiples: Comparing Trades
concepts.definition: R is the initial risk. Dividing each result by the risk taken lets you compare trades of different dollar size.

concepts.name: R With Partials, Breakeven And Costs
concepts.definition: A trade closed in pieces has a result equal to each piece's R weighted by its size. Costs come off before the result is written in R, so a breakeven stop is a small loss.

concepts.name: Probability For Traders
concepts.definition: For independent results, chances multiply. The chance of at least one win is 1 minus the chance of losing every time. Past results do not change the next chance.

concepts.name: Mean, Median And Outliers
concepts.definition: The mean is pulled by big results. The median is the middle one. Compare them before trusting an average.

concepts.name: Spread And Standard Error
concepts.definition: Standard deviation measures how spread out results are. Standard error measures how uncertain their average is, and it shrinks only with the square root of the number of trades.

concepts.name: Expectancy
concepts.definition: Expectancy is the average result per trade: win rate × average win minus loss rate × average loss. It needs both how often and how much.

concepts.name: Break-Even Win Rate And Payoff
concepts.definition: Every payoff ratio has a win rate at which expectancy is zero: 1 ÷ (1 + payoff). Costs push that rate higher.

concepts.name: Profit Factor
concepts.definition: Profit factor is total won divided by total lost. It is a ratio, not an average, and a few large winners can inflate it.

concepts.name: Drawdown And Recovery
concepts.definition: A drawdown is a fall from a high point. The gain needed to recover is bigger than the fall, and grows quickly as the fall deepens.

concepts.name: Compounding And Position Sizing Over Time
concepts.definition: Gains and losses compound on the balance you have at the time. Risking a percent of the current balance changes the size of every later bet.

concepts.name: Risk Of Ruin
concepts.definition: The chance of a ruinous drawdown depends on win rate, payoff and, above all, the risk per trade. It is only as reliable as the estimates that go into it.

concepts.name: What A Chart Shows
concepts.definition: A chart records where price traded against time. It is a record of what happened, not a forecast.

concepts.name: Timeframes And Aggregation
concepts.definition: Each candle covers a fixed interval. A bigger candle is the first open, the highest high, the lowest low and the last close of the smaller ones inside it.

concepts.name: Open, High, Low, Close
concepts.definition: A candle keeps four prices. The open is the first, the close is the last, and the high and low are the extremes reached in between.

concepts.name: Body, Wicks And Range
concepts.definition: Body = |close − open|. Range = high − low. The wicks are the parts of the range outside the body. Ratios such as body ÷ range describe the shape.

concepts.name: Bullish And Bearish Candles
concepts.definition: A candle is bullish if it closed above its open and bearish if below. Colours are a convention, and small bodies are described by ratio.

concepts.name: Candles Are Summaries, Not Signals
concepts.definition: Many different tick paths make the same candle. A named candle pattern is a label for a shape. What follows it is a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

concepts.name: Consolidation And Expansion
concepts.definition: Compare the average candle range of a stretch with the whole chart. A definition with a stated threshold makes the count repeatable, and a different threshold gives a different count.

concepts.name: Impulse And Correction
concepts.definition: An impulse is a leg between two swings and a correction is the counter-leg. A retracement is the correction as a fraction of the impulse: (B − C) ÷ (B − A).

concepts.name: Swing Highs And Swing Lows
concepts.definition: A swing high beats n highs on each side; a swing low beats n lows. It is confirmed only n bars later. Until then the newest extreme is provisional.

concepts.name: HH, HL, LH, LL
concepts.definition: Compare each swing with the previous swing of the same kind: higher or lower. The labels describe a sequence and predict nothing.

concepts.name: Trends And Ranges
concepts.definition: Rising highs and lows are bullish; falling are bearish; level ones are a range; mixed ones are unclear. Unclear is a valid answer.

concepts.name: Breakouts And Pullbacks
concepts.definition: A breakout is the first close beyond a stated level (or a wick, under another convention). A pullback is a counter-move that has not broken structure. Conventions change the count.

concepts.name: Observation, Interpretation, Hypothesis
concepts.definition: A chart reading has three layers. The swing sequence is an observation. Calling it a trend is an interpretation. Saying it will continue is a hypothesis. Keep them apart.

concepts.name: Swing Points And Structural Points
concepts.definition: Order-1 swings are the size-n swings. Structural swings are the order-1 swings that stand beyond their neighbours of the same kind. The scale is a convention that depends on the chart.

concepts.name: Confirmed And Provisional Swings
concepts.definition: The newest extreme is always provisional. Labelling a swing before it is confirmed uses knowledge from the future: look-ahead bias.

concepts.name: Bullish Structure
concepts.definition: Rising confirmed structural highs and lows. The latest structural low is the level that holds the sequence up.

concepts.name: Bearish Structure
concepts.definition: Falling confirmed structural highs and lows. The latest structural high is the level that holds the sequence down.

concepts.name: Range Structure
concepts.definition: A range has boundaries: highs that are about level and lows that are about level, within a stated tolerance. A borderline case is unclear.

concepts.name: Break Of Structure
concepts.definition: A break of structure is a bar that closes beyond the latest confirmed structural swing. Under a wick convention the count can differ. It is an observable event, not a prediction.

concepts.name: Structural Shifts And Invalidation
concepts.definition: Invalidation is the level whose break ends the current description. A shift is a description of what happened. A reversal is a hypothesis about what comes next.

concepts.name: Multi-Timeframe Structure
concepts.definition: Each timeframe has its own structure. When they differ, state both readings with their timeframes. A conflict is a description, not a signal.

concepts.name: Analysis At The Live Edge
concepts.definition: At the live edge the future is hidden. State the structure, the latest confirmed swings, the invalidation and what would change your view. Then reveal, and judge the reading, not the result.

concepts.name: Technical Analysis As A Description
concepts.definition: Technical analysis here uses price, time and levels to DESCRIBE what the market did and to state hypotheses that can be tested. It cannot promise what happens next.

concepts.name: From Observation To Conclusion
concepts.definition: Observation, hypothesis, test, result, conclusion. A hypothesis must be written so that a count can refute it, and a conclusion may honestly be "insufficient evidence".

concepts.name: Support And Resistance As Reaction Zones
concepts.definition: A level is a band where price reacted before. That is an observation. That it will react again is a hypothesis, and levels drawn after the fact prove nothing. Compare with random levels.

concepts.name: Previous Highs And Lows
concepts.definition: The previous day's and previous week's high and low are reference levels. Which candle made them depends on where the day starts.

concepts.name: Liquidity: Three Meanings
concepts.definition: Liquidity can mean market depth (observable), orders resting near obvious levels (interpretation) or price being drawn to them (hypothesis). Keep the three meanings apart.

concepts.name: Volatility, Compression And Expansion
concepts.definition: Volatility is the size and speed of price change. Compression and expansion are found by comparing candle ranges with a recent average, using stated thresholds.

concepts.name: Momentum As Price Speed
concepts.definition: Momentum here is displacement per unit time, or a run of closes in one direction. It describes what price did and forecasts nothing.

concepts.name: Breakouts, Failed Breakouts, Continuation And Reversal
concepts.definition: Each event needs a price rule and a time rule. "Failed" needs a stated failure condition. Two definitions can classify the same event differently.

concepts.name: Forex Sessions
concepts.definition: Sessions are windows defined on each market's own clock. Activity differing across the day is a tested regularity, not a law, and it needs a sample to measure.

concepts.name: Session Time Versus Your Time
concepts.definition: Each session sits on its own market's clock and follows that market's daylight saving. Guyana stays at UTC−4, so the gap to a market changes twice a year, and in the weeks when the US and the UK are out of step.

concepts.name: Session Highs And Lows
concepts.definition: A session's high and low come from the candles inside its window. A different window gives different levels. The Session Levels overlay draws them as references, never as signals.

concepts.name: A Map Of Currency Drivers
concepts.definition: Rates, inflation, growth, policy, risk sentiment and flows can all move a currency, often at once. Each link is an expectation, not a certainty.

concepts.name: Interest Rates And Central Banks
concepts.definition: A central bank sets a policy rate. The gap between two economies' rates is one input, and what the market EXPECTS rates to do matters as much as where they are.

concepts.name: Inflation
concepts.definition: CPI measures the prices of a basket. Its yearly percent change is inflation. Central banks respond to it, and markets respond to how it compares with expectations.

concepts.name: Employment
concepts.definition: Payrolls, unemployment and wages describe the labour market. Policy makers watch them because they bear on growth and inflation.

concepts.name: GDP And Economic Growth
concepts.definition: GDP is the output of an economy. It is a lagging measure and is often revised, so the first figure is not the last.

concepts.name: Monetary Policy And Its Tone
concepts.definition: Tightening and easing describe policy. Hawkish and dovish describe TONE. Forward guidance shapes expectations. Both words are descriptions, not forecasts.

concepts.name: Risk Sentiment And Currency Strength
concepts.definition: Risk-on and risk-off describe investor mood. Relationships between currencies change across eras, so a measured relationship describes the window it was measured in. That is an interpretation.

concepts.name: The Big US Events: CPI, NFP, FOMC
concepts.definition: The US inflation report, the employment report and the central bank decision are widely watched because they bear on the path of US rates.

concepts.name: ECB, BoE And Other Releases
concepts.definition: Rate decisions, press conferences, growth and employment releases elsewhere follow their own schedules and clocks.

concepts.name: Reading An Economic Calendar
concepts.definition: A calendar row gives impact, forecast, previous, actual, revision and a release time on a stated clock. Convert the time for the date, including daylight saving.

concepts.name: Expectations, Surprise And Reaction
concepts.definition: Price reacts to the surprise (actual minus forecast), not the figure itself. The first move can reverse, and the direction cannot be read from the number alone.

concepts.name: News And Execution Conditions
concepts.definition: Around a release, spreads widen, slippage grows and stops can fill far from their price. Standing aside, reducing or trading is a rule decided in advance.

concepts.name: The News Event Lab
concepts.definition: An event study compares price around every event with ordinary periods. It counts all events, states its sample, and needs a verified list of timestamps.

concepts.name: Risk Per Trade
concepts.definition: Fixed-fraction risk means the same percent of the current balance on each trade. The choice comes from surviving a losing streak, not from the gains you hope for.

concepts.name: Position Sizing In Practice
concepts.definition: Size from the risk budget and the stop, convert the pip value into your account currency, round lots DOWN to the lot step, and check the realized risk after rounding.

concepts.name: The Stop Is Invalidation
concepts.definition: Place the stop just beyond the level that ends the idea, then size the position to fit it. A stop chosen from a dollar amount, or a fixed distance, is a warning sign.

concepts.name: Maximum Daily And Weekly Loss
concepts.definition: A circuit breaker stops you after a stated loss. Say whether it counts closed trades or open losses too, and what happens when it is hit.

concepts.name: Drawdown Rules
concepts.definition: After a drawdown you reduce risk, never raise it to make the loss back. The gain needed to recover is bigger than the fall.

concepts.name: Account Exposure And Open Risk
concepts.definition: Open risk is the sum of the risk on every open trade. Cap it, so that one bad day cannot reach your daily limit from open trades alone.

concepts.name: Correlation And Exposure By Currency
concepts.definition: Positions in different pairs can be one bet on a single currency. Count exposure by currency across all positions. Relationships between currencies are not stable.

concepts.name: Concentration Risk And Leverage
concepts.definition: Notional is not risk: risk depends on the stop. But a large notional makes gaps and slippage costly, and leverage available is not leverage to use.

concepts.name: Risk Of Ruin Revisited
concepts.definition: Simulated ruin curves across risk levels, win rates and payoffs. The output depends on assumed inputs, and the risk per trade changes it a great deal.

concepts.name: The Losing-Streak Simulator
concepts.definition: Apply 1, 3, 5, 8 and 10 losses in a row at different risk settings, state how many you could survive BEFORE the animation, and compare with the result.

concepts.name: Drawdown Distributions
concepts.definition: Many simulated runs of the same rules give a spread of maximum drawdowns and longest losing streaks. Plan for the unlucky end of the spread, not the middle.

concepts.name: Planned Versus Realized Risk
concepts.definition: Spread, slippage, gaps and rounding make the risk you actually take differ from the risk you planned. Build a buffer, and measure it.

concepts.name: Building A Risk Plan
concepts.definition: A Risk Plan is your own written limits, made consistent with each other and approved by your mentor. It is what the journal later enforces.

concepts.name: Process Quality Against Trade Outcome
concepts.definition: A decision is judged by whether the plan was followed. The result is judged separately, and one result proves little about a method.

concepts.name: Outcome Bias
concepts.definition: Judging a decision by its result. Hindsight makes the answer look obvious. Grade the decision blind to the result first.

concepts.name: FOMO
concepts.definition: Entering because price has already moved. Signature: an entry far from the planned level, after a fast move, with no valid setup logged. Rule: no plan level, no order.

concepts.name: Revenge Trading And Raising Risk After Losses
concepts.definition: Trading to recover a loss, or raising size after one. Signature: a trade soon after a loss with larger size or no valid setup. Rule: a pause after a loss, and risk never rises inside a drawdown.

concepts.name: Overtrading
concepts.definition: More trades than the plan allows. Signature: trades per day above the plan's maximum. Rule: a maximum trades per day, written in the plan.

concepts.name: Moving Stops
concepts.definition: Widening a stop after entry. Signature: stop distance increased after entry. Rule: stops move only to reduce risk.

concepts.name: Cutting Winners And Holding Losers
concepts.definition: Exiting winners early and holding losers hoping. It lowers expectancy in R even when the win rate is unchanged. Rule: management rules written before entry, and a stop set with the order.

concepts.name: Fear Of Losing And Loss Aversion
concepts.definition: A loss feels heavier than an equal gain, so you skip valid setups after losses or hold losers. Signature: losers held longer than winners. Check: compare the average time in trade of winners and losers.

concepts.name: Recency Bias And The Gambler's Fallacy
concepts.definition: Weighting the last few trades too heavily, and believing a win is "due". Independent trades owe nothing. Signature: size raised after a losing streak. Rule: size depends on the plan, never on the last result.

concepts.name: Confirmation Bias
concepts.definition: Seeking evidence that agrees and discounting the rest. Signature: the disconfirming-evidence field left empty. Rule: write the strongest case against the trade before entry.

concepts.name: Rules, Checklists And Pre-Commitment
concepts.definition: Turn each countermeasure into an if-then rule written in advance, and run a checklist before every order. The moment of temptation is the worst time to decide.

concepts.name: Naming The Behavior And The Rule
concepts.definition: From a short story, name the behavior, name the rule that answers it, and score the process.

concepts.name: The Post-Trade Review
concepts.definition: Score process first, from the plan. Note the outcome second. Then decide what evidence the trade adds, which is usually very little on its own.

concepts.name: The Ten Components Of A Strategy
concepts.definition: Market, timeframe, session, setup, entry, stop, target, sizing, management and no-trade conditions. A strategy is a procedure that specifies every one.

concepts.name: A Belief Against A Strategy
concepts.definition: "Price will go up" is a belief. "Buy when A, B and C are true" is a strategy. The second can be applied, tested and found wrong.

concepts.name: Choosing A Market And Timeframe
concepts.definition: Choose by costs, liquidity, session activity, data available and how many opportunities each gives, and write the reason down.

concepts.name: Session And Time Rules
concepts.definition: Name the time zone and the window. "The London open" is ambiguous once the clocks change. Say the zone and the hours.

concepts.name: Setup Against Entry Trigger
concepts.definition: A setup is the context that makes a trade possible and can last for hours. A trigger is the single event that fires the order.

concepts.name: Stop And Target Conditions
concepts.definition: The stop is where the hypothesis is invalid, tied to a level. A target trades win rate against R: a nearer target wins more often and pays less, and expectancy decides.

concepts.name: Sizing And Management As Rules
concepts.definition: Position sizing links to the Risk Plan. Every management action, such as a partial exit, a stop move or a trail, is a rule written before entry. Discretionary changes make results untestable.

concepts.name: No-Trade Conditions
concepts.definition: At least three, each testable: news, spread, session, loss limits or missing data. They are decided before, not during.

concepts.name: Making Rules Testable: The Two-Person Test
concepts.definition: Could two people apply these rules to the same chart and reach the same decision? Replace strong, clear and good with numbers, levels and clock times.

concepts.name: Hypotheses And Expectations
concepts.definition: Before any test, write the win rate range you expect, the average R, the smallest sample you will accept and what result would count as failure. A test with no stated failure cannot fail.

concepts.name: Critiquing A Strategy
concepts.definition: Look for missing components, ambiguity, discretionary management and overfitting warning signs: many precise parameters, hundreds of variants tried, one short period, a narrow window that looks fitted.

concepts.name: What A Backtest Can And Cannot Show
concepts.definition: A backtest shows how a precise rule would have behaved on past data, under stated assumptions. It cannot show that the rule will work, and it is only as honest as the protocol used.

concepts.name: Sample Size And Randomness
concepts.definition: A small sample can show an edge that is not there. The interval around an average shrinks only with the square root of the number of trades, and a random-outcome generator produces "strategies" that look skilled.

concepts.name: Hindsight And Look-Ahead Bias
concepts.definition: Using information not available at decision time: a swing before it is confirmed, a day's high before the day ends. Hindsight makes old charts look easy.

concepts.name: Cherry-Picking And Survivorship Bias
concepts.definition: Choosing the good examples, leaving out the failures and the setups never logged, or testing only what survived.

concepts.name: Data Snooping And Overfitting
concepts.definition: Try many variants and keep the best, or fit many parameters to one sample, and you fit noise. The fix is data the rule has never seen.

concepts.name: In-Sample And Out-Of-Sample
concepts.definition: Split the data before you look. Build on the in-sample part. Freeze the rule. Run the out-of-sample part once. An out-of-sample set you have looked at, and then changed the rule because of, is no longer out-of-sample.

concepts.name: Costs And Realistic Fills
concepts.definition: Spread, commission and slippage take R from every trade, and a small edge can vanish. When a candle reaches both the stop and the target, take the stop: the conservative rule.

concepts.name: Running A Manual Backtest Properly
concepts.definition: Pre-register the hypothesis, fix the window and the split, step bar by bar, log every valid setup and every skip with a reason, then conclude in-sample, unlock the out-of-sample data, run it once, and state the interval.

concepts.name: The Trading Journal
concepts.definition: Every field exists for a reason: a filter, a check or a flag needs it. The accuracy audit compares prices, R, stop side, sizing and session tag, and failures are notes to fix.

concepts.name: Performance Statistics And Their Uncertainty
concepts.definition: Trades, win rate, average R, expectancy, profit factor, maximum drawdown and streaks, each with the number of trades it rests on. The interval on expectancy and the sign-flip test say how sure you can be.

concepts.name: Interpreting A Result
concepts.definition: Ask eight questions: what information, what outcomes are possible, what would invalidate it, what is the risk, what does the historical evidence say, is there an edge, how large is the sample, could it be random. Most results on small samples answer "cannot say".

concepts.name: The Ladder Of Evidence
concepts.definition: Backtest, out-of-sample, replay, demo forward test, small live, then scaling. Each rung catches a different problem. Completing this curriculum is not a profitable strategy, and nothing here encourages funded accounts or significant capital.

concepts.name: Planning With The Future Hidden
concepts.definition: Decide the setup, the stop, the target and the size before the future is shown. The process is scored first and the outcome second, and the two are kept apart because one outcome says almost nothing.

concepts.name: Recognising Bias In A Supplied Test
concepts.definition: Given a description of a test, name what is wrong: hindsight, look-ahead, cherry-picking, survivorship, snooping, overfitting, a contaminated out-of-sample set, ignored costs or a sample too small.

concepts.name: Charting, Platform And Broker
concepts.definition: Three different things. A charting platform draws charts. A trading platform sends orders. A broker holds your account and fills or routes the order. An alert is a notification, not a signal.

concepts.name: Setting Up A Chart Honestly
concepts.definition: Set the time zone, read the timeframe, show the sessions you use, and know what replay does and does not show. Menus differ by version: verify on your own copy.

concepts.name: Server Time
concepts.definition: The platform's server clock differs from market time and from yours. Find its offset from UTC, write it down, and convert before using any time rule.

concepts.name: Accounts, Leverage And Specifications
concepts.definition: Account currency, the leverage setting, smallest lot and lot step, and the contract specification of each symbol decide what a trade costs and how it can be sized.

concepts.name: What A Demo Does Not Show
concepts.definition: A demo teaches mechanics. It may not reproduce real fills, slippage or spreads, and it cannot reproduce the feeling of real money.

concepts.name: Placing And Managing A Trade
concepts.definition: Attach the stop and target to the order, check the ticket against your planned R and risk, move a stop only to reduce risk, and record what you did.

concepts.name: Reading The Account Panel
concepts.definition: Equity is balance plus floating profit or loss. Free margin is equity minus margin used. Margin level is equity divided by margin.

concepts.name: Exporting Trade History
concepts.definition: An exported statement is the platform's own record. Check that every trade is there, which clock its times use, and that costs are shown, before copying anything into your journal.

concepts.name: Regulation: Verify At The Source
concepts.definition: A regulator keeps a public register. Look up the firm's exact legal name and license number on the regulator's own register, which you reach yourself. Regulation does not guarantee profit or fair fills, and jurisdictions differ.

concepts.name: Costs And Execution, Measured
concepts.definition: Spread, commission and swap are read from the terms. Spread and slippage are measured on a demo, at your hours, over many orders. A quoted figure is a claim. A measured one is evidence.

concepts.name: Deposits, Withdrawals And Restrictions
concepts.definition: Read the conditions for moving money in and out, the fees, the time a withdrawal takes, and the restrictions on styles, news trading, leverage and inactivity. Test a small withdrawal before relying on it.

concepts.name: Funded-Account Programs And Expected Value
concepts.definition: Expected value is the chance of passing times the payout, minus the fee. Use your own honest inputs. The fee is paid every time, so most people who pay it lose it.

concepts.name: The Path To Live
concepts.definition: Written readiness criteria in numbers, capital only that can be lost completely, small live testing rules, a rule for going back to demo, and scaling last. Completing this curriculum is not a profitable strategy.

concepts.name: The Platform Practice Lab
concepts.definition: The lab is a checklist done on your own demo account: a demo opened, a trade placed, modified and closed, the history exported, and two providers evaluated on the worksheet. Your mentor verifies it with you on the screen. Nothing in it is taken on trust.

glossary.definition: One complete action: you enter a position, hold it, and exit it.
A place, real or online, where buyers and sellers agree prices.
The level at which a buyer and a seller last agreed to trade.
The price at which you start a trade.
The price at which you finish a trade.
A trade that is currently open.
What a trade made or lost. It is fixed only when you exit.
The most you are willing to lose on one trade, set before you enter.
Buying something to own for a long time, for growth and income.
Risking money on an uncertain result with no measured advantage, often with the odds set against you.
The built-in advantage that makes a casino game pay out less than it should on average.
Taking a risk on a price move in the hope of a profit.
Taking a position to protect against a price move that would hurt you elsewhere.
The way buyers and sellers together reveal what something is worth right now.
A country's official bank. It manages the currency and interest rates.
A pool of money managed for many people.
A set of rules a computer follows to place trades automatically.
An average gain per trade, after costs, that is supported by evidence.
The average result of a bet if it were repeated many times.
How often something happens over many tries, as a fraction or a percent.
The share of trades that make money.
The set of results you are looking at. A small sample can mislead.
Results that do not affect each other.
Several losing trades in a row.
How spread out results are. High variance means results swing a lot.
The plan and rules you followed to make a decision.
What happened: the profit or the loss.
Knowing how something turned out, which makes it look obvious in retrospect.
Two currencies quoted together, such as EUR/USD. The price says how much of the second one buys one of the first.
The second currency in a pair. Prices and profits first come out in this currency.
The currency your trading account is held in.
The standard step of a currency price: 0.0001 on most pairs, 0.01 on yen pairs.
A standard size for a position. One standard lot is 100,000 units.
What one pip is worth in money, for your position size, in your account currency.
The clock rule of a place. Guyana is four hours behind UTC all year.
Moving the clocks forward in summer. Some countries do it and some do not, and on different dates.
The first currency in a pair. It is the one being priced.
The second currency in a pair. The price is counted in this currency.
In this program: one of the seven most traded pairs, each with the US dollar in it.
A pair of two major currencies that does not include the US dollar. Also called a cross.
A major currency paired with the currency of a smaller or emerging economy.
The same price turned round: USD/EUR is 1 divided by EUR/USD.
A price worked out from two other prices that share a currency.
Something you can check directly in the data.
How a person reads what they observe. It is a judgment, not a fact.
A testable claim about what will happen. It may turn out wrong.
Something of value that people buy and sell.
A group of similar assets, such as stocks or bonds.
The thing whose price you are exposed to, such as gold or a company's shares.
What you actually trade to get exposure to the underlying: the thing itself, a fund, or a contract.
A small piece of ownership in a company. Also called a stock.
A part of a company's profit paid out to its owners.
An organised market with set rules and opening hours where standard products trade.
Exchange-traded fund: a basket of assets that trades on an exchange like a single share.
A number that measures the combined price of a basket of assets. You cannot buy an index itself.
A physical good traded in standard grades, such as oil, gold or wheat.
The price for buying something right now, for immediate delivery.
A loan to a government or company. It pays interest and is repaid on a set date.
The yearly interest a bond pays, usually stated as an amount on its face value.
The yearly income from an asset divided by the price you pay for it.
The main interest rate a central bank sets. Other interest rates follow it.
A standard agreement, made on an exchange, to buy or sell something at a set price on a set future date.
The date a futures contract ends.
Closing a contract that is about to expire and opening the next one, to stay in the market.
A deposit you put up to hold a position. It is not the full price of the position.
A body that stands between the buyer and the seller of an exchange-traded contract, so each side deals with it and not with the other.
Contract for difference: a contract that pays or charges the change in price between when it opens and when it closes. You never own the underlying.
Controlling a position larger than the money you put up. Gains and losses are on the whole position.
A daily charge or credit for holding a leveraged position overnight.
The other side of your trade or contract.
A digital asset recorded on a shared ledger called a blockchain.
Who holds an asset for you, and who holds the keys to it.
The price at which you can SELL. It is the lower of the two prices in a quote.
The price at which you can BUY. It is the higher of the two prices in a quote.
The gap between the ask and the bid. It is a cost you pay every time you trade.
One tenth of a pip. It is the fifth decimal place on most pairs and the third on yen pairs.
One single unit of a currency, such as one euro.
How many units are in one standard lot. For currencies it is usually 100,000.
The full value of a position, in a currency: units times price.
A trade that starts with a buy. It gains when the price rises.
A trade that starts with a sell. It gains when the price falls.
Your account balance plus the floating profit or loss of your open trades.
The margin currently held for your open positions.
Equity minus used margin. It is what you have left to open new positions or absorb losses.
Equity divided by used margin, as a percent. Brokers watch it to protect themselves.
A warning from the broker when the margin level falls to a set level. Each broker sets its own.
The level at which a broker closes your positions automatically. Each broker sets its own.
A charge or credit for holding a position overnight. It comes from the difference in interest rates between the two currencies, plus the broker's markup.
A fee some brokers charge per lot, on top of the spread.
The difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got. It can help or hurt.
The profit or loss of a trade that is still open. It changes with every price move.
A price you choose in advance where you will exit a losing trade. Level 4 covers how it works.
The most money you are willing to lose on one trade, often set as a percent of your account.
The smallest change your broker allows in position size, such as 0.01 lots.
The money or pips a trade makes if it reaches its target.
The reward divided by the risk. A trade risking 20 pips to make 60 has a ratio of 3 : 1.
A result measured in units of the risk you took. Risk $25 and make $75 is +3R. Risk $25 and lose $25 is −1R.
An order to trade right now at the best price available.
An order that waits until the price reaches a level you chose.
A pending order that fills at your price or BETTER. It waits for the price to come to you.
A pending order that becomes a market order when the price reaches your level, so it fills at your price or WORSE.
A buy order placed BELOW the current price. It waits for a pullback.
A sell order placed ABOVE the current price. It waits for a rally.
A buy order placed ABOVE the current price. It buys when the price rises through your level.
A sell order placed BELOW the current price. It sells when the price falls through your level.
An order that closes a trade at a profit target. It is a limit order.
An entry order with a stop-loss and a take-profit attached.
A stop order with a limit price. Once triggered it fills only at your limit or better, so it may not fill at all.
A jump in price with no trading in between, such as over a weekend or after big news.
How easily you can trade without moving the price. Deep markets have plenty of orders on both sides. Thin markets do not.
How far and how fast a price moves.
The daily cut-off when positions are rolled to the next day. Many brokers show wider spreads around it.
A broker's reply of a new price when the price you asked for is no longer available.
The way a broker turns your order into a fill: for example market, instant or request execution.
A department at a broker that may take the other side of client trades.
The clock a platform uses to stamp its candles. It may differ from market time and from your time.
The change divided by the STARTING value, times 100.
A way to compare two amounts, such as 1 : 3. The parts add up to a whole.
Closing part of a position and leaving the rest open.
A stop moved to your entry price, so the rest of the trade cannot lose money before costs.
The chance that several independent things all happen: multiply their chances.
The average: the total divided by the number of results.
The middle result once the results are put in order.
A result far bigger or smaller than the rest.
A measure of how far results typically sit from their mean. Bigger means more spread out.
How uncertain an average is. It equals the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of results.
The average result per trade, in R, weighted by how often each outcome happens.
The average win divided by the average loss. A method with a 2 : 1 payoff wins twice what it loses.
The win rate at which expectancy is exactly zero, for a given payoff ratio. It equals 1 ÷ (1 + payoff).
Total won divided by total lost. Above 1 the method made money in the sample. Below 1 it lost.
A fall from a high point of the balance (or the running total) to a later low point.
The biggest peak-to-trough fall in a set of results.
Growth (or loss) that is earned on a balance that already includes earlier growth (or loss).
Risking the same PERCENT of your current balance on every trade, so the dollar risk rises and falls with the account.
The chance that an account suffers a drawdown large enough to count as ruin. You must define the size of that drawdown first.
A drawing of four prices for one interval of time: the open, the high, the low and the close.
The first price, the highest price, the lowest price and the last price of one interval.
The length of time each candle covers, such as 1 minute, 15 minutes, 1 hour or 1 day.
Combining smaller candles into one bigger one: the first open, the highest high, the lowest low and the last close.
The part of a candle between the open and the close. Its length is |close − open|.
The thin line above or below the body, reaching to the high or to the low.
The distance from the low to the high of a candle, wicks included.
A candle whose body is tiny compared with its range. In this course: a body of 10% of the range or less.
The clock time at which a platform starts a new daily candle. It differs between platforms.
A stretch of a chart whose average candle range is well below the chart's average. In this course: below 0.7 of it.
A stretch whose average candle range is well above the chart's average. In this course: above 1.4 times it.
A leg of price movement in one direction, between two swings.
The counter-move after an impulse, back against it.
How much of the impulse the correction gave back, as a fraction of the impulse.
A candle whose high is above the highs of the n candles on each side of it. Confirmed n bars later.
A candle whose low is below the lows of the n candles on each side of it. Confirmed n bars later.
The newest extreme, which does not yet have n bars after it, so it is not a confirmed swing.
A swing high above the previous swing high (HH), and a swing low above the previous swing low (HL).
A swing high below the previous swing high (LH), and a swing low below the previous swing low (LL).
In this course: an ordered run of rising swings (bullish) or falling swings (bearish).
In this course: highs that are about level and lows that are about level.
The first close (or, under another convention, the first trade) beyond a stated level.
A counter-move that has not broken the structure it moved against.
In this course: the sequence of confirmed swing highs and swing lows, described as bullish, bearish, range or unclear.
A swing under the size rule of Level 6: it beats n bars on each side.
In this course: an order-1 high that is above the order-1 highs on either side of it, or an order-1 low that is below the order-1 lows on either side. The scale is a convention.
Using information from later candles to label an earlier moment, so the analysis looks better than it could have been at the time.
The last candle on the chart. Everything to its right is unknown.
Swing highs (or lows) that differ by no more than the range tolerance: 15% of the recent swing range in this course.
A bar that closes (or, under another convention, trades) beyond the latest confirmed structural swing. A continuation if it agrees with the structure, a shift if it goes against it.
A break that goes against the existing structure. A description of what happened, not a prediction of a reversal.
The level whose break ends the current description of the structure.
The bigger and smaller candles of the same market. Each has its own structure.
A result from a test with a stated method and sample size, such as "39 of 63 visits reacted". It is stronger than an observation but is only as good as the test.
A claim written so that a stated count or measurement on data could confirm or refute it.
A band of prices, not a single line, where price has recently turned or stalled. An observation about the past.
The highest and lowest prices of the completed day. Where the day starts is a convention.
How easily you can trade at a price without moving it. Observable through spread and, where available, volume.
The idea that orders rest near obvious highs and lows. An interpretation: in an over-the-counter market it cannot be seen directly.
The idea that price is pulled towards those levels. A hypothesis that can be tested by counting.
A stretch where candle ranges are well below their recent average. In this course: below 0.7 of it.
Price displacement per unit of time, such as pips per bar. It describes how fast price moved. It does not forecast.
A number of consecutive candles that close in the same direction.
A breakout followed, within a stated number of bars, by a close back on the other side of the level.
The structure's sequence extended after a pullback, for example a new higher high after a higher low.
An invalidation breach followed by a confirmed opposite structure. An event that needs both parts.
A window of the day, defined on a market's own clock, such as London 08:00–17:00. A convention.
A window defined on one fixed clock, such as 20:00–02:00 New York time. It stays fixed on that clock and drifts against other markets' clocks.
The highest and lowest prices of the candles whose open time falls inside a session window. Final only after the window closes.
A factor that traders believe pushes a currency up or down: interest rates, inflation, growth, policy, risk sentiment or money flows. Several act at once.
The difference between two economies' policy rates. One input among many, and expectations of it matter as much as its level.
A measure of the prices of a basket of goods and services. Its yearly change is the inflation rate.
A monthly US report on how many jobs were added outside farming.
The total value of what an economy produces in a period. A lagging measure that is often revised.
A description of a central bank's TONE: leaning towards higher rates or tighter policy.
A description of a central bank's TONE: leaning towards lower rates or easier policy.
What a central bank says about its likely future path, which shapes expectations.
A description of investor mood. Risk-on: money moving towards riskier assets. Risk-off: money moving away from them.
The committee of the US central bank that sets US interest-rate policy. It meets on a published schedule.
The committee of the Bank of England that sets UK interest-rate policy.
The body of the European Central Bank that decides euro-area interest-rate policy.
The three figures of a calendar row: what analysts expected, the last figure, and the released one.
A later change to a figure that was released before.
The gap between the actual figure and the forecast. Price reacts to this gap more than to the figure itself.
A rule written in advance for what to do around a scheduled release: stand aside, reduce size, or trade, and how.
A comparison of what price did around a set of events with what it did in ordinary periods, counting every event.
Risking the same percent of your current balance on each trade. The dollar amount rises and falls with the account.
The risk actually taken after lots are rounded down, and after spread and slippage. It can differ from the planned risk.
A stop placed just beyond the level that shows your idea was wrong. The position size is worked out to fit it.
A written limit that stops you trading for a period once a loss is reached: a daily or weekly loss limit.
A written rule for what changes when the account falls from its high: you trade smaller, and never larger, to get it back.
The total amount at risk across all open trades, if every stop were hit: the sum of the risk on each.
How much of one currency you are long or short across ALL open positions, counting each pair's two currencies and each position's direction.
The chance that price jumps past your stop, so the loss is bigger than planned.
A written document with your own limits: risk per trade, daily, weekly and drawdown limits, open risk, exposure by currency, and a news rule. The journal later checks your trades against it.
How well a decision followed the written plan: a valid setup, the planned size, a stop at the invalidation level, and rules obeyed. It is judged BEFORE the result is looked at.
Judging a decision by how it turned out. A good decision can lose and a poor one can win.
Entering because price has moved and you fear missing out, not because a rule fired.
Trading to win back a loss: taking trades that break the plan, or raising size after a loss.
Taking more trades than the plan allows, or trades with no valid setup.
Widening a stop after entry, so the trade can be wrong for longer. The stop marked where the idea fails.
Feeling a loss more strongly than an equal gain. In trading it shows as skipping valid setups after losses, and holding losers to avoid taking the loss.
Believing that after a run of losses a win is "due". Independent trades do not owe you anything.
Giving the last few trades more weight than the whole record.
Looking for evidence that agrees with what you already think, and discounting the evidence that does not.
A decision made before the situation arises, written as an if-then rule, so you do not have to decide it while under pressure.
Scoring a trade in a fixed order: process first, then the outcome, then what evidence the trade adds.
A written procedure that says, for a given market and time, exactly when to trade, how, and when to stay out. It is a procedure, not a prediction.
The context conditions that make a trade possible. A state that can last for hours.
The single event at a moment that fires the order, once the setup is in place.
A written, testable condition that means you stay out, for example a news release or a wide spread.
The test of a written rule set: could two people apply it to the same chart and reach the same decision? If not, it is not yet testable.
Writing your expectations and what would count as failure BEFORE you look at any test result.
Fitting rules so closely to past data that they describe its noise, and then fail on new data.
A simulation of a written strategy on past data. It can show how a rule would have behaved. It cannot show how it will behave.
Using information in a test that was not available at the moment of the decision.
Testing only on what survived, such as companies that are still listed, so the failures are missing.
Trying many variants on the same data and keeping the best. The best of many looks good by chance alone.
The data you use to build and look at the rule. Results here are flattered by the looking.
Data kept apart and not looked at until the rule is frozen. Run once. If you look at it and change the rule, it is no longer out-of-sample.
The share of recent journal entries whose prices, R, stop side, sizing and session tag all agree with each other.
A range of values the true average could plausibly take, given the sample. The real answer to "how sure am I?".
Historical backtest, then out-of-sample test, chart replay, demo forward test, small live trading and only then any scaling. Each rung can catch something the one below cannot.
How well a plan followed the rules, graded before the outcome is known. It measures what you control.
Software that draws charts from a data feed. It may also send orders, but drawing and ordering are separate jobs.
Software that sends your orders to a broker and shows your account.
A practice account with pretend money. It shows mechanics and does not reproduce every real fill, or any emotion.
The public list a regulator keeps of the firms it has licensed. You reach it yourself, not through a link the firm gives you.
The difference between the price you asked for and the price you were filled at, recorded over many orders on your own demo.
A paid challenge that offers access to someone else's capital if you meet its rules. The fee is paid whether or not you pass.
Your written plan for how you would ever trade real money: readiness criteria, the capital rule, small live rules, when to go back, and scaling last.

jpy-pip-100x.label: using 0.0001 as the pip size on a yen pair
jpy-pip-100x.fix: On yen pairs a pip is 0.01, not 0.0001.

pip-pipette-10x.label: treating a pipette as a pip
pip-pipette-10x.fix: A pip is ten pipettes. The fifth decimal (third on yen pairs) is the pipette.

no-conversion.label: forgetting to convert into the account currency
no-conversion.fix: Pip value first comes out in the pair's second currency. Convert it to your account currency.

per-lot-only.label: giving the value for one lot, not the whole trade
per-lot-only.fix: Multiply the per-lot value by the number of lots.

wrong-way-conversion.label: converting with the rate the wrong way round
wrong-way-conversion.fix: Divide by the pair price when the account currency is the first currency in the pair.

sign-error.label: getting the sign wrong on a gain or a loss
sign-error.fix: A loss is negative. A profit is positive.

percent-as-decimal.label: mixing up a percent and a decimal
percent-as-decimal.fix: 0.5% is 0.005 as a decimal. Divide a percent by 100.

ev-forgot-probability.label: adding the outcomes without weighting them by their chances
ev-forgot-probability.fix: Multiply each outcome by its probability, then add.

confuse-win-loss.label: giving the number of losses when the wins were asked for
confuse-win-loss.fix: Read the question again: which side is being asked for?

added-not-multiplied.label: adding chances that should be multiplied
added-not-multiplied.fix: For independent results in a row, multiply the chances.

outcome-bias.label: judging a decision by its result
outcome-bias.fix: Judge the decision by the information and plan you had, not by how it turned out.

gamblers-fallacy.label: treating a win as due after a losing streak
gamblers-fallacy.fix: Independent trades have no memory. A streak does not change the odds on the next one.

small-sample.label: drawing a conclusion from a handful of results
small-sample.fix: A few results can be luck. An edge shows only over many trades.

hindsight-story.label: treating an after-the-fact story as a prediction
hindsight-story.fix: A neat explanation of a move that already happened does not tell you what happens next.

win-rate-is-edge.label: treating a high win rate as the same as an edge
win-rate-is-edge.fix: Edge depends on how much you win and lose, not only how often. Multiply and add.

ignoring-costs.label: forgetting that every trade has a cost
ignoring-costs.fix: Spreads and fees are paid every time. Your average trade has to beat them.

belief-as-edge.label: treating a feeling or a story as an edge
belief-as-edge.fix: An edge is a measured average over many recorded trades, not a conviction.

trading-as-gambling.label: acting on luck or a hunch with no plan or limit
trading-as-gambling.fix: A plan with a fixed risk is what separates a trade from a bet.

certainty-thinking.label: expecting a certain result from a single trade
certainty-thinking.fix: A single trade is one draw from a range of possible outcomes.

profit-means-good.label: assuming a profit means the decision was good
profit-means-good.fix: A rule-breaking trade can win by luck. Check the process first.

loss-means-bad.label: assuming a loss means the decision was bad
loss-means-bad.fix: A well-planned trade can lose. Losses are part of any edge.

price-yield-same-way.label: thinking a bond's price and yield rise together
price-yield-same-way.fix: The coupon is fixed. If you pay more for the same income, the yield is lower.

own-vs-contract.label: mixing up owning an asset with holding a contract on it
own-vs-contract.fix: Ask what you really hold: the thing itself, or a contract that follows its price.

inverted-quote.label: reading a currency quote the wrong way round
inverted-quote.fix: The first currency is the one being priced. The price counts how many units of the second currency it takes to buy one of the first.

both-move.label: saying both currencies rose or fell together
both-move.fix: A pair compares two currencies. When one strengthens against the other, the other weakens against it.

rate-as-change.label: treating a price level as a change
rate-as-change.fix: A quote is a level: how many units of one currency buy one unit of the other.

bigger-number-stronger.label: judging a currency's strength by the size of the number
bigger-number-stronger.fix: A price only compares two currencies. A bigger number does not mean a stronger economy.

one-currency-only.label: thinking only the first currency moves in a pair
one-currency-only.fix: The price is a comparison. Both currencies are described by the same move, in opposite directions.

swap-base-quote.label: mixing up the base and the quote currency
swap-base-quote.fix: Base first, quote second. The price is counted in the quote currency.

no-units.label: forgetting that a price has units
no-units.fix: A currency price is counted in the second currency of the pair.

forgot-to-invert.label: giving the original price when asked for the reverse quote
forgot-to-invert.fix: The reverse quote is 1 divided by the original price.

subtracted-not-inverted.label: subtracting when you should divide 1 by the price
subtracted-not-inverted.fix: The reverse of a price is 1 ÷ price.

cross-upside-down.label: dividing the two prices the wrong way round in a cross rate
cross-upside-down.fix: For X/Y from X/USD and Y/USD, divide X/USD by Y/USD.

multiplied-cross.label: multiplying when a cross rate needs a division
multiplied-cross.fix: When both prices are against the same currency, divide.

cross-wrong-op.label: using the wrong operation in a cross rate
cross-wrong-op.fix: Follow the currency through: X to USD, then USD to JPY. Multiply when the middle currency is second in the first pair and first in the second.

cross-check-wrong.label: comparing a quote with the wrong number
cross-check-wrong.fix: Work out the cross rate first, then compare the quote with it directly.

inverted-ratio.label: dividing the wrong way round
inverted-ratio.fix: Yield is the income divided by the price.

lot-size-mixup.label: using the wrong number of units for a lot
lot-size-mixup.fix: A standard lot is 100,000 units. A mini lot is 10,000 and a micro lot is 1,000.

forgot-contract-size.label: forgetting that one lot is 100,000 units

forgot-price.label: forgetting to multiply by the price
forgot-price.fix: The units are in the base currency. Multiply by the price to get the value in the quote currency.

forgot-leverage.label: forgetting to divide by the leverage
forgot-leverage.fix: Margin is the position value divided by the leverage.

wrong-side.label: going the wrong way from the entry price
