wrong-side.fix: Above means a higher price. Below means a lower price.

lots-not-rounded.label: not rounding the lot size to the lot step
lots-not-rounded.fix: Round DOWN to the lot step your broker allows.

lots-rounded-up.label: rounding the lot size up
lots-rounded-up.fix: Always round DOWN, so the risk never goes above your limit.

forgot-pip-value.label: forgetting the pip value
forgot-pip-value.fix: Each pip on one lot is worth money. Multiply pips by the pip value.

rr-inverted.label: dividing risk by reward
rr-inverted.fix: Reward-to-risk is reward divided by risk.

r-vs-pips.label: giving the result in pips or money when R was asked for
r-vs-pips.fix: R is the result divided by the risk taken.

margin-level-inverted.label: dividing margin by equity
margin-level-inverted.fix: Margin level is equity divided by used margin.

floating-ignored.label: ignoring the floating profit or loss
floating-ignored.fix: Equity is the balance plus the floating result of open trades.

nights-forgotten.label: forgetting to multiply by the number of nights
nights-forgotten.fix: Swap is charged for each night the position is held.

round-trip-forgotten.label: counting commission once when it is charged twice
round-trip-forgotten.fix: Commission per side is charged when you open and again when you close.

cost-omitted.label: leaving one of the costs out of the total
cost-omitted.fix: Add the spread, the commission, the swap and the slippage.

bid-ask-swap.label: mixing up which price opens and which closes a trade
bid-ask-swap.fix: A long trade opens at the ask and closes at the bid. A short trade opens at the bid and closes at the ask.

no-spread-thinking.label: forgetting that there are two prices
no-spread-thinking.fix: You buy at the higher price and sell at the lower price. The gap is the spread.

off-by-ten.label: an answer ten times too big or too small
off-by-ten.fix: Check your answer against the pip value: it should give about the risk you chose.

long-short-mixup.label: ignoring the direction of the trade
long-short-mixup.fix: A long trade gains when the price rises. A short trade gains when it falls.

label-model-mixup.label: mixing up the execution models
label-model-mixup.fix: Market execution fills at the available price. Instant execution can requote. Request execution sends a price for you to accept.

limit-stop-swap.label: mixing up a limit order and a stop order
limit-stop-swap.fix: A limit waits for a BETTER price (a pullback). A stop waits for the price to move THROUGH a level (a breakout).

side-swap.label: choosing an order for the wrong direction
side-swap.fix: Decide first whether you want to buy or sell, then whether you are waiting for a pullback or a breakout.

order-price-guaranteed.label: thinking a pending order always fills at its level
order-price-guaranteed.fix: A pending order fills at the first available price once triggered. A limit gives you your price or better. A stop gives you your price or worse.

stop-limit-guarantee.label: thinking a stop-limit always fills
stop-limit-guarantee.fix: Once triggered, a stop-limit fills only at its limit or better. If the price jumps past the limit, it may not fill at all.

stop-guaranteed.label: thinking a stop-loss guarantees the exit price
stop-guaranteed.fix: A stop-loss becomes a market order when triggered. In a gap it fills at the first available price, which can be far past the stop.

wrong-side-of-market.label: placing a pending order on the wrong side of the market
wrong-side-of-market.fix: Buy limits and sell stops go below the price. Buy stops and sell limits go above it.

risk-invariant.label: thinking a drawdown in R means the same fall in the account whatever you risk
risk-invariant.fix: The same drawdown in R is a bigger fall in percent when you risk more per trade.

streak-rounded-down.label: rounding down a count that has to be reached
streak-rounded-down.fix: A count that does not quite reach the target is not enough. Round UP to the first whole number that gets there.

avg-of-ratios.label: averaging the win size and the loss size without weighting them
avg-of-ratios.fix: Weight each outcome by how often it happens before you combine them.

winrate-as-expectancy.label: treating a win rate as if it were the edge
winrate-as-expectancy.fix: Expectancy depends on how much you win and lose, not only how often. Weight each outcome by its chance.

pct-of-wrong-base.label: measuring a percent against the wrong starting value
pct-of-wrong-base.fix: A percent change is measured against the STARTING value. A drawdown is measured against the PEAK.

ratio-not-change.label: giving the new value as a percent when the change was asked for
ratio-not-change.fix: The change is the new value minus the old, divided by the old.

ratio-not-share.label: dividing one part by the other instead of by the whole
ratio-not-share.fix: A share divides a part by the total of all the parts.

gain-loss-symmetry.label: expecting a fall and an equal rise to cancel out
gain-loss-symmetry.fix: A rise is measured on the balance you have AFTER the fall, so it does not undo it.

dollars-not-r.label: comparing trades by dollars instead of by R
dollars-not-r.fix: Divide each result by the risk taken. R makes trades of different sizes comparable.

avg-not-weighted.label: averaging exits equally instead of by size
avg-not-weighted.fix: Weight each part of the trade by how much of the position it was.

partial-only.label: counting only one part of a trade that was closed in pieces
partial-only.fix: Add the result of every part, each weighted by its size.

hot-hand.label: believing a run of losses means the next trade is worse
hot-hand.fix: Independent trades have no memory. Past results do not change the next chance.

mean-median-mixup.label: mixing up the mean and the median
mean-median-mixup.fix: The mean is total ÷ count. The median is the middle value once sorted.

sum-not-mean.label: giving the total when the average was asked for
sum-not-mean.fix: Divide the total by the number of results.

sd-population.label: dividing by n instead of n − 1 for a sample
sd-population.fix: For a sample of trades, divide the sum of squared gaps by n − 1.

variance-not-sd.label: giving the variance instead of the standard deviation
variance-not-sd.fix: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

se-divided-by-n.label: dividing by n instead of the square root of n

se-times.label: multiplying by √n instead of dividing
se-times.fix: More trades make the average MORE certain, so divide by √n.

be-inverted.label: giving the reward share instead of the break-even win rate

be-inverse.label: turning the break-even formula upside down
be-inverse.fix: Rarer wins must be bigger. Check that your answer moves the right way.

pf-vs-payoff.label: giving the payoff ratio or the average instead of the profit factor
pf-vs-payoff.fix: Profit factor = total profit of the winners ÷ total loss of the losers.

pf-count-ratio.label: comparing the number of winners with the number of losers
pf-count-ratio.fix: Compare the total R won with the total R lost, not the counts.

pct-recover-same.label: thinking a gain equal to the fall gets you back
pct-recover-same.fix: The gain needed is bigger than the fall, because it is earned on a smaller balance.

dd-not-peak-to-trough.label: giving the worst single trade instead of the peak-to-trough fall
dd-not-peak-to-trough.fix: A drawdown is the biggest fall from a high point of the running total.

fixed-vs-percent.label: using the same dollar amount when the risk is a percent of the balance
fixed-vs-percent.fix: A percent of the current balance shrinks after a loss and grows after a win.

simple-vs-compound.label: adding the same amount each period when growth compounds
simple-vs-compound.fix: Compounding means each period's growth is earned on a bigger balance.

provisional-swing.label: marking a swing that is not confirmed yet
provisional-swing.fix: The newest extreme has fewer than n bars after it, so it is provisional. Only mark swings that have all n bars on each side.

older-swing.label: marking a confirmed swing that is not the most recent
older-swing.fix: Read from the right-hand edge of the chart. The most recent confirmed swing comes before any older ones.

not-a-swing.label: marking a bar that is not a swing under the stated size
not-a-swing.fix: A swing must beat n bars on each side. Count the bars before you mark.

missed-swing.label: missing a swing that meets the definition
missed-swing.fix: Scan the chart from left to right and test every peak against the n bars on each side.

compared-wrong-swing.label: comparing a swing with the wrong earlier swing
compared-wrong-swing.fix: A high is compared with the previous HIGH, and a low with the previous LOW.

direction-flip.label: reading a rising sequence as falling, or the reverse
direction-flip.fix: Compare each swing with the one before it of the same kind. Rising highs and lows are bullish. Falling highs and lows are bearish.

range-as-trend.label: calling a level sequence a trend
range-as-trend.fix: If the last two highs are about level and the last two lows are about level, that is a range.

trend-as-range.label: calling a moving sequence a range
trend-as-range.fix: A range keeps its highs and lows about level. Steadily rising or falling ones are not a range.

refused-clear.label: answering "unclear" when the swings agree
refused-clear.fix: Unclear is for charts where the swings disagree. When they clearly point one way, say so.

forced-a-call.label: forcing a direction on a chart that is mixed
forced-a-call.fix: When highs rise and lows fall (or the reverse), the structure is unclear. That is a valid, correct answer.

wrong-supporting-swing.label: citing swings that do not support the classification
wrong-supporting-swing.fix: Use the last two CONFIRMED swing highs and the last two CONFIRMED swing lows.

wrong-swing.label: marking the wrong swing
wrong-swing.fix: Use the latest confirmed swing under the stated definition.

wrong-invalidation.label: marking the wrong level as the invalidation
wrong-invalidation.fix: A bullish structure is held up by its latest confirmed structural low. A bearish one is held down by its latest structural high.

wick-not-close.label: counting a wick as a break when the rule needs a close
wick-not-close.fix: Under the close convention a wick beyond the level does not count. The bar must CLOSE beyond it.

close-not-wick.label: waiting for a close when the rule counts a wick
close-not-wick.fix: Under the wick convention the first trade beyond the level counts, even if the bar closes back inside.

wrong-break-bar.label: marking a bar that does not meet the break rule
wrong-break-bar.fix: Check each bar against the stated rule and the level in force at that moment.

range-state-wrong.label: misreading how big the candles are compared with the rest of the chart
range-state-wrong.fix: Compare the average candle RANGE of the stretch with the average over the whole chart. Direction does not matter.

retracement-from-wrong-end.label: measuring a retracement from the wrong end of the leg
retracement-from-wrong-end.fix: A retracement is how much of the leg was given back from its extreme: (B − C) ÷ (B − A).

body-vs-range.label: mixing up the body and the range of a candle
body-vs-range.fix: The body is open to close. The range is low to high, wicks included.

wrong-wick.label: measuring the wrong wick, or the whole range as a wick
wrong-wick.fix: The upper wick is above the body. The lower wick is below it. Each is only part of the range.

wick-share.label: giving the wick share instead of the body ratio
wick-share.fix: Body ratio = body ÷ range. The wicks are what is left over.

pips-vs-price.label: giving a price difference where pips were asked
pips-vs-price.fix: One pip is 0.0001 (0.01 on yen pairs). Multiply the price difference by 10,000 for pips.

confirm-at-formation.label: thinking a swing is confirmed the moment it forms
confirm-at-formation.fix: A swing needs n more bars to close after it. It is confirmed at the close of bar i + n.

high-as-close.label: mixing up the high and low with the first and last prices
high-as-close.fix: Open = first price. Close = last price. High = highest price reached. Low = lowest.

aggregate-last-open.label: using the wrong candle's open when combining candles
aggregate-last-open.fix: The combined candle opens with the FIRST small candle.

aggregate-first-close.label: using the wrong candle's close when combining candles
aggregate-first-close.fix: The combined candle closes with the LAST small candle.

aggregate-average.label: averaging the highs and lows when combining candles
aggregate-average.fix: The combined high is the highest high and the combined low is the lowest low.

tf-inverted.label: dividing the short period by the long one
tf-inverted.fix: To count how many short candles fit in a long one, divide the long period by the short one.

direction-vs-body.label: mixing up the direction of a candle with the size of its body
direction-vs-body.fix: Colour comes from close versus open. A doji is decided by the body ratio.

lookahead-label.label: labelling a swing with knowledge from later candles
lookahead-label.fix: A swing can only be labelled once n bars have closed after it. Labelling it sooner uses information you did not have.

layer-mixup.label: mixing up observation, interpretation and hypothesis
layer-mixup.fix: Observation: what the prices show. Interpretation: what you say it means now. Hypothesis: what you think comes next.

ratio-inverted.label: putting the two numbers of a ratio the wrong way round
ratio-inverted.fix: Say what goes on top: the thing you are measuring goes on the top, the yardstick underneath.

ignored-dst.label: ignoring that a market's clock changed on that date
ignored-dst.fix: Each session sits on its own market's clock and follows that market's daylight saving. Work out the offset on the date asked, not for the time of year you usually think of.

converted-wrong-way.label: moving the clock the wrong way when converting
converted-wrong-way.fix: Decide which clock is ahead, then move from the market's time to yours in the right direction. Check that the answer makes sense.

outside-window.label: taking the extreme of the whole day instead of the session
outside-window.fix: A session high is the highest candle INSIDE the session window, not the highest of the day.

wrong-session-window.label: placing the session window in the wrong place
wrong-session-window.fix: Find the start and end of the window on the chart's own clock first. Then take the extreme of the candles inside it.

wrong-day-anchor.label: using a different day start from the one stated
wrong-day-anchor.fix: A day's high and low depend on where the day starts. Use the day start stated in the exercise.

wrong-day-window.label: taking the previous day's extreme over the wrong stretch of the chart
wrong-day-window.fix: Find where the previous day starts and ends under the stated day start, then take its extreme.

event-rule-misapplied.label: not applying the stated event rule bar by bar
event-rule-misapplied.fix: Check the marked bar against the rule exactly: a close, not a touch, and the stated number of bars for a failure.

points-not-percent.label: giving a change in points where a percent was asked
points-not-percent.fix: A percent change divides the change by the starting value and multiplies by 100.

surprise-sign.label: subtracting the forecast from the actual the wrong way round
surprise-sign.fix: The surprise is actual minus forecast. A positive surprise means the figure came in above the forecast.

level-not-surprise.label: reading the level of a figure instead of the surprise
level-not-surprise.fix: Price reacts to how far the figure was from expectations, not to the figure itself.

diff-sign.label: subtracting the two rates the wrong way round
diff-sign.fix: A differential is the first economy's rate minus the second's. State which way you took it.

open-risk-cap.label: letting open risk exceed the daily loss limit
open-risk-cap.fix: If every open stop were hit, the total should not go beyond what your daily limit allows.

revenge-trade.label: trading to win a loss back
revenge-trade.fix: After a loss, risk stays the same or falls. A rule about the limit or the drawdown is written for exactly this moment.

plan-drift.label: drifting away from a written rule because it feels fine
plan-drift.fix: A rule is followed as written. Changing it in the moment is how plans stop working.

account-currency-ignored.label: not converting the pip value into the account currency
account-currency-ignored.fix: A pip is worth a fixed amount in the currency the pair is quoted in. Convert that into your account currency before you size.

stop-from-dollars.label: choosing a stop from a dollar amount
stop-from-dollars.fix: Place the stop where the idea is wrong. Then size the position to fit that distance, never the reverse.

stop-fixed-pips.label: using the same stop distance on every trade
stop-fixed-pips.fix: A stop belongs at the level that invalidates THIS idea, so its distance changes from trade to trade.

stop-at-entry.label: putting the stop at the entry price
stop-at-entry.fix: A stop at the entry is hit by noise and does not mark where the idea fails.

off-by-one-limit.label: stopping one loss short of, or beyond, a loss limit
off-by-one-limit.fix: Round UP to the first count of losses that reaches the limit.

largest-only.label: counting only the biggest position when adding risk
largest-only.fix: Open risk is the total across every open trade.

exposure-sum-abs.label: adding position sizes without their direction
exposure-sum-abs.fix: A short in a currency cancels a long in the same currency. Net exposure keeps the signs.

exposure-per-pair.label: treating each pair as a separate bet
exposure-per-pair.fix: Exposure is counted by CURRENCY across all your positions, not pair by pair.

fomo-entry.label: entering because price has moved
fomo-entry.fix: An entry needs a plan level and a valid setup. A fast move is not a rule.

fear-skip.label: skipping a valid setup because of an earlier feeling
fear-skip.fix: A valid setup under the plan is taken. Your feelings about an earlier move are not a rule.

loss-averse-skip.label: skipping a valid setup after losses
loss-averse-skip.fix: A valid setup is taken at the planned size whatever the last few trades did. Skipping them makes the record meaningless.

recency-bias.label: weighting the last few trades over the whole record
recency-bias.fix: Judge a method on its whole record, and size from the plan, not from the last few results.

confirmation-bias.label: looking only for evidence that agrees
confirmation-bias.fix: Write the strongest case against the trade before entry, and look for the evidence you would rather not see.

behavior-mixup.label: naming the wrong behavior
behavior-mixup.fix: Match the signature in the story to the behavior: what was done, when, and after what.

stop-widened.label: treating a wider stop as good management
stop-widened.fix: The stop marks where the idea fails. Moving it away only makes the loss larger.

process-outcome-mixup.label: reversing the verdict on a decision
process-outcome-mixup.fix: Judge the decision by the plan: followed means a good decision, broken means a poor one, whatever the result.

planned-not-actual.label: giving the plan's figure where the achieved figure was asked
planned-not-actual.fix: Use the sizes the trader actually took, not the sizes the plan called for.

belief-mixup.label: treating a prediction as a strategy
belief-mixup.fix: A strategy says what you will do under stated conditions. A prediction says what price will do.

component-mixup.label: naming the wrong component
component-mixup.fix: Ask what question the line answers: where, when, what triggers, where it is wrong, where it ends, how big, what happens after entry, when to stay out.

setup-trigger-mixup.label: confusing a setup with a trigger
setup-trigger-mixup.fix: A setup is a state that can last. A trigger is the single event that fires the order.

reward-only-expectancy.label: counting only the winners
reward-only-expectancy.fix: Expectancy is win rate × reward minus loss rate × risk. The losers count.

still-vague.label: keeping a judgement word in a rule
still-vague.fix: Replace words like strong, good or nearby with a number, a level or a clock time.

cherry-picking.label: accepting chosen examples
cherry-picking.fix: Ask how many trades there were in all and who chose the ones shown.

survivorship.label: missing the failures that are not in the data
survivorship.fix: A test on survivors only leaves out the failures. Ask what was dropped along the way.

data-snooping.label: trusting the best of many tries
data-snooping.fix: The best of many is what chance alone produces. Test it on data it has never seen.

overfitting.label: trusting a tuned rule
overfitting.fix: Many precisely tuned numbers fit noise. Keep the rule simple, and test it on new data.

lookahead-bias.label: using information before it was known
lookahead-bias.fix: A test may use only what was available at the moment of the decision.

oos-contaminated.label: reusing out-of-sample data
oos-contaminated.fix: Out-of-sample data can be used once. If it shaped the rule, it is now in-sample.

bias-mixup.label: naming the wrong problem in a test
bias-mixup.fix: Ask what information was used (look-ahead, hindsight), what was left out (cherry-picking, survivorship), or how the result was chosen (snooping, overfitting, a contaminated test).

interval-misread.label: reading an interval wrongly
interval-misread.fix: Work out the two ends and look at whether zero is between them. A positive average alone is not evidence.

costs-ignored.label: leaving the costs out of a result
costs-ignored.fix: Net R is gross R minus the spread (and other costs) expressed in R on every trade.

forgot-square.label: not squaring the ratio
forgot-square.fix: The number of trades needed is (2.8 × SD ÷ effect)².

offset-sign.label: subtracting a clock offset the wrong way
offset-sign.fix: Server time minus UTC is positive when the server clock is ahead of UTC.

pips-not-money.label: leaving slippage in pips when dollars were asked
pips-not-money.fix: Multiply pips by lots and by the pip value per lot.

fee-ignored.label: leaving out the fee in an expected value
fee-ignored.fix: The fee is paid every time. Subtract it from the expected payout.

pass-as-certain.label: treating a chance of passing as a certainty
pass-as-certain.fix: Multiply the payout by the probability of passing, then subtract the fee.

believe-not-verify.label: believing a claim instead of checking it
believe-not-verify.fix: Check at the source, or measure it yourself. Repetition and appearance are not evidence.

lessons.title: How This Program Works
lessons.aim: Know how the lessons, levels, ranks and daily Warm-Up fit together.

blocks.text: Each lesson is short. You read a little, try something, then answer a few questions. This is the cycle: **understand**, **practice**, **test**, **demonstrate**, **advance**.
The program has 13 levels. Each one ends with an assessment. Pass it and the next level opens.
As you pass levels you earn ranks, from Beginner up to Apprentice. A rank shows what you have learned. It does not show that you can make money.
Each day the app asks about ten questions from earlier lessons. It takes about five minutes.
Old material comes back on purpose. Knowing something today does not mean you will know it next month.
Your mentor marks your written answers and can help when you are stuck. Written answers are marked by a person, not by the app.

steps.title: Put The Cycle In Order
steps.intro: Tap the steps in the order they happen.

exercise.prompt: Put the learning cycle in order.

items.text: Understand
Practice
Test
Demonstrate
Advance

exercise.explanation: Each level follows this cycle. You only move on after you have shown you can do it.

points: Lessons are short: read, try, check.
Each level ends with an assessment.
The daily Warm-Up brings old material back on purpose.
A rank shows what you have learned, not that you can profit.

lessons.title: What This Program Is Not
lessons.aim: Read and accept what this program does and does not promise.

blocks.text: A course in how markets work, how to measure risk and evidence, and how to think clearly about decisions.

items: It will not tell you what to trade.
It will not promise income.
It will not make trading look easy.

blocks.text: You will not be given signals. You will be taught to reason.

blocks.title: Please Read This
blocks.text: Completing this program shows you understand the material. It does not mean you have a profitable strategy, and it is not a signal to trade real money.
Even good decisions lose sometimes. You will see this again and again in the lessons ahead.
The goal is to make good decisions repeatedly and to keep losses small enough to keep going.

exercise.statement: If you pass every level of this program, you have a profitable strategy.
exercise.prompt: True or false? Then choose the reason.

reasons.text: Passing shows you understand the material. It says nothing about whether a strategy makes money.
Passing proves you can beat the market.
The app checks your trades against real markets.

reasonFeedback.b: Passing an exam tests understanding, not market results.
reasonFeedback.c: The app does not test any strategy against live markets.

exercise.explanation: Understanding the material and having a profitable strategy are two different things.

steps.text: I have read the honest statement and I understand it.

points: The program teaches how to think, not what to trade.
It does not promise income.
Finishing it does not mean you have a profitable strategy.

lessons.title: Set Your Clocks
lessons.aim: Set your time zone and read market time against your own.

blocks.text: Markets keep the time of the place they are in. London trades on London time. New York trades on New York time. Your own clock is a third clock.
This app always shows **market time** and **your time**, each with its zone beside it.
Guyana is four hours behind UTC all year. It never changes its clocks.
Many countries do change theirs, in spring and autumn, and not on the same dates.
For a few weeks a year the US and the UK are on different clock offsets, so the gap between New York and London is four hours instead of five.
Your clock does not move, so the times markets open shift on your clock. Later lessons train you to convert these correctly.

steps.title: Choose Your Zone
steps.intro: Pick your time zone. Guyana is set by default.

steps.title: Convert Three Times
steps.intro: Work out what these market times are on your clock today.

points: Markets keep their own clock. So do you.
Guyana is UTC−4 all year.
Other countries change their clocks on different dates, which shifts market times on your clock.

lessons.title: The Analyst's Frame
lessons.aim: Use eight questions to turn a hunch into a reasoned decision.

blocks.text: This program never asks "what is the right trade?" It asks you to think. These eight questions are how.

items: What information do I have?
What are the possible outcomes?
What would show my idea is wrong?
What is my risk?
What does the evidence say?
Is there actually an edge?
How large is my sample?
Could this result be random?

blocks.text: Decide whether to carry an umbrella to work. Look at the sky, the forecast and your past experience. Then answer the eight questions in your own words.

steps.title: Your First Analyst's Frame
steps.scenario: You are deciding whether to carry an umbrella to work. It is cloudy. The forecast says a 60% chance of rain this afternoon.

fields.q: What would show my idea is wrong?

fields.hint: What is the most I could lose?
What have I actually measured or tested?
Or is it only a belief?
How many results is this based on?

blocks.text: In the early levels the questions come with hints. Later the hints fade, and you answer on your own.
You will use the same eight questions on trades, on test results and on your own journal.

points: Eight questions turn a hunch into a decision.
They work on any decision, not only trades.
The hints fade as you get better.

lessons.title: Number Check
lessons.aim: See which number skills are strong and which need practice.

blocks.text: This is not a test. It shows where your number skills are strong and where a little practice will help.
You can use the keypad. There is no time limit.

points: Weak spots here are normal and fixable.
Percentages, decimals and negative numbers come up in every level.
A short Number Skills track will be offered for any weak area.

lessons.title: What Is Trading?
lessons.aim: Say what trading is and name the parts of every trade.

blocks.text: Trading is buying or selling something to profit from a change in its price, over a short or medium time.
You are not trying to own it for life. You are trying to profit from the price moving.
Every trade has the same six parts.

items: **Market:** what you trade.
**Direction:** buy or sell.
**Size:** how much.
**Entry:** the price where you start.
**Exit:** the price where you finish.
**Risk limit:** the most you will lose, set before you start.

blocks.text: You enter, you hold, you exit. While a trade is open its profit or loss keeps changing.
It only becomes final when you exit.

blocks.title: Buy, hold, sell
steps: You buy 10 units at $50. You spend $500.
You sell all 10 at $53. You receive $530.

blocks.text: You can also sell first and buy back later if you expect a fall. That comes in Level 3.

steps.title: The Life Of A Trade
steps.intro: Tap the steps in the order they happen.

exercise.prompt: Put the life of a trade in order.

items.text: Decide what to trade
Choose direction and size
Enter the trade
Hold it, with a risk limit in place
Exit the trade
Review the result

exercise.explanation: You plan first, then enter, then exit, then review. The plan and the risk limit come before the entry.

steps.title: Name The Parts
steps.intro: Match each piece of the story to its part of a trade.

exercise.prompt: Sam trades shares of Company A. Sam buys 100 shares at $20, and sells them at $21. Sam also decides to sell if the price falls to $19.

right.text: Market
Direction
Size
Entry
Exit
Risk limit

exercise.explanation: Every trade can be described with these six parts.

points: Trading is buying or selling to profit from a price change.
Every trade has a market, direction, size, entry, exit and risk limit.
A trade is only final when you exit.

lessons.title: Trading Versus Investing
lessons.aim: Tell trading and investing apart and say why neither is safe or easy.

blocks.text: **Investing** means buying something to own for a long time. The return comes from growth and income, such as company profits or interest, as well as price changes.
**Trading** means aiming to profit from price moves over a shorter time. You decide more often.

items: **Time held:** years for an investor. Minutes to weeks for a trader.
**Where the return comes from:** growth and income for an investor. Price moves for a trader.
**How often you decide:** rarely for an investor. Often for a trader.
**Costs:** they matter to both, and more the more often you trade.

blocks.title: Neither Is Safe Or Easy
blocks.text: Investing is not automatically safe. Trading is not fast money. Either can lose.
Some people hold for months and call it trading. Some trade every day and call it investing.
What matters is what you are doing and why: your time frame, your reason and your plan.

steps.title: Trading, Investing Or Both?
steps.intro: Tap a statement, then tap where it belongs.

exercise.prompt: Sort each statement.

items.text: Aims to profit from short price moves
Holds for many years
May receive dividends or interest
Can lose money
Makes decisions often, even daily
Focuses on a business growing over the long term
Needs a plan for when to sell
Pays a cost every time you buy or sell

itemFeedback.i6: Both need a plan. An investor also needs a reason to sell.

exercise.explanation: The line is not sharp, but time frame, purpose and plan tell you which one you are doing.

points: Investors hold for growth and income. Traders aim to profit from price moves.
Neither is safe. Neither is easy.
What matters is your time frame, your reason and your plan.

lessons.title: Trading Versus Gambling
lessons.aim: Explain what trading and gambling share and what can set them apart.

blocks.text: In both you do not know what happens next. The uncertainty is the same.

items: In a game like roulette, the payouts are set so the house wins on average. That built-in advantage is the **house edge**. You cannot change it.
In trading, nobody sets the odds against you. You choose what to trade, when, and how much to risk.
In trading you can record your results over many trades and check whether you have an advantage. Lesson 1.07 shows how.

blocks.text: Every trade has a cost, such as the gap between the buy price and the sell price. It is small, but you pay it each time.
Your average trade has to beat those costs before it earns anything.

steps.title: A Trader Can Act Like A Gambler

items: Doubling the stake after every loss.
Risking everything on one trade.
Trading on a hunch with no plan.

blocks.text: That is gambling, in any market. The difference is your method, not the market.

blocks.title: Not A Promise
blocks.text: Trading does not pay just because it is not a casino. This program teaches you to measure whether you have an edge. It does not tell you that you will.
The **expected value** of a bet is its average result if you could repeat it many times. Multiply each result by its chance, then add.

steps.title: Work Out An Expected Value
steps.intro: Use the keypad. Use the − key for a negative number.

steps.title: Gambler Or Trader?
steps.intro: Tap a behavior, then tap where it belongs.

exercise.prompt: Which behaviors belong to a trader with a method, and which to a gambler?

items.text: Writes down the plan and the maximum loss before entering
Doubles the stake after every loss to win it back
Bets everything on one outcome
Reviews results across many trades
Trades because it "feels lucky"
Skips the trade when the plan says there is no setup

exercise.explanation: A plan, a limit and a review are what turn a bet into a trade.

points: Trading and gambling share uncertainty.
In trading you choose and cap your risk, and a measured edge is possible.
Costs are paid on every trade.
Acting on a hunch with no plan is gambling in any market.

lessons.title: Why Financial Markets Exist
lessons.aim: Explain the jobs a market does and where a trader fits.

steps.title: A Market Is A Meeting Place

blocks.text: A market is where buyers and sellers meet and agree a price. It can be a place or a screen.

items: **Exchange:** people swap one thing for another, such as one currency for another.
**Set prices:** buyers and sellers together show what something is worth right now.
**Raise money:** a company can sell shares to fund a project.
**Pass on risk:** someone can pay to avoid a price change that would hurt them.

blocks.title: An importer
steps: An importer must pay a foreign supplier in US dollars next month.
The importer worries the exchange rate will move against them.
A market lets them agree a rate now, which protects them from the move.

blocks.text: The importer is not trying to profit from the rate. They want certainty.
Markets did not appear so that people could trade for profit. Traders are one kind of participant among many, and they are on the other side of trades made for other reasons.

steps.title: Match The Job To The Example

exercise.prompt: Match each job of a market to an example.

right.text: A traveller swaps dollars for euros
Buyers and sellers agree today's price of oil
A company sells new shares to build a factory
A farmer agrees a price now for a crop delivered later

exercise.explanation: Each example is a different job that a market does.

points: A market is where buyers and sellers agree prices.
Markets let people exchange, set prices, raise money and pass on risk.
Traders are one kind of participant, not the reason markets exist.

lessons.title: Who Participates In Markets?
lessons.aim: Name the main kinds of participants and their different motives.

items: **Central banks:** manage a country's money and interest rates.
**Banks and dealers:** buy and sell for customers and for themselves.
**Companies:** exchange money to pay suppliers and receive customers' payments.
**Funds:** manage pooled money for many people.
**Individual traders:** people trading their own money, like you.
**Automated firms:** computers that follow rules and trade very fast.

steps.title: Not Everyone Wants A Profit From The Price

blocks.text: A company paying a supplier is not speculating. A central bank follows policy goals. A fund follows its own rules. Each has its own reason to buy or sell.
An individual trader is a very small participant. Your orders will not move the price.
You will be trading against people and firms with more information and better tools. That is why measuring an edge matters so much.
A big order made for a non-trading reason, such as paying a supplier, can move a price without carrying any message about the future. You cannot see anyone's motive from the price alone.

steps.title: Match The Participant To The Motive

exercise.prompt: Match each participant to what it typically wants.

right.text: To pay a foreign supplier without a surprise
To carry out its policy for the country's money
To profit from price moves with their own money
To manage pooled money by its rules
To follow rules and trade at high speed

exercise.explanation: Motives differ. Many participants have no interest in short-term price moves.

points: Central banks, banks, companies, funds, individuals and automated firms all trade.
Most do not aim to profit from short price moves.
An individual is a very small participant.

lessons.title: Why Do Prices Move?
lessons.aim: Explain a price move as buying against selling, and say why after-the-fact stories are not predictions.

steps.title: A Price Is Where A Trade Happened

blocks.text: The price is the level at which a buyer and a seller last agreed to trade.
When more people want to buy than sell, buyers must pay more to get filled. The price rises.
When more want to sell than buy, sellers must accept less. The price falls.

items: New information, such as a news release.
Changed expectations about the future.
Needs that have nothing to do with the price, such as paying a bill.
Large players changing their positions.

blocks.text: After a move, people explain it with a tidy story about the news.
In real time the cause is often unclear, and several forces act at once. A story that explains a move that already happened is **hindsight**. It is not a forecast.

steps.title: Buying Against Selling
steps.intro: First choose what you expect. Then run it.

points: A price is where a buyer and seller last agreed.
More buying than selling pushes it up. More selling pushes it down.
Many forces act at once, and the cause is often unclear in real time.
A story after the fact is not a prediction.

lessons.title: What Is An Edge?
lessons.aim: Define an edge and tell it apart from a belief.

blocks.text: An edge is an average gain per trade, after costs, that is supported by evidence.
An edge is not a property of one trade. It is what happens on average across many.
A trade can lose while the method still has an edge. A trade can win with no edge at all.

blocks.title: Two statements
steps: **Edge:** "Across 300 recorded trades, this method averaged +$4 per trade after costs."

blocks.text: The first is a feeling. The second is a measurement. (The numbers here are an illustration, not a real result.)
Real edges are small. Even a real edge produces runs of losses. A small edge takes many trades to show up.
That is why a few good results prove nothing. Level 13 shows you how to measure this properly.
Expected value is the tool for asking "does this bet pay on average?" A positive expected value, after costs, is what an edge looks like in numbers.
A high win rate is not the same thing. It depends how much you win and lose too. You will see this in Level 5.

steps.title: Two Coins
steps.intro: One coin lands heads 50% of the time. The other, 52%. Can you tell which is which?

steps.title: Another Expected Value
steps.intro: Use the − key for a negative number.

points: An edge is a measured average gain per trade after costs.
A belief is a feeling. An edge is evidence.
A real edge is small and noisy, and needs many trades to show.
A high win rate is not the same as an edge.

lessons.title: Probability And Uncertainty
lessons.aim: Explain why one result cannot be predicted but many results can.

blocks.text: A 60% chance means about 6 in 10 over many tries. It says nothing certain about the next one.
You cannot predict one coin flip. But 100 flips will land close to 50 heads.
One result is unpredictable. The spread of many results is predictable.
For this lesson, treat each trade as its own draw, and do not let the last result change your view of the next. Results like this are called **independent**.

steps.title: A Loss Streak Does Not Make A Win Due

blocks.text: After four losses in a row, the fifth is not "due" to win. The market has no memory of your results. This mistake has a name, the **gambler's fallacy**. You will meet it again in Level 11.

steps.title: The Probability Lab
steps.intro: Choose a win rate and a number of trades. Predict first. Then run 1,000 tries.

points: Probability is how often something happens over many tries.
One result cannot be predicted. The spread of many can.
Independent results do not remember the past.
A loss streak does not make a win due.

lessons.title: Why Traders Experience Losing Streaks
lessons.aim: Show with a simulation that runs of losses are normal, even for a method that wins on average.

blocks.text: Flip a fair coin 100 times and you will see runs of heads and runs of tails. Nothing is wrong with the coin. Random results just cluster.

steps.title: A Winning Method Still Has Losing Runs

blocks.text: Even a method that wins 6 times in 10 will have several losses in a row now and then. A losing run does not mean the method has stopped working.
The lower the win rate, the longer the losing runs tend to be. Some good methods win less than half the time.
Give twenty traders the same rules and the same odds. Their results will still look very different, because of luck.
That is why one person's good or bad run tells you little about their skill.

steps.title: The Streak Simulator
steps.intro: Choose a win rate. Predict the longest losing streak. Then run twenty identical traders.

points: Random results come in runs.
A method that wins on average still has losing runs.
Lower win rates make longer losing runs.
Traders with identical rules get different results from luck alone.

lessons.title: A Good Trade Versus A Profitable Trade
lessons.aim: Judge a decision by its quality, separately from its result.

blocks.text: Was the decision good? And did it make money? They are different questions.
A good decision can lose. A poor decision can win. Neither result changes the quality of the decision.

items: It followed a plan that was tested.
Risk stayed within the limit.
It used only the information available at the time.

blocks.text: If you judge by results, you learn the wrong lessons. You keep habits that got lucky, and you drop good ones that lost. Over time that costs you.

steps.title: Sort Twelve Decisions
steps.intro: Tap a decision, then tap the box where it belongs.

exercise.prompt: Each trader made a decision. Sort them by the quality of the decision and the result.

items.text: Followed every rule in the plan. The trade made money.
Followed every rule in the plan. The trade lost.
Ignored the plan and traded on a hunch. It made money.
Ignored the plan and doubled the size. It lost.
Waited for the setup, risked the planned amount, and lost.
Skipped the trade because the plan said there was no setup. The price then rose.
Entered late out of excitement, with no limit. It made money.
Moved the risk limit further away to avoid a loss. It lost more.
Traded the planned size with the limit in place. It made money.
Took a large risk on a tip. It lost.
Sat out a news release because the plan says to. The price jumped.
Traded without checking the plan, and the trade paid off.

itemFeedback.i1: Following the plan was right. A loss is part of any method.
itemFeedback.i2: The win was luck. The decision was still poor.
itemFeedback.i5: The plan said no. The price rising afterwards does not make the decision poor.

exercise.explanation: Judge the decision first. The result is a separate question.

steps.title: In Your Own Words
steps.prompt: Why can a trader have a losing trade while following a method that is profitable on average? Write a few sentences.
steps.modelAnswer: Each trade is only one draw from a range of possible results. A method that wins on average still loses some of its trades, and even runs of them, because results vary. So one loss does not show the method is broken, and one win does not show it is good. You judge the method over many trades and you judge each decision by whether it followed the plan.
rubric: Each trade is one draw from a range of outcomes.
An edge shows over many trades, not one.
Losing trades are an expected part of a profitable method.
Judge the decision by process, not by one result.
Small samples can mislead in either direction.

points: Decision quality and result are separate questions.
A good decision can lose. A poor decision can win.
Judging by results teaches the wrong lessons.
A good decision follows a tested plan at acceptable risk.

lessons.title: Currency Pairs: Base And Quote
lessons.aim: Read a currency quote and say exactly what it means.

steps.title: A Currency Has No Price Alone

blocks.text: You cannot say what a euro costs without saying **in what**. A currency's price is always in another currency.
That is why currencies are quoted in **pairs**, such as EUR/USD.
In EUR/USD, the first currency is the **base**. The second is the **quote**.
The price of a pair is how many units of the quote currency it takes to buy one unit of the base.

blocks.title: EUR/USD is 1.1750
steps: Base: EUR, the euro. Quote: USD, the US dollar.
Read it as: **one euro costs 1.1750 US dollars.**

blocks.text: Use this sentence every time: one *base* costs *price* *quote*.
Each currency has a three-letter code.

items: EUR euro, USD US dollar, GBP British pound.
JPY Japanese yen, CHF Swiss franc.
AUD Australian dollar, NZD New Zealand dollar, CAD Canadian dollar.

steps.title: What Does The Price Say?
steps.intro: Choose the sentence that reads the price correctly.

steps.title: Convert An Amount
steps.intro: Use the keypad. Multiply when you change the base into the quote.

points: A currency is always priced in another currency.
In a pair, the first currency is the base and the second is the quote.
The price is how many quote units buy one base unit.
Say it as: one base costs price quote.

lessons.title: Major, Minor And Exotic Pairs
lessons.aim: Group currency pairs as major, minor or exotic, and say that the groups are a convention.

blocks.text: There are many currency pairs. Traders sort them into three groups by how heavily they trade.
In this program the seven majors are EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY, USD/CHF, AUD/USD, USD/CAD and NZD/USD.
Each includes the US dollar. They are the most heavily traded pairs.
A **minor** (or cross) pairs two major currencies without the dollar, such as EUR/GBP or GBP/JPY.
An **exotic** pairs a major currency with one from a smaller or emerging economy, such as USD/MXN or USD/ZAR.

blocks.title: Lists Differ
blocks.text: Other sources draw the lines differently. Some leave out NZD/USD or USD/CAD from the majors. The groups are a convention, so this program says which one it uses.
The more heavily a pair trades, the narrower its spread usually is. You can check this on any platform's quote list.

steps.title: Sort The First Ten
steps.intro: Under this program's definition, sort each pair.

exercise.prompt: Sort each pair using the definition in this program.

items.text: EUR/USD
GBP/JPY
USD/ZAR
AUD/USD
EUR/GBP
USD/MXN
USD/CAD
EUR/JPY
USD/JPY
USD/TRY

exercise.explanation: Majors include the dollar and are the most traded. Minors are two major currencies without the dollar. Exotics pair a major with a smaller economy.

points: Pairs are grouped as major, minor or exotic.
In this program the majors are the seven most traded pairs that include the dollar.
Minors are major currencies without the dollar. Exotics include a smaller economy.
The groups are a convention. Sources differ.

lessons.title: Reading Exchange Rates
lessons.aim: State exactly what happened to each currency when a pair's price moves.

blocks.title: EUR/USD rises from 1.1750 to 1.1800
steps: One euro used to cost 1.1750 dollars. Now it costs 1.1800.
The euro has **strengthened** against the dollar.
The move is 50 pips. (A pip is the usual small step of a price. You will measure it in Level 3.)

blocks.text: When the price of a pair rises, the base currency has strengthened against the quote currency. When it falls, the base has weakened.

steps.title: The Other Currency Moves The Other Way

blocks.text: One move, two readings. In the same example, the dollar has **weakened** against the euro.
A pair compares two currencies. If one gains on the other, the other loses to it.

blocks.title: USD/JPY rises from 150.00 to 151.00
steps: One dollar used to cost 150 yen. Now it costs 151.
The dollar strengthened against the yen. The yen weakened against the dollar.

steps.title: A Bigger Number Is Not A Stronger Currency

blocks.title: Do Not Judge By Size
blocks.text: A pair at 150 does not mean the base is stronger than one at 1.17. The number only says how many quote units one base unit costs.

steps.title: What Happened?
steps.intro: Read the move and choose the statement that is true.

points: When a pair's price rises, the base strengthened against the quote.
The quote currency moved the other way.
A bigger number does not mean a stronger currency.
State every move as one currency against another.

lessons.title: Inverse Quotes And Cross Rates
lessons.aim: Turn a quote round, and work out a cross rate from two prices.

blocks.text: If one euro costs 1.1750 dollars, how many euros does one dollar cost?
Divide 1 by the price. That gives the **reverse quote**.
Sometimes a pair is not quoted directly, but you can work it out from two others that share a currency.
That is a **cross rate**.

blocks.title: EUR/USD 1.1750 and GBP/USD 1.3500
steps: So one euro is worth 1.1750 ÷ 1.3500 = **0.8704 pounds**.

blocks.text: If EUR/USD, GBP/USD and EUR/GBP are all quoted, they must agree with each other.
If they did not, someone could make a risk-free profit by trading around the triangle, so traders and providers keep them in line.

steps.title: Try A Reverse Quote
steps.intro: Use the keypad. Divide 1 by the price.

steps.title: A Cross Rate, One Step At A Time
steps.intro: Change euros into dollars, then dollars into pounds, then read off the rate.

points: The reverse quote of a price is 1 divided by it.
A cross rate comes from two prices that share a currency.
Divide when both prices are against the same currency. Multiply when you chain one currency into the next.
Prices that disagree would offer a risk-free profit, so they are kept in line.

lessons.title: Currency Strength Is Relative
lessons.aim: Explain why "the dollar rose" needs a counterpart, and label what you can and cannot conclude.

blocks.text: A currency has no price by itself. It only has a price **against another currency**.
So "the dollar rose" is an incomplete sentence. Rose against what?
To say something about one currency, look at its moves against several others.
If the dollar rose against all of them, that says more than a rise against one.
A statement about a market can be three different things. This program labels them every time.

items: **Observable:** you can check it in the data.
**Interpretation:** how someone reads what they see.
**Hypothesis:** a testable claim about what happens next.

blocks.title: Three pairs on one day (teaching example)
steps: Each one says the dollar weakened against that currency.

blocks.text: Saying "the dollar weakened against the euro, pound and yen today" is an **observation**. Saying "the dollar was weak" is an **interpretation**. Saying "it will keep falling" is a **hypothesis**.

steps.title: Label The Conclusion
steps.intro: Use the table, then sort each statement into its layer.

exercise.prompt: Here are three pairs on one teaching day. Sort each statement into its layer.

items.text: EUR/USD rose 0.4%, GBP/USD rose 0.3% and USD/JPY fell 0.5%.
The dollar was broadly weak today.
The dollar will keep weakening next week.
The dollar weakened against the euro, the pound and the yen.
Traders must have been selling dollars because of an interest rate story.
If the dollar falls for three days, it usually keeps falling.

exercise.explanation: What the data shows is an observation. A reading of it is an interpretation. A claim about the future is a hypothesis, and it needs testing.

stimulus.title: One Day, Three Pairs
head: Pair
Change
Dollar Against It
stimulus.foot: Invented numbers for practice. Not market data.

points: A currency only has a price against another currency.
Look at several pairs before saying anything about one currency.
Label each statement: observable, interpretation or hypothesis.
A conclusion about the dollar is an interpretation, not a fact.

lessons.title: What Is An Asset Class?
lessons.aim: Tell owning an asset apart from holding a contract on its price.

blocks.text: An **asset** is something of value that people buy and sell. A group of similar assets is an **asset class**.
This level covers the main ones: stocks, funds, indices, commodities, bonds, futures, CFDs, crypto and currencies.
There are two ways to gain from a price. You can **own the thing**, such as a share in a company or a bar of gold.
Or you can hold a **contract** whose value follows the price, such as a futures contract or a CFD. You own the contract, not the thing.

blocks.title: Same Price, Different Position
blocks.text: Owning a share and holding a contract on that share can both move with the price. But they carry different risks and different costs.
The **underlying** is the thing whose price matters. The **instrument** is what you actually trade.
Gold is an underlying. A gold bar, a gold fund and a gold contract are three instruments that follow it.

blocks.title: The price of gold rises from $2,000 to $2,050 an ounce (teaching example)
steps: Gold bar: you own the metal. You must store it and insure it.
Gold fund: you own a share of a fund that holds gold.
Gold CFD: you own a contract with a provider. It pays you the difference in price.

blocks.text: All three gain when gold rises. All three lose when it falls. The risks around them are different.

steps.title: What Do You Actually Own?
steps.intro: Match each holding to what you really have.

exercise.prompt: Match each holding to what you actually own.

right.text: A small piece of the company
The metal itself
A contract with a provider
A contract to buy or sell oil later

exercise.explanation: Some holdings are the thing itself. Others are contracts that follow its price.

points: An asset class is a group of similar assets.
You either own the thing or hold a contract on its price.
The underlying is the thing. The instrument is what you trade.
Different instruments on the same underlying carry different risks.

lessons.title: Stocks And ETFs
lessons.aim: Explain what a share and a fund are, and what each one costs and risks.

blocks.text: A **share** (or stock) is a small piece of a company. If the company does well, the price of its shares may rise.
Some companies also pay a **dividend**, a part of their profit paid to owners.
Shares trade on an **exchange**. It has set opening hours on working days, and it is closed at night and on weekends.
So a share price can jump between one close and the next open. You cannot trade in the gap.
An **ETF** is a basket of assets that trades like a single share. One fund can hold hundreds of companies.
If you buy one share of the fund, you own a small slice of the whole basket.

items: An ETF charges a small yearly fee.
It may not match its index perfectly. The gap is called tracking difference.
Every trade has a spread or a commission.

blocks.text: A basket lowers the harm from one company failing. It does not protect you when the whole market falls.

steps.title: Share, Fund, Or Both?
steps.intro: Sort each statement.

exercise.prompt: Which asset does each statement describe?

items.text: Gives you part-ownership of one company
Holds a basket of many assets
Trades on an exchange in set hours
Can pay you a dividend
Charges a yearly fund fee
Can lose value

itemFeedback.i3: Some funds pass on dividends from the companies they hold, but a share of one company is the plain example.

exercise.explanation: A share is one company. A fund is a basket. Both trade on an exchange and both can lose value.

points: A share is part-ownership of a company.
Shares trade on exchanges with set hours.
An ETF is a basket that trades like one share.
A basket spreads company risk but not market risk, and it has fees.

lessons.title: Indices
lessons.aim: Explain what an index is and how people trade it.

blocks.text: An **index** measures a group of assets as one number. A stock index tracks a group of large companies.
For example, the S&P 500 follows 500 large US companies. It is quoted in **points**, not dollars.
An index is a calculation. There is nothing to hand over.
To trade its moves you use an instrument that follows it: an **ETF**, a **futures contract** or a **CFD**. The index is the underlying.
Many indices give large companies more weight. A big company's price change moves the index more than a small one's.
Some indices give every company equal weight. The rules are published by whoever runs the index.

blocks.title: Two shares, equal weight (teaching example)
steps: Share A goes from $40 to $44. That is +10%.
Share B goes from $60 to $57. That is −5%.
The index is the average of the two changes: (10% + −5%) ÷ 2 = **+2.5%**.

steps.title: Which Can You Buy?
steps.intro: Tap all that you can trade directly.

exercise.prompt: Which of these can you trade directly? Choose all that apply.

options.text: An ETF that tracks an index
A futures contract on an index

optionFeedback.d: An index is only a calculation. You trade something that follows it.
optionFeedback.e: It is a measure, not a product.

exercise.explanation: You trade an instrument that follows the index, never the index itself.

points: An index is a number that measures a basket.
You cannot buy an index. You trade an ETF, futures contract or CFD that follows it.
Many indices give big companies more weight.

lessons.title: Commodities
lessons.aim: Explain what commodities are and what pushes their prices.

blocks.text: A **commodity** is a physical good that is traded in standard grades. Oil, gold, copper, wheat and coffee are commodities.
Because the grade is standard, one barrel or one ounce is treated the same as another.
Commodity prices are pushed by sudden changes in how much is available or how much is wanted.

items: A drought cuts a harvest.
A mine strike stops output.
A new pipeline adds supply.
Demand jumps when travel restarts.

blocks.text: Less supply, with the same demand, tends to push a price up. More supply tends to push it down.

steps.title: Most People Never Touch The Goods

blocks.text: Nobody wants a truck of wheat delivered to their door. Traders use **futures**, **funds** or **CFDs** that follow the price.
Each of these is an instrument. The commodity is the underlying.
The **spot price** is the price for delivery now. A futures contract sets a price for delivery later.
The two prices can differ. So a fund or contract that follows a commodity may not match the spot price exactly.

steps.title: Likely Up Or Likely Down?
steps.intro: Sort each shock by its likely effect on price, other things equal.

exercise.prompt: Other things equal, how does each event tend to push the price?

items.text: A drought cuts the wheat harvest
A record coffee crop
A mine strike halts copper output
A new pipeline doubles oil supply
Demand for jet fuel jumps as travel returns
A large stock of oil is released from storage

exercise.explanation: Less supply or more demand tends to lift a price. More supply or less demand tends to lower it. This is a tendency. Other things move at the same time.

points: Commodities are physical goods in standard grades.
Supply and demand shocks push their prices, as a tendency.
Most traders use futures, funds or CFDs, not the goods.
An instrument can differ from the spot price.

lessons.title: Bonds And Interest Rates
lessons.aim: Explain what a bond is and why its price and yield move in opposite directions.

blocks.text: A **bond** is a loan you make to a government or a company. In return it pays you interest, and it repays the loan on a set date.
The interest is called the **coupon**. It is usually a fixed yearly amount.

blocks.title: A teaching example
steps: A bond has a face value of $100.
It pays a coupon of $5 every year.
So it pays 5% of its face value each year.

blocks.text: The **yield** is the yearly income divided by the price you pay.
When a bond's price rises, its yield falls. When its price falls, its yield rises.
The coupon stays the same. Only the price changes, so the income is a bigger or smaller share of what you pay.
A central bank sets a **policy rate**. When it raises the rate, new bonds pay more.
Older bonds that pay less become less attractive. Their prices tend to fall until their yield catches up. You will see this again in Level 9.

steps.title: Move The Price
steps.intro: Slide the price. Watch the yield.

points: A bond is a loan that pays a coupon and is repaid on a set date.
Yield is the yearly income divided by the price paid.
When price rises, yield falls. When price falls, yield rises.
Higher policy rates tend to push older bond prices down.

lessons.title: Futures
lessons.aim: Explain what a futures contract is, what margin does, and what expiry means for a trader.

blocks.text: A **futures contract** is an agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a set date in the future.
It is standard. The exchange decides the size, the quality and the date. Only the price is negotiated by the market.
You do not pay the full value to open a futures position. You put up a smaller deposit called **margin**.
But your gain or loss is on the full size of the contract. So a small move in price can make a large change in your account.
A **clearing house** stands between buyer and seller. Each side deals with the clearing house, not with each other.
That is why exchange-traded futures are open to many people who do not know or trust each other.
A futures contract **expires**. On that date it settles: some settle in cash, some by delivering the goods.
Most traders close before then. To stay in the market they **roll**: close the old contract and open the next one.

steps.title: The Life Of A Futures Position
steps.intro: Put the steps in order.

exercise.prompt: Put the life of a futures position in order.

items.text: Deposit margin
Open the position
Hold it while the price moves
Close it or roll it before expiry
The contract settles or is replaced

exercise.explanation: You deposit margin, open, hold, then close or roll before the contract expires.

points: A futures contract is a standard agreement for a set price on a set date.
You put up margin, but gains and losses are on the full contract.
A clearing house stands between buyer and seller.
Every contract expires, so traders close or roll.

lessons.title: CFDs And Leveraged Derivatives
lessons.aim: Explain what a CFD is and spot the flaws in a CFD advertisement.

steps.title: A Contract On The Price Change

blocks.text: A **CFD** is a contract that pays or charges you the change in price between when you open it and when you close it.
You never own the underlying. You hold a contract, and usually the other side of it is the company that offers it.
CFDs use **leverage**: you put up a small deposit and hold a larger position. Gains and losses are on the whole position.
So leverage makes small moves bigger, in both directions. Level 3 shows the numbers.

items: The **spread**: you buy a little higher than you sell.
**Financing**: holding a position overnight is charged or credited each day.
Sometimes a commission on top.

blocks.text: Some countries limit the leverage on CFDs for ordinary clients. Some do not allow them at all.
Always check the rules that apply to you. A product being advertised does not mean it is allowed where you live.

steps.title: Spot The Flaws In An Advertisement
steps.intro: Read each statement. Is it fine, or does it contain a flaw? The advertisement is invented for this exercise.

exercise.prompt: This is an invented advertisement from "Example Markets". Judge each statement.

claims.text: Our top clients doubled their money in a week.
You can trade shares, oil and currencies without owning any of them.
With leverage, a small price move can bring a large profit.
Commission-free trading, with no other charges.
Our simple method always works.
Prices include a spread, and holding a position overnight can add a financing charge.

claimFeedback.c0: It shows only the best results, with no evidence and no sample.
claimFeedback.c1: This is a fair description of what a CFD is.
claimFeedback.c2: Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains. Only the gains are mentioned.
claimFeedback.c3: The spread and financing are costs. "No other charges" is false.
claimFeedback.c4: No method always works. Any promise of certainty is a red flag.

exercise.explanation: Look for promises of certainty, one-sided leverage, missing costs and results with no evidence.

points: A CFD pays the change in price. You never own the underlying.
The provider is usually the other side of your contract.
Leverage magnifies gains and losses. Costs are the spread and financing.
Rules vary by country. Watch for one-sided and guaranteed claims.

lessons.title: Crypto
lessons.aim: Describe what crypto assets are and the main risks around holding and trading them.

blocks.text: A **crypto asset** is a digital asset recorded on a shared ledger called a blockchain.
You hold it with a set of secret keys. Whoever controls the keys controls the asset.
Crypto markets trade around the clock, every day of the week. There is no closing bell.
That means a price can move while you sleep, and there is no quiet gap to review your plan.
If you keep crypto on an exchange, the exchange holds the keys. If you keep the keys yourself, you are responsible for them.
This question is called **custody**. Exchanges have failed, been hacked or stopped withdrawals in the past.
You can buy the asset itself. You can also trade futures or CFDs that follow its price.
Those are contracts, so the earlier lessons apply: leverage, expiry, financing and who the counterparty is.

blocks.title: Check First
blocks.text: Regulation of crypto varies a great deal by country and keeps changing. Check the rules that apply where you live before you do anything.

steps.title: Which Kind Of Risk?
steps.intro: Sort each risk.

exercise.prompt: Which kind of risk is each one?

items.text: The price falls 20% in a day
An exchange freezes withdrawals
A country restricts trading
You lose the keys to your wallet
A new law changes what you can buy
Prices swing while you sleep

exercise.explanation: Market risk is about price. Custody and platform risk is about who holds the asset. Rule risk is about what the law allows.

points: Crypto assets are digital assets held with keys.
Markets trade around the clock.
Custody and platform failure are major risks.
You can trade the asset or contracts on it. Rules vary and change.

lessons.title: Comparing Instruments
lessons.aim: Compare instruments on ownership, leverage and hours, and match an instrument to a job.

blocks.text: So far each instrument has been a separate lesson. Now compare them side by side.

items: Do you **own** the asset?
Is **leverage** built in?
Are there **set hours**?
Who is on the **other side**?

blocks.text: Each instrument does a different job. A share suits long ownership. A fund suits a broad basket. A contract suits a short-term view on a price.
Choose by the job you need done, not by habit or by what an advertisement calls exciting.

steps.title: Fill In The Matrix
steps.intro: For each instrument, choose Yes, No or Depends for each feature.

blocks.text: Next, four short situations. For each, choose the instrument whose features fit the job, and say why.

steps.title: Choose By The Job
steps.intro: Read the situation and choose.

exercise.prompt: Sam wants to own a small part of a business for many years and receive any dividends. Which fits best?

options.text: A futures contract on a stock index

optionFeedback.b: A CFD gives no ownership and no dividend rights.
optionFeedback.c: That is a short-dated contract on an index.
optionFeedback.d: That is not part-ownership of a business.

exercise.explanation: Ownership and dividends point to the share itself.

points: Compare instruments on ownership, leverage, hours and counterparty.
There is no best instrument. Each does a different job.
Choose by the job, and check the costs and rules that apply to you.

lessons.title: Why This Program Starts With Forex
lessons.aim: State the honest reasons this program teaches with Forex, and what those reasons do not mean.

blocks.text: This program uses currency pairs to teach trading. There are practical reasons.

items: One kind of market to learn, not thousands of companies.
No company reports to surprise a price in the middle of a lesson.
Sessions follow the clock, which teaches time.
Position sizes can be small, so risk can be small.
Pips and lots carry over to other markets.

blocks.title: Not Easier, Not Safer
blocks.text: Forex is not easier than other markets. It is not safer. It is not more profitable. Leverage and costs apply, and most of what you learn here works in any market.

steps.title: A Market With No Single Tape

blocks.text: Forex is not on one exchange. Banks and providers quote prices to each other and to you.
So two providers can show slightly different prices at the same moment. You will meet this again in Level 4.
Forex is a convenient place to practise the skills. The skills are decision-making, risk and evidence.
If you ever trade another market, the same ideas apply.

steps.title: Spot The Unsupported Claims
steps.intro: Read each statement about Forex. Is it fine, or does it contain a flaw? The text is invented.

exercise.prompt: These statements are invented for this exercise. Judge each one.

claims.text: Forex is the easiest market to make money in.
Currencies can be traded on weekdays around the clock through providers and banks.
Small position sizes let you keep risk small while you learn.
Leverage lets even a small account earn a big income.
Follow our method and you will win.
Forex is safer than shares because it never crashes.

claimFeedback.c0: No evidence is given, and no market is easy.
claimFeedback.c1: A fair description of how the market is open.
claimFeedback.c2: This is a fair practical point.
claimFeedback.c3: Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains, and income is never assured.
claimFeedback.c5: No evidence is given, and currencies can move a long way.

exercise.explanation: Spot the promises of certainty, the one-sided leverage claims and the claims with no evidence.

points: The reasons for starting with Forex are practical.
Forex is not easier, safer or more profitable.
There is no single tape, so providers can show slightly different prices.
The skills carry over to any market.

lessons.title: Bid, Ask And The Spread
lessons.aim: Read a two-way quote, and say who pays the spread and when.

blocks.text: A platform shows two prices for a currency pair, not one.

items: The **bid** is the price you can sell at.
The **ask** is the price you can buy at.

steps.title: You Buy High And Sell Low

blocks.text: The ask is always higher than the bid. When you **buy**, you pay the higher price. When you **sell**, you get the lower one.
Whoever is on the other side of your trade earns that gap.
The gap between the two prices is the **spread**.

blocks.title: EUR/USD quoted 1.17494 / 1.17506
steps: Traders call this 1.2 pips. The next lesson explains pips.

blocks.title: Buy 10,000 euros, then sell them straight away
steps: You buy at the ask: 1.17506 dollars for each euro.
You sell at the bid: 1.17494 dollars for each euro.
You lose 0.00012 × 10,000 = **$1.20**, and the market has not moved at all.

blocks.text: So every trade starts a little behind. Your average trade has to earn more than the spread before it earns anything.

steps.title: The Quote Board
steps.intro: Predict, then buy and close.

points: A quote has a bid (you sell here) and an ask (you buy here).
The ask is higher. The gap is the spread.
You pay the spread the moment you open a trade.
A trade must first earn back the spread before it earns anything.

lessons.title: The Pip And The Pipette
lessons.aim: Count pips between two prices, on any pair, without a tool.

blocks.text: Prices move in small steps. The usual small step has a name: the **pip**.

items: On most pairs a pip is **0.0001**, the fourth decimal place.
On pairs with the yen, a pip is **0.01**, the second decimal place.

blocks.text: Many platforms show one more digit. That extra digit is a **pipette**: one tenth of a pip.

blocks.title: EUR/USD at 1.17452
steps: The fourth decimal is the pip: 1.1745.
The fifth decimal, 2, is a pipette: two tenths of a pip.

blocks.title: EUR/USD moves from 1.17452 to 1.17721
steps: Divide by the pip size: 0.00269 ÷ 0.0001 = **26.9 pips**.

blocks.title: Watch For These
blocks.text: Yen trap: using 0.0001 on a yen pair makes your answer 100 times too big. Pipette trap: counting the fifth decimal as a whole pip makes it 10 times too big. The app will name these mistakes if you make them.

steps.title: Count The Pips
steps.intro: Use the keypad. One decimal place.

steps.title: A Yen Pair
steps.intro: The pip is 0.01 here.

points: A pip is 0.0001 on most pairs and 0.01 on yen pairs.
A pipette is one tenth of a pip.
Count pips by dividing the price gap by the pip size.
Watch the yen trap (100 times) and the pipette trap (10 times).

lessons.title: Lots And Contract Size
lessons.aim: Convert between lots and units, and say what a position is worth.

blocks.text: You do not buy currency one unit at a time. Positions are measured in **lots**.

items: A **standard lot** is 100,000 units of the base currency.
A **mini lot** is 10,000 units, or 0.1 lot.
A **micro lot** is 1,000 units, or 0.01 lot.

blocks.text: Those sizes are the usual ones. Some brokers allow smaller or odd sizes. Always check the contract size on your own platform.
The **position value** is the units times the price. It is much larger than the money you need to open it.

steps.title: Lots To Units
steps.intro: Use the keypad.

steps.title: The Value Of A Position
steps.intro: Lots × 100,000 × the price.

points: A standard lot is 100,000 units. A mini is 10,000. A micro is 1,000.
Lots × 100,000 gives units.
Position value = units × price.
Check the contract size on your own platform.

lessons.title: Long And Short
lessons.aim: Explain what going long and short mean, and which price opens and closes each.

blocks.text: Buying EUR/USD means **buying the euro and selling the dollar**. You gain if the euro gets stronger against the dollar, so if the price rises.
A trade that starts with a buy is a **long** trade.
You can also **sell first** and buy back later. That is a **short** trade. You gain if the price falls.
In a currency pair you always have both sides at once. Selling EUR/USD means selling euros and buying dollars.

items: A **long** trade opens at the **ask** (you buy) and closes at the **bid** (you sell).
A **short** trade opens at the **bid** (you sell) and closes at the **ask** (you buy back).

blocks.title: Long EUR/USD from 1.1750 to 1.1780
steps: The price rose 30 pips. A long trade gains: **+30 pips**.

blocks.title: Short EUR/USD from 1.1750 to 1.1780
steps: The same price rise hurts a short trade: **−30 pips**.

steps.title: Which Prices?
steps.intro: Choose how the platform opens and closes the trade.

points: Long means buy first. Short means sell first.
Long gains when the price rises. Short gains when it falls.
Long opens at the ask and closes at the bid. Short opens at the bid and closes at the ask.
In a pair you always buy one currency and sell the other.

lessons.title: Pip Value
lessons.aim: Work out what one pip is worth in your account currency.

blocks.text: **Pip value** is what one pip is worth in money for your position, in your account currency.
It depends on three things:

items: The pip size of the pair.
The size of your position, in lots.
The second currency in the pair, compared with your account currency.

blocks.text: Trade EUR/USD with a US-dollar account. The second currency is already dollars.
Half a lot is $5 per pip. Two lots is $20 per pip.

steps.title: Case Two: Convert To Your Currency

blocks.text: When the second currency is not your account currency, the pip value first comes out in that currency. Then you convert it.

blocks.title: USD/JPY at 150, one lot
steps: Yen pair, so the pip size is 0.01.
One dollar buys 150 yen, so 1,000 yen is 1,000 ÷ 150 = **$6.67**.

blocks.text: Ask one question: how many dollars is one unit of that second currency worth?

items: **Yen:** one yen is 1 ÷ 150 dollars, so **divide** by the USD/JPY price.
**Canadian dollars:** one is 1 ÷ 1.36 dollars, so **divide** by the USD/CAD price.
**Pounds:** one pound is 1.35 dollars, so **multiply** by the GBP/USD price.

blocks.title: The Yen Trap
blocks.text: On a yen pair the pip is 0.01, not 0.0001. Using the wrong one makes your answer 100 times too small.

blocks.title: USD/JPY at 150, half a lot, dollar account
steps: In dollars: 1,000 ÷ 150 = $6.67 per pip for one lot.

steps.title: Guided Calculator
steps.intro: Fill in each step. If one step is off, the next steps are still marked against your own number.

steps.title: Try One More
steps.intro: Use the keypad.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Try different pairs and lot sizes. Open Show Working to see each step.

points: Pip value depends on pip size, lots, and the second currency.
Second currency = your account currency: nothing to convert.
Otherwise, convert. Divide when dollars are the first currency, multiply when dollars are the second.
Yen pairs use a 0.01 pip.

lessons.title: Profit And Loss In Money
lessons.aim: Turn a result in pips into money, for a long or a short trade.

blocks.text: Profit or loss in money = result in pips × pip value per lot × number of lots.

blocks.title: Long 0.5 lots of EUR/USD, up 30 pips (dollar account)

steps.title: A Loss Uses The Same Steps

blocks.title: The same trade, but the price falls 20 pips

blocks.text: Keep the minus sign all the way through. A loss is a negative number.
The direction only changes the sign of the pips.

items: **Long:** price up is a gain, price down is a loss.
