**Short:** price down is a gain, price up is a loss.

steps.title: The Spread Is Already In It

blocks.text: If you use the prices you actually traded at, the spread is already included. A long trade opens at the ask and closes at the bid.

blocks.title: The chart mid-price rises 30 pips, and the spread is 1.2 pips
steps: You paid the spread on entry, so the result is about 30 − 1.2 = 28.8 pips.

blocks.title: Charts Hide The Spread
blocks.text: A chart shows one price. A real trade uses the bid and the ask. Level 4 explains why this matters.

steps.title: Pips To Money
steps.intro: Use the keypad and the − key for a loss.

points: Profit or loss = pips × pip value × lots.
Direction sets the sign: long gains on a rise, short gains on a fall.
Prices at the bid and ask already include the spread.
A chart price does not show the spread.

lessons.title: Leverage And Margin
lessons.aim: Explain leverage and margin, and why leverage swings an account harder.

steps.title: A Bigger Position Than Your Deposit

blocks.text: **Leverage** lets you hold a position larger than the money you put up. A ratio of 100 : 1 means the position can be 100 times the deposit.
The deposit is called **margin**.
Margin = position value ÷ leverage.

steps.title: Leverage Does Not Change A Pip

blocks.text: At every leverage, one pip on one lot of EUR/USD is worth $10.
What leverage changes is **how large a position the account is allowed to hold**. The size you choose decides how far your account swings.

blocks.title: A $2,000 account holds 1 lot. The price moves 50 pips.

blocks.text: Leverage magnifies gains and losses by the same amount.

steps.title: The Leverage Lens
steps.intro: Predict first, then move the market.

steps.title: Work Out The Margin
steps.intro: Position value ÷ leverage.

points: Leverage lets a small deposit (margin) control a bigger position.
Margin = position value ÷ leverage.
A pip is worth the same at every leverage.
Bigger positions swing the account more, in both directions.

lessons.title: Balance, Equity, Free Margin, Margin Level
lessons.aim: Read an account panel and predict what a price move does to it.

items: **Balance:** your money from closed trades.
**Equity:** balance plus the floating result of open trades.
**Used margin:** the deposit held for open positions.
**Free margin:** equity minus used margin.
**Margin level:** equity ÷ used margin × 100.

blocks.title: Balance $2,000. One lot of EUR/USD, leverage 100 : 1. The price falls 40 pips.

blocks.text: Brokers watch the margin level to protect themselves. At a set level they warn you (a **margin call**). At a lower level they close your positions (a **stop-out**).

blocks.title: Levels Vary By Broker
blocks.text: Some warn around 100% and close positions around 50%, but every broker sets its own. Look up yours before you trade.

steps.title: The Account Panel
steps.intro: Predict first, then slide the price.

steps.title: Margin Level
steps.intro: Equity ÷ used margin × 100.

points: Balance changes when trades close. Equity moves with every open trade.
Free margin = equity − used margin.
Margin level = equity ÷ used margin × 100.
Margin-call and stop-out levels are set by each broker.

lessons.title: Swap And Commission
lessons.aim: Work out what holding a trade overnight, and trading it, costs.

blocks.text: When you hold a position past the daily cut-off, the broker applies a **swap**. It can be a charge or a credit.
It comes from the difference between the interest rates of the two currencies, plus the broker's markup.

blocks.title: You hold 2 lots for 3 nights. The swap is −$4.50 per lot per night.

blocks.text: A minus sign means a charge. A plus sign means a credit.

blocks.title: Check Your Broker
blocks.text: Some brokers charge three nights of swap on one night of the week to cover the weekend. Which night varies by broker.
Some brokers charge a **commission**, a fee per lot, on top of the spread.

blocks.title: $3.50 per lot each way. You trade 0.5 lots.

steps.title: Add Up The Swap
steps.intro: Use the − key for a charge.

points: Holding a position overnight earns or costs swap.
Total swap = lots × nights × swap per lot per night.
Commission is usually charged per lot, on opening and again on closing.
Check your own broker's swap and commission tables.

lessons.title: Slippage And Total Trade Cost
lessons.aim: Add up every cost of a trade, and say how much of your 1R they take.

blocks.text: **Slippage** is the difference between the price you expected and the price you got. It happens when the market moves between your click and your fill.
It can help you or hurt you. Over many trades it usually costs a little.
Total cost = spread + commission + swap + slippage.
So a trade that wins 2R before costs really wins about 1.86R. A trade that loses 1R loses about 1.14R.
Costs are about the same whether your stop is close or far. So with a tight stop they take a larger share of your risk.

blocks.title: Do Not Ignore This
blocks.text: A strategy that looks good before costs may not survive them. You will meet this again in Levels 4, 5 and 13.

steps.title: The Cost Bar
steps.intro: Slide the stop and watch the share of 1R.

steps.title: Total Cost
steps.intro: Add the four costs.

points: Total cost = spread + commission + swap + slippage.
Compare the cost with the money you risk to see how much of 1R it takes.
Costs matter more when stops are tight.
A strategy must beat its costs before it earns anything.

lessons.title: Dollar Risk And Percentage Risk
lessons.aim: Turn a risk percentage into dollars, and dollars back into a percentage.

blocks.text: Before you enter, you decide the most you are willing to lose on the trade. This is your **risk per trade**.
Many traders state it as a percent of the account, so the amount adjusts as the account grows or shrinks.
Dollar risk = account balance × risk % ÷ 100.
Risk % = money at risk ÷ account balance × 100.

blocks.title: A trade risks $80 in a $4,000 account
0.5% Is Not 0.5
blocks.text: To use a percent in a calculation, divide it by 100 first. 0.5% is 0.005. Mixing these up makes your answer 100 times wrong.
This app lets your mentor set a cap on risk per trade. The default is 1%. It only warns you. It is not advice about what your risk should be.
Level 10 shows what different risk settings do to an account, so you can choose for yourself.

steps.title: Percent To Dollars
steps.intro: Use the keypad.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Try a few accounts and risk percentages.

points: Dollar risk = balance × risk% ÷ 100.
Risk % = money at risk ÷ balance × 100.
Divide a percent by 100 before you use it.
A cap is a guardrail, not advice.

lessons.title: Stop-Loss Distance And Position Size
lessons.aim: Work from two prices to a position size and the risk you actually take.

blocks.text: Do not pick a size and then hope. Decide where you would be **wrong** first. That price is your stop.
Then choose a size so that hitting the stop loses only the amount you decided to risk.

blocks.title: Order Matters
blocks.text: The stop comes from the market. The size comes from the stop. Never the other way round.

steps.title: The Spread Adds To The Risk

blocks.text: Chart prices show the bid. A long trade enters at the ask, which is higher. So a small extra distance is at risk.
Lots = risk amount ÷ (stop distance in pips × pip value per lot).

blocks.title: Account $10,000, risk 0.5%, EUR/USD, risk distance 25.8 pips
steps: One lot loses 25.8 × $10 = $258 at the stop.

blocks.text: Your broker lets you change size in steps, often 0.01 lots. **Always round down**, so the risk never goes above your limit.

blocks.title: 0.1938 rounds down to 0.19 lots
steps: Realized risk: 0.19 × 25.8 × $10 = **$49.02**, which is 0.49% of the account.

blocks.title: Never Round Up
blocks.text: Rounding 0.1938 up to 0.20 would risk $51.60, which is over your $50 limit.

steps.title: Estimate First
steps.intro: A quick guess protects you from a slip of ten times.

steps.title: Size A Trade Step By Step
steps.intro: Work through each step. A step that is right for your own earlier number still earns its credit.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Change the stop or the risk and watch the lots and the realized risk.

points: Choose the stop from where you would be wrong. Then size to it.
Stop distance = price gap ÷ pip size, plus the spread for a long trade from a bid chart.
Lots = risk ÷ (stop pips × pip value), rounded DOWN.
Check the risk you actually take after rounding.

lessons.title: Reward, Risk-Reward And R-Multiple
lessons.aim: Measure a trade's reward against its risk, and state any result in R.

blocks.text: The **reward** is what the trade makes if it reaches its target. Measure it in pips, then in money, the same way as risk.
Reward-to-risk = reward ÷ risk.

steps.title: R: The Risk As A Unit

blocks.text: The money you risk on a trade is called **1R**. Every result can then be written as a multiple of it.
R lets you compare trades of different sizes. A +2R trade is +2R whether you risked $10 or $1,000.
Costs come off the result before you write it in R. A +2R trade with costs of 0.15R is +1.85R.

steps.title: Result In R
steps.intro: Use the − key for a loss.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Try a trade and see the result in R.

points: Reward-to-risk = reward ÷ risk.
R is a result divided by the risk taken. Risk $25 and make $75 is +3R.
Write a loss as a negative R.
Costs come off before you write the result in R.

lessons.title: Calculator Mastery Lab
lessons.aim: Reach mastery in every calculator problem family before the assessment.

blocks.text: The arithmetic in this level is the foundation of everything after it. So before the assessment, you practise each kind of problem until it is automatic.
There are six problem families: pips and lots, pip value and profit, risk and position size, reward and R, margin, and costs.

items: Each session is 20 mixed problems. Families you are weakest in come up more often.
A family is **mastered** at 90% or better over its last 10 problems.
Those problems must be spread over **at least two different days**.
Every wrong answer is named, so you can see what to fix.

blocks.title: Come Back Another Day
blocks.text: Your first session will not finish the lab. That is on purpose. What you can do on two different days is what you really know.

steps.title: The Lab
steps.intro: Start a session. It ends after 20 problems.

points: Mastery is 90% over the last 10 problems in a family, over at least two days.
The lab returns to your weakest families and names your mistakes.
The Level 3 assessment opens when every family is mastered and every lesson is done.
You can return to the lab any time from the Practice tab.

lessons.title: Market Orders
lessons.aim: Explain what a market order does and why the fill can differ from the price on screen.

blocks.text: A **market order** says: trade right now at the best price available.

items: A buy fills at the ask.
A sell fills at the bid.

steps.title: The Price On Screen Is Old

blocks.text: Between your click and your fill, a little time passes. It may be a fraction of a second. The price can move in that time.
The difference between the price you saw and the price you got is **slippage**. You met it in Level 3.
When the market is quiet, the fill is usually close to the price you saw. When it is moving fast, the fill can be several pips away, and it can go against you or for you.
A market order gives you certainty of a fill, but not certainty of the price.
Use one when getting in or out matters more than the exact price.

steps.title: Buy At Market
steps.intro: Try a quiet market and a fast one.

steps.title: Measure The Slippage
steps.intro: Use the keypad.

points: A market order trades now at the best price available.
A buy fills at the ask. A sell fills at the bid.
The fill can differ from the price you saw. That is slippage.
It gives certainty of a fill, not of the price.

lessons.title: Pending Orders: Limit Versus Stop
lessons.aim: Tell a limit order from a stop order, and say which side of the market each sits on.

blocks.text: A **pending order** waits until the price reaches a level you choose. Then it becomes a trade.
A **limit** order waits for a BETTER price than now. It is for buying cheaper or selling higher.

items: Buy limit: below the price. You wait for a pullback.
Sell limit: above the price. You wait for a rally.

steps.title: Stop: A Move Through A Level

blocks.text: A **stop** order waits for the price to move THROUGH a level. It is for joining a move that has already started.

items: Buy stop: above the price. You buy if it keeps rising.
Sell stop: below the price. You sell if it keeps falling.

blocks.title: Bargain Or Confirmation
blocks.text: A limit waits for a bargain: a better price than now. A stop waits for confirmation: the price moving through your level.

blocks.title: EUR/USD is at 1.1750
steps: Buy limit at 1.1720: below. You want to buy cheaper.
Buy stop at 1.1780: above. You want to buy if it breaks higher.
Sell limit at 1.1780: above. You want to sell higher.
Sell stop at 1.1720: below. You want to sell if it breaks lower.

steps.title: Which Side Of The Market?
steps.intro: Tap a price where the platform would accept the order.

steps.title: Which Order?
steps.intro: Read the idea and choose the order.

points: A limit waits for a BETTER price. A stop waits for a move THROUGH a level.
Buy limit and sell stop sit below the price.
Sell limit and buy stop sit above the price.
The platform rejects an order on the wrong side.

lessons.title: Buy Limit And Sell Limit
lessons.aim: Place limit orders on the right side, and explain that they may never fill.

blocks.text: A **buy limit** sits below the market. If the price falls to your level, you buy. If it does not, you do not.
A **sell limit** sits above the market. If the price rises to your level, you sell.
A limit order fills at your price or **better**. If the market jumps past your level, you get the better price.
The price you get is never worse than the level you set.

blocks.title: It May Never Fill
blocks.text: If the price turns before it reaches your level, the order just sits there. You did not lose money, but you missed the move. A limit gives you price control and gives up the certainty of a trade.

steps.title: Place A Limit Order
steps.intro: Choose a limit order and a level.
steps.question: Choose a limit order and a price for it. If you choose the wrong side, the platform will say so.

steps.title: Where Can It Sit?
steps.intro: Tap a valid price.

points: A buy limit sits below the price. A sell limit sits above it.
A limit fills at your price or better.
It may never fill.
A limit gives price control and gives up certainty of a trade.

lessons.title: Buy Stop And Sell Stop
lessons.aim: Place stop orders on the right side, and explain that they can fill at a worse price than your level.

blocks.text: A **buy stop** sits above the market. If the price rises to your level, your order becomes a market buy.
A **sell stop** sits below the market. If the price falls to your level, your order becomes a market sell.
A stop order turns into a market order when it is triggered. So it fills at the next price available, which can be **worse** than your level.

blocks.title: A buy stop at 1.1770
steps: The order is filled at about **1.1790**, 20 pips worse than your level.

steps.title: A Stop-Loss Is A Stop Order

blocks.text: The stop-loss you attach to a trade is itself a stop order. It becomes a market order when the price reaches it. So it has the same weakness.

blocks.title: Gaps
blocks.text: Over a weekend or after big news the price can jump past your stop. Your stop then fills at the first available price, and the loss can be bigger than you planned.

steps.title: Place A Stop Order
steps.intro: Choose a stop order and a level.
steps.question: Choose a stop order and a price for it. Watch what happens when the price runs through your level.

steps.title: A Gap Through Your Order
steps.intro: What price is the order filled at?

points: A buy stop sits above the price. A sell stop sits below it.
A stop becomes a market order when the price reaches it.
It fills at your level or WORSE, especially in a gap.
A stop-loss is a stop order, so it has the same weakness.

lessons.title: Stop-Loss And Take-Profit Orders
lessons.aim: Attach a stop-loss and a take-profit to an entry, and explain what neither one guarantees.

blocks.text: A **stop-loss** closes the trade if it goes against you, so your loss has a limit. A **take-profit** closes it when it reaches a target.
Together with the entry they make a **bracket**.

items: The stop-loss is a **stop** order: it becomes a market order when triggered.
The take-profit is a **limit** order: it fills at your price or better.

blocks.text: So the stop-loss can fill worse than its level. The take-profit cannot.
On a chart, a candle shows only its open, high, low and close. If one candle contains both your stop-loss and your take-profit, the chart cannot tell you which was hit first.

blocks.title: Say What You Assume
blocks.text: When you test a plan on candles, you must choose a rule for this case. The careful rule is to assume the stop was hit first. You will use it again in Levels 6, 12 and 13.

steps.title: Build A Bracket
steps.intro: Choose an entry, a stop and a target.
steps.question: Choose an entry order, then a stop-loss and a take-profit.

steps.title: The Ratio Of A Bracket
steps.intro: Use the keypad.

points: A stop-loss caps a loss. A take-profit closes at a target. Together with an entry they make a bracket.
The stop-loss is a stop order. The take-profit is a limit order.
Neither is guaranteed to fill at its level.
If both are inside one candle, the chart cannot say which came first.

lessons.title: Stop-Limit Orders
lessons.aim: Explain what a stop-limit does, and what you give up to get price control.

blocks.text: A **stop-limit** order has two prices: a **trigger** and a **limit**.

items: When the price reaches the trigger, the order wakes up.
It then becomes a limit order: it fills only at your limit price or better.

blocks.text: A plain stop can fill at a bad price in a fast move. A stop-limit will not: it refuses any price beyond your limit.

blocks.title: It May Not Fill
blocks.text: If the price jumps past your limit, the order stays unfilled. You keep price control, but you might not get the trade at all. In a stop-loss, that would leave you with no protection.
Not every platform offers stop-limit orders. Availability and behaviour vary, so check your own.

steps.title: Stop Against Stop-Limit
steps.intro: Set the same trigger for both. See what a fast move does.

steps.title: What Happens?
steps.intro: Read the jump and choose.

points: A stop-limit has a trigger and a limit.
Once triggered it fills only at the limit or better.
It protects you from a bad price, but it may not fill at all.
Check whether your platform offers it.

lessons.title: Choosing The Correct Order Type
lessons.aim: Choose an order type from an idea, and check it is on the right side of the market.

blocks.text: Do not start from the order. Start from what you want to happen, then find the order that does it.

items: Do you want in **now**? A market order.
Do you want a **better price** than now, waiting for a pullback? A limit order.
Do you want to join a move that **breaks through** a level? A stop order.
Do you want the breakout, but **not at any price**? A stop-limit.
Do you already have a trade and want a **cap and a target**? A stop-loss and a take-profit.

blocks.text: In the lab you will get twelve situations. Each one is marked on whether your order matches your idea and sits on the right side of the market.
It is not marked on whether the price would later have gone your way. A sound choice can lose. A poor one can win.

steps.title: The Order Lab
steps.intro: Twelve situations. Choose the order for each.

points: Start from the idea, then choose the order.
Now: market. Pullback: limit. Breakout: stop. Breakout with a price limit: stop-limit.
Check the order is on the correct side of the market.
The order choice is judged on logic, not on the outcome.

lessons.title: Liquidity And Volatility As Execution Conditions
lessons.aim: Explain how thin markets and fast markets change the price you get.

blocks.text: **Liquidity** is how easily you can trade without moving the price. A **deep** market has many orders on both sides. A **thin** market has few.
**Volatility** is how far and how fast a price moves. A calm market moves in small steps. A volatile one jumps.
Neither is fixed. The same pair can be deep at one hour and thin at another, calm in the morning and volatile after a news release.
Thin markets and fast markets tend to give worse fills, especially for large orders.
Retail platforms usually do not show the orders waiting in the market, so the next widget is a model. It shows the idea: a big order in a thin market fills at a worse average price.

steps.title: Thin Against Deep
steps.intro: Change the market and the size.

points: Liquidity is how easily you can trade without moving the price. Volatility is how far and fast it moves.
Both change through the day.
Thin or fast markets tend to give worse fills.
Large orders feel this most.

lessons.title: Spread Expansion, News And Slippage
lessons.aim: Explain how wider spreads around news raise cost and can stop you out, and state the cost in R.

blocks.text: Around big news and around the daily **rollover**, spreads often widen. A spread of 1 pip can become 10.

blocks.title: Stop 20 pips. The spread widens from 1 pip to 9 pips.
steps: 8 ÷ 20 = **0.4R** of extra cost, before the trade has done anything.

steps.title: A Short Stop Is A Buy

blocks.text: A stop-loss on a SHORT trade is a **buy** order, so it triggers on the **ask**. If the spread widens, the ask can rise to your stop while the bid, the price on your chart, barely moves.

blocks.title: The Chart May Not Show It
blocks.text: A chart usually draws the bid. It may show that price never reached your stop, even though your short was stopped out.
Fast news moves also bring gaps and slippage. Your fills can be worse at exactly the moments the market is moving most.

steps.title: Replay A News Event
steps.intro: Choose a stop, then replay.

steps.title: The Cost Of A Wide Spread
steps.intro: Extra spread divided by the stop.

points: Spreads often widen around news and rollover.
A wider spread is a cost, and can be stated in R.
A short stop-loss triggers on the ask.
News also brings gaps and slippage.

lessons.title: Broker Execution Models
lessons.aim: Describe the main ways brokers fill orders, and read an execution claim for what can be verified.

blocks.text: An **execution model** is the way a broker turns your order into a fill. Three names come up often.

items: **Market execution:** the order fills at the price available when it arrives. No requote.
**Instant execution:** you ask for a price and get it, or the broker sends a **requote** if it has moved.
**Request execution:** the broker sends you a price first and you accept or decline it.

blocks.text: Marketing labels such as "no dealing desk" describe a **model**, a way the broker says it works. They do not promise you a better price.
You can measure execution on a demo or a small account. Send orders, record the price you saw and the price you got, and note the time. Then you have evidence.

steps.title: Read An Execution Claim
steps.intro: Judge each statement. The text is invented.

exercise.prompt: These statements are invented for this exercise. Judge each one.

claims.text: Orders are filled at the best price available when they reach us.
No dealing desk means we never take the other side and you can never be requoted.
Zero slippage on every order, guaranteed.
Our fills are the fastest in the industry.
You can test our execution on a free demo account before you deposit.
Instant execution means you always get the price on your screen.

claimFeedback.c0: This describes a way of working. You can measure whether it holds.
claimFeedback.c1: A label names a model. "Never" is an absolute that only measurement can support.
claimFeedback.c2: No broker can guarantee zero slippage in fast markets.
claimFeedback.c3: No evidence or measurement is given.
claimFeedback.c4: This is checkable and lets you gather evidence.
claimFeedback.c5: With instant execution the broker can send a requote instead.

exercise.explanation: A model or a label is a description. A guarantee or an absolute needs proof, and you can test it.

points: Brokers fill orders by different models: market, instant or request execution.
A requote is a new price sent when yours is no longer available.
Labels like "no dealing desk" describe a model. They do not guarantee a fill or a price.
Test on a demo to gather evidence.

lessons.title: TradingView Versus Broker Prices
lessons.aim: Explain why a chart and a broker can disagree about whether a level was touched.

blocks.text: A charting service and your broker each take prices from their own sources. Two honest feeds can differ by a pip or two, or more in fast markets.
A chart may draw the bid, the middle price or the ask. Most draw one price, so the spread is not drawn at all.
Your broker fills buys at the ask and sells at the bid. So a buy stop is triggered by the ask, which the chart may not show.
Platforms stamp candles with their own clock, called **server time**. A daily candle can start at a different hour on two platforms. So daily highs and lows can differ.

steps.title: Two Feeds
steps.intro: Move a level near the high and see what each feed says. The differences are calculated live.

points: Chart feeds and broker feeds can differ.
A chart usually draws one price, so the spread is not shown.
A buy is filled at the ask, which the chart may not show.
Platforms may stamp candles with different server times.

lessons.title: Why Backtest Fills Differ From Live Fills
lessons.aim: List what makes a backtest fill better than a live one, and test one plan under three fill rules.

blocks.text: On a chart, price "touched" your level. In real life, that does not always mean you were filled.

items: The chart hides the **spread**.
Real fills have **slippage** and **delay**.
A candle cannot show what came **first** inside it.
Your broker's feed can differ from the chart.
**Touch fills:** a fill whenever price touches the level. No spread, no slippage. The most generous.
**Spread included:** buys use the ask, sells the bid.
**Conservative:** spread, slippage, and a fill only if price trades a little beyond the level. Stop first if both levels are in one candle.

blocks.title: A Backtest Is Only As Honest As Its Fill Rule
blocks.text: A result that depends on generous fills may vanish in real trading. When you test anything in this program, write down which fill rule you used, and prefer the conservative one.

steps.title: Same Plan, Three Rules
steps.intro: Change the plan and compare the results.

points: Touched is not filled.
Charts hide the spread. Live trading has slippage and delay. A candle cannot say what came first.
State your fill rule, and prefer the conservative one.
A backtest that depends on generous fills may not survive real trading.

lessons.title: Percentages, Ratios And Decimals
lessons.aim: Move between percentages, ratios and decimals, and see why a fall and an equal rise do not cancel.

blocks.text: 50% is 50 out of every 100. As a decimal it is 0.50. As a fraction it is one half.
Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. It is always measured against the STARTING value.
A **ratio** compares parts of a whole. Risking 1 to make 3 is a ratio of 1 : 3.

blocks.title: The ratio 1 : 3
steps: The risk is 1 of 4 parts: **25%**. The reward is 3 of 4: **75%**.

blocks.title: They Do Not Cancel
blocks.text: A rise is measured on the smaller balance you have after the fall. You will see this again in the lesson on drawdown.

steps.title: Percent Change
steps.intro: Use the − key for a fall.

points: A percent is a hundredth. Divide by 100 to use it.
Percent change is measured against the starting value.
A ratio compares parts of a whole: 1 : 3 is 25% and 75%.
A fall and an equal rise do not cancel out.

lessons.title: R-Multiples I
lessons.aim: Convert between money and R, and compare trades of different sizes in R.

blocks.text: **R** is the amount you risked at the start of the trade. It is set before you enter and it does not change.

items: Risk $25 and make $75: **+3R**.
Risk $25 and lose $25: **−1R**.

blocks.text: Trade A risked $200 and made $200. Trade B risked $25 and made $75.
In dollars A looks bigger. In R, A is +1R and B is **+3R**. B did better with the risk it took.
R removes the size of your account and your position from the comparison. It compares each decision with the risk it carried.

steps.title: Which Did Better?
steps.intro: Compare in R.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Try a few trades and see each result in R.

points: R is the money you risked at the start, used as a unit.
Result in R = result in money ÷ money risked.
R lets you compare trades of different dollar size.
A loss equal to your risk is −1R.

lessons.title: R-Multiples II
lessons.aim: Work out the R of a trade with partial exits, a breakeven stop and costs.

blocks.text: You can close part of a position early and let the rest run. Each piece has its own result in R.
Result = (share closed first × its R) + (share left × its R).

blocks.title: Close half at +1R. The other half finishes at +3R

blocks.text: Moving your stop to your entry means the rest of the trade cannot lose before costs.

blocks.title: Close half at +1R and move the stop to breakeven. The rest is stopped at breakeven
Breakeven Is Not Free
blocks.text: A trade that ends at your entry price still pays the spread and any fees. The result in R is slightly negative.

steps.title: A Trade In Pieces, Step By Step
steps.intro: Work out each piece, then the total.

steps.title: One More
steps.intro: Weight each piece.

points: A trade closed in pieces is a weighted average of its pieces.
A breakeven stop removes the chance of a loss, but not the costs.
Costs come off the result before you write it in R.
R lets you compare trades however they were managed.

lessons.title: Probability For Traders
lessons.aim: Use independence and compound probability, and state the gambler's fallacy precisely.

blocks.text: When results are **independent**, what happened on one trade does not change the chance on the next.
A method that wins 40% of the time has a 40% chance on every trade, whatever came before.
For independent results, the chance that all of them happen is their chances multiplied.

blocks.title: Each trade loses 60% of the time. What is the chance of 3 losses in a row?

blocks.text: The chance of at least one win is 100% minus the chance of losing every time.

blocks.title: Wins 40%. Six trades.
steps: Chance of at least one win: 100% − 4.7% = **95.3%**.

blocks.title: A method wins 40% of the time. Over 50 trades

blocks.text: This is an average. Any one run will differ.

blocks.title: Precisely
blocks.text: Before the trades, five losses in a row was unlikely. Once they have happened, the next trade still has its usual chance. A win is not "due". Independent results have no memory.

steps.title: The Streak Simulator
steps.intro: Twenty identical traders. See how long the losing streaks get.

steps.title: At Least One Win
steps.intro: Use the keypad.

points: For independent results, chances multiply.
At least one win = 100% minus the chance of losing every time.
Expected losses = trades × loss rate.
Past results do not change the next chance. A win is never "due".

lessons.title: Mean, Median And Outliers
lessons.aim: Work out the mean and median of a set of results, and say when they disagree.

blocks.text: The **mean** is the total divided by the number of results. The **median** is the middle result once they are in order.
A single very large result is an **outlier**. It drags the mean a long way. It barely moves the median.
If the mean and the median are far apart, one or two results are doing the work. An average alone can hide that.
Look at the mean, the median and the biggest result together.

steps.title: Move One Trade
steps.intro: Predict, then slide the tenth trade.

steps.title: Find The Mean
steps.intro: Use the − key if negative.

points: Mean = total ÷ count. Median = the middle result.
One big result pulls the mean and barely moves the median.
When they disagree, a few results dominate.
Check both before trusting an average.

lessons.title: Spread And Standard Error
lessons.aim: Measure how spread out results are, and see how many trades an average needs before you can lean on it.

blocks.text: Two methods can have the same average result and feel completely different. One gives steady small results. The other swings between big wins and big losses.
The average does not show that. You need a measure of how **spread out** the results are.
Standard deviation is the typical distance of a result from the mean. The bigger it is, the more spread out the results are.

items: Find the mean.
Find each result's gap from the mean.
Square each gap, so all are positive.
Add the squares.
Divide by n − 1.
Take the square root.

blocks.title: Results in R: −1, 0, +1, +2
steps: For a sample, divide by n − 1 = 3: 5 ÷ 3 = 1.67.

blocks.text: Your trades are a **sample** of everything the method could produce. A small sample rarely catches the extremes, so it understates the spread. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n corrects for that.
Standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n. It tells you how uncertain the AVERAGE is, given n trades.
Four times the trades halves the uncertainty. Doubling the trades does not.

steps.title: Ten Traders, One Method
steps.intro: Predict first. Then see what different sample sizes do to the same method.

blocks.text: The method wins 40% of the time, +2R on a win and −1R on a loss. Its true average is **+0.2R**, and its standard deviation is about **1.47R**.

blocks.title: The uncertainty of its average
steps: At 30 trades: 1.47 ÷ √30 = about **0.27R**. That is bigger than the edge itself.

blocks.text: A small average from a few trades tells you very little. Its margin of error can be as large as the average.

steps.title: Standard Error
steps.intro: Divide by the square root of n.

steps.title: Standard Deviation
steps.intro: Take your time. Follow the steps in the lesson.

points: Standard deviation measures how spread out results are.
Standard error = SD ÷ √n. It measures how uncertain the average is.
Four times the trades halves the standard error.
An average from a few trades can be mostly noise.

lessons.title: Expectancy
lessons.aim: Calculate the average result per trade from a win rate and the size of wins and losses.

blocks.text: **Expectancy** is the average result of one trade, in R, if you took the method many times.
Expectancy = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).
The method that wins most often loses money on average. The method that wins least often makes it. A win rate says nothing on its own.

blocks.title: Expectancy +0.2R. You risk $50 on each trade.
An Average, Not A Trade
blocks.text: No single trade pays $10. The $10 appears only across many trades, and it carries the margin of error you met in the last lesson.
The win rate and the average win and loss in the formula are estimates from past trades. They are only as reliable as the number of trades behind them.
An expectancy from 30 trades is a rough guess. Ask how many trades stand behind it, and how big its standard error is.

steps.title: Use The Calculator
steps.intro: Change the win rate and the payoff. Find a combination with zero expectancy.

steps.title: Expectancy
steps.intro: Use the − key if it is negative.

points: Expectancy = win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss.
It is the average result per trade, in R.
A high win rate can still lose money. Sizes matter as much as frequency.
It is an estimate. Ask how many trades stand behind it.

lessons.title: Break-Even Win Rate And Payoff
lessons.aim: Find the win rate a payoff needs, and the payoff a win rate needs, including costs.

blocks.text: Every reward-to-risk ratio has a win rate at which expectancy is exactly zero. Win more often than that and the method makes money. Win less often and it loses.
Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + reward-to-risk).

items: 0.5 : 1 (a small target) needs **66.7%**.

blocks.text: If you know your win rate, the payoff you need is (1 − w) ÷ w.

blocks.title: A method wins 25% of the time

blocks.text: Rarer wins have to be bigger.

blocks.title: At 2 : 1, costs take 0.1R from every trade
Zero Is Not Break-Even
blocks.text: A method at exactly the theoretical break-even rate loses money once costs are counted. Its real break-even win rate is higher.

steps.title: The Expectancy Table
steps.intro: Find the lowest profitable win rate for each payoff.

steps.title: Break-Even Win Rate
steps.intro: One decimal place.

steps.title: The Payoff You Need
steps.intro: A rarer win has to be bigger.

points: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + payoff). At 2 : 1 it is 33.3%.
The payoff needed = (1 − w) ÷ w. Rarer wins must be bigger.
Costs push the real break-even win rate higher.
A profitable region on a table is not a promise. It only shows what would be needed.

lessons.title: Profit Factor
lessons.aim: Calculate profit factor, read it beside expectancy, and see why a few big winners flatter it.

blocks.text: Profit factor = the total of all winning trades ÷ the total of all losing trades (without the minus sign).

items: **1.0** means the sample broke even.
Above 1 means it made money. Below 1 means it lost money.
Above 1 does not mean the method has an edge. It describes the sample you have.

blocks.text: In the example above the expectancy is (8 − 6) ÷ 10 trades = **+0.2R**. Both say the sample made money.
They answer different questions. Expectancy is R per trade. Profit factor is a ratio with no units. Read them together.

blocks.title: Eight trades: six losses of −1R, and two winners of +6R and +4R
Fragile
blocks.text: A healthy-looking profit factor from few trades can hang on one result. Ask what it becomes without the largest winner.

steps.title: Profit Factor From A List
steps.intro: Total the winners, then the losers.

steps.title: Profit Factor From Rates
steps.intro: Per 100 trades, count the R won and the R lost.

points: Profit factor = total won ÷ total lost.
Above 1 means the sample made money. It says nothing about the future.
Read it beside expectancy and the number of trades.
A few big winners can inflate it. Test it without the largest one.

lessons.title: Drawdown And Recovery
lessons.aim: Measure a drawdown in R and in percent, and calculate the gain needed to recover from it.

blocks.text: A drawdown is a fall from a high point of the balance to a later low point. The maximum drawdown is the biggest such fall.

blocks.title: Results in R: −1, +2, −1, −1, −1, +3
steps: The highest point was +1 (after the second trade). The lowest point after it was −2.

blocks.title: The balance peaked at $10,000, then fell to $7,500

blocks.text: A drawdown is always measured against the PEAK.
Getting back to the peak needs a bigger gain than the fall, because the gain is earned on a smaller balance.
Gain needed = 1 ÷ (1 − fall) − 1.

items: A 10% fall needs **+11.1%**.
A 20% fall needs **+25%**.
A 30% fall needs **+42.9%**.
A 50% fall needs **+100%**.
A 75% fall needs **+300%**.

blocks.title: A 10R drawdown, and each loss is 1R of the current balance

blocks.text: The R drawdown is the same. What it does to your account depends on how much you risk per trade.

steps.title: Build A Drawdown
steps.intro: Make a run of trades that ends ahead but suffers a deep drawdown.

blocks.text: Drawdowns are a normal part of a method with an edge. The question is whether your risk per trade lets you survive one.

steps.title: Gain To Recover
steps.intro: One decimal place.

steps.title: Drawdown From A Run
steps.intro: Track the running total and its highest point.

steps.title: Drawdown In Percent
steps.intro: Against the peak.

points: A drawdown is a fall from a high point. Measure it from the peak.
Maximum drawdown is the biggest such fall in the sample.
The gain needed to recover is bigger than the fall: −50% needs +100%.
The same drawdown in R can be a small or a huge fall in percent, depending on your risk per trade.

lessons.title: Compounding And Position Sizing Over Time
lessons.aim: See how gains and losses compound, and what changes when you risk a percent of the current balance or a fixed dollar amount.

blocks.title: $1,000 grows 10% each month, and the growth stays in the account

blocks.text: Each month's growth is earned on a bigger balance. That is **compounding**.

blocks.title: $10,000. You lose 10% of the CURRENT balance five times in a row
steps: Taking $1,000 from the start each time would leave $5,000.

blocks.text: A percent of a shrinking balance is a smaller and smaller amount. So a run of percent losses cannot take an account exactly to zero. It can still take it a very long way down.

items: **Percent of the current balance**: risk 2% of whatever you have now. Bets grow after wins and shrink after losses.
**Fixed dollars**: risk 2% of the STARTING balance every time. Bets never change.

steps.title: The Same Trades, Two Ways
steps.intro: Run the same 80 trades with both rules and different risks.

steps.title: The Order Of The Same Trades

blocks.title: Four trades at 10% risk: two of −1R and two of +1.5R
steps: Order −, −, +, +: the balance ends at $10,712 and the worst fall was **19%**.
Order −, +, −, +: the same $10,712, and the worst fall was **10%**.

blocks.text: With a percent of the current balance, the final balance does not depend on the order. The worst drawdown does.

blocks.title: A Projection Is Not A Promise
blocks.text: A projection that grows 5% a month for ten years assumes the edge is real, constant and correctly measured. None of that is known. Use compounding to understand risk, not to promise growth.

steps.title: Growth On Growth
steps.intro: Round to the nearest dollar.

steps.title: Losses On Losses
steps.intro: Each loss is a percent of what is left.

points: Compounding earns growth on growth, and takes losses out of a shrinking balance.
A percent of the current balance grows after wins and shrinks after losses.
The final balance does not depend on the order of the trades. The drawdown does.
A compounding projection assumes the edge is real. Use it to understand risk.

lessons.title: Risk Of Ruin
lessons.aim: Define ruin, see how risk per trade changes the chance of it, and say what a simulated number can and cannot tell you.

blocks.text: "Ruin" has no single meaning. Before you calculate its chance you must say what it is. In this lesson, ruin is **a drawdown of a size you choose**, such as 30% or 50%.
You could also define it as the drawdown at which you would stop trading.
How many losses in a row, each a percent of the current balance, does it take to reach a 30% drawdown?

items: At 1% risk: **36** losses.
At 2% risk: **18** losses.
At 5% risk: **7** losses.
At 10% risk: **4** losses.

blocks.text: Halve the risk and you roughly double the number of losses it takes.

items: The **win rate**.
The **payoff**: the size of wins against the size of losses.
The **risk per trade**.

blocks.text: The first two come from the method and can only be estimated. The third is entirely yours.

steps.title: The Ruin Explorer
steps.intro: Predict first. Then run the simulation.

blocks.text: The simulation plays the method many times, assuming the win rate and payoff you type in are TRUE. Real ones are estimates with a standard error.
A simulated chance of ruin is a way to compare settings, not a forecast. The same method can look safe or dangerous depending on what you assumed.
This program starts with a **1% cap** on the risk in any one trade. The cap is a starting default. You can change it in Settings, and this lesson shows what you would be changing.

steps.title: Losses To A Drawdown
steps.intro: Round up to the first whole number that gets there.

points: Define ruin before you calculate it, for example a 30% drawdown.
The risk per trade is the lever you control, and it changes the chance of ruin a lot.
A simulation is only as good as the win rate and payoff you feed it.
The 1% cap is an editable default.

lessons.title: The Expectancy Lab
lessons.aim: Work out every statistic for a run of trades by hand, and say what the statistics do and do not show.

blocks.text: You are given forty trades in order. Work out the statistics yourself, using the calculators from the lessons. The engine then checks each one.

items: The number of winners and the win rate.
The expectancy in R.
The profit factor.
The maximum drawdown in R.
The longest losing streak.

blocks.text: A wrong answer is information. Find out where the working went astray.

steps.title: The Forty Trades
steps.intro: Do it by hand first. Check after.

steps.title: A Mixed Set
steps.intro: Eight questions drawn from the whole level.

steps.title: Questions To Ask
steps.prompt: A friend shows you 25 trades with a profit factor of 2.1 and an expectancy of +0.6R. Write the questions you would ask before you believed it.
rubric: Asks how many trades stand behind it, and what the standard error is.
Asks what the results are without the largest winners.
Asks whether costs and realistic fills were included.
Asks whether the rules were fixed before the results were seen.
Asks about the drawdown, not only the average.
steps.modelAnswer: Twenty-five trades is a small sample, so the standard error of that +0.6R is probably large. I would ask what the profit factor is without the biggest winner, whether costs and realistic fills were in the numbers, and whether the rules were written down before the trades were taken. I would also ask for the maximum drawdown, because an average says nothing about how bad the worst stretch was.

points: Expectancy, profit factor and drawdown answer different questions. Read them together.
Every statistic comes with the question: how many trades?
A wrong figure in the lab is a signal to find the slip in your working.
Level 5 is the arithmetic. Later levels use it to judge evidence.

lessons.title: What A Chart Shows
lessons.aim: Say what the lines and candles on a chart record, and what they cannot tell you.

blocks.text: A price chart has time across the bottom and price up the side. Each point says: at this time, price traded here.
Prices arrive one at a time as trades happen. These arrivals are called **ticks**. A chart is a way to see a great many ticks at once.

steps.title: One Market, Three Drawings
steps.intro: Twenty ticks, drawn as a line, as bars and as candles.

items: A **line** joins single prices. It shows the path and hides nothing, but it is crowded.
A **bar** groups ticks and keeps four prices: open, high, low, close.
A **candle** keeps the same four prices as a bar and draws them so that the body is easy to see.

blocks.text: A chart shows where price traded. That is a record of the past.
Saying "it is trending" or "it is stuck" is an interpretation of that record.
Saying "it will keep going" is a hypothesis. A chart cannot confirm it.

blocks.title: The Right-Hand Edge
blocks.text: Everything to the right of the last candle is unknown. A pattern that looks obvious on the left was chosen with the help of what came after it.

points: A chart is a record of prices against time.
Lines, bars and candles are three ways to draw the same ticks.
What a chart shows is an observation. What it means is an interpretation. What comes next is a hypothesis.

lessons.title: Timeframes
lessons.aim: Combine small candles into a bigger one by hand, and say why the same market looks different at different timeframes.

blocks.text: Every candle covers a fixed length of time: a minute, fifteen minutes, an hour, a day. That length is the **timeframe**.
A 15-minute chart draws one candle for every 15 minutes of trading.

steps.title: The Same Market, Four Ways
steps.intro: Tap between timeframes. Only the size of each candle changes.

blocks.text: A bigger candle = the FIRST open, the HIGHEST high, the LOWEST low and the LAST close of the smaller candles inside it.

blocks.title: Three 5-minute candles (pips above 1.10000): O10 H16 L8 C14, then O14 H19 L12 C17, then O17 H18 L11 C13

blocks.text: A daily candle is 24 hours of trading, but WHEN the day starts is a choice. One platform may cut days at midnight in its own server time. Another may cut them at 5 p.m. New York time.

blocks.title: Two Platforms, Two Daily Candles
blocks.text: Because the cut differs, the same market can show a different daily open, high, low and close on two platforms. Neither is wrong. Always ask which anchor a chart is using.

steps.title: How Many Fit?
steps.intro: Divide the longer period by the shorter one.

steps.title: Combine Three Candles
steps.intro: First open, highest high, lowest low, last close.

points: Each candle covers a fixed interval: the timeframe.
A bigger candle = first open, highest high, lowest low, last close.
Where a day starts depends on the platform's day anchor.

lessons.title: The Candlestick: Open, High, Low, Close
lessons.aim: Build a candle from a list of prices, and say what each of its four numbers records.

blocks.text: A candle keeps four prices from its interval: the OPEN (first), the HIGH (highest), the LOW (lowest) and the CLOSE (last).

steps.title: Build A Candle
steps.intro: Nine prices arrive one at a time. Watch the four numbers change.

blocks.text: The candle does not keep the ORDER of the prices between the open and the close. It does not keep how many times price turned. It does not say whether the high came before the low.

blocks.title: A Summary
blocks.text: Four numbers stand in for hundreds of ticks. The next lessons use them carefully.

steps.title: Find A Price
steps.intro: Read the six prices in order.

points: A candle records the open, high, low and close of an interval.
The open is the first price and the close is the last.
The high and low can come at any point in between.

lessons.title: Body And Wicks
lessons.aim: Measure the body, the wicks and the range of a candle in pips, and work out the body ratio.

items: The **body** runs from the open to the close. Its length is |close − open|.
The **upper wick** runs from the top of the body to the high.
The **lower wick** runs from the bottom of the body down to the low.
The **range** runs from the low to the high, wicks included.

blocks.text: Two candles of different size can have the same shape. A ratio compares the parts with the range.
Body ratio = body ÷ range. In the example: 6 ÷ 14 = 43%.
A small body ratio means most of the range is wick. A body ratio near 100% means there are almost no wicks.

steps.title: Measure A Candle
steps.intro: Range, body or a wick, in pips.

steps.title: Body Ratio
steps.intro: Body ÷ range, as a percent.

points: Body = |close − open|. Range = high − low. Wicks are the rest.
Body ratio = body ÷ range.
The range equals the body plus the two wicks.

lessons.title: Bullish And Bearish Candles
lessons.aim: Describe a candle as bullish, bearish or a doji using stated rules, and treat colours as a convention.

blocks.text: A candle is BULLISH if the close is above the open, BEARISH if the close is below the open.
These are words for what the candle did. They do not say who is in control or what happens next.
This app draws bullish candles teal and bearish candles rose. Other platforms use green and red, or white and black, or hollow and filled. The choice is arbitrary.
You can switch the app to hollow bullish candles in the chart controls. The information is identical.
When the body is tiny compared with the range, the open and close are almost the same. Calling it bullish or bearish would say more than the candle does.
In this course a candle is a **doji** when its body is 10% of its range or less.

blocks.title: A Rule, Not A Law
blocks.text: Some traders use 5% and some use 15%. What matters is that you state the rule. A different threshold changes which candles you call a doji.

steps.title: Describe The Candle
steps.intro: Compare close with open, then check the 10% rule.

points: Bullish: close above open. Bearish: close below open.
A doji has a body of 10% of the range or less (in this course).
Colours are a convention and the words describe, they do not predict.

lessons.title: Candles Are Summaries, Not Signals
lessons.aim: Explain why many different tick paths make the same candle, and turn a named candle pattern into a testable hypothesis.

steps.title: One Candle, Many Paths
steps.intro: Predict first. Then see three paths that make exactly the same candle.

blocks.text: A candle keeps four numbers. Any path that starts at the open, touches the high and low and ends at the close makes the same candle.
The candle tells you the four prices. It does not tell you the order in which the high and the low happened.
Traders give names to shapes.

items: A **hammer** has a small body and a long lower wick.
A **doji** has a tiny body.
An **engulfing** candle has a body that covers the one before.

blocks.text: A name is a **label** for a shape. Each one can be defined with ratios, like the doji rule.
Some traders say a hammer marks a turn upwards. That is a HYPOTHESIS about what follows a shape. This course makes no claim that it is true.
To test one, you must do four things.

items: Define the shape exactly, with numbers.
Count every time it occurred.
Record what price did afterwards, over a fixed horizon.
Compare that with what price does after ANY candle.

blocks.title: Stories Are Cheap
blocks.text: It is easy to remember the times a pattern worked. The times it did not are forgotten. Only counting every occurrence shows whether it means anything.

steps.title: A Testable Hypothesis
steps.prompt: Pick one named candle pattern. Write it as a testable hypothesis: define the shape with numbers, say what you think follows and over how many bars, and describe the test you would run.
rubric: Defines the shape with measurable rules (for example a body ratio and a wick length).
States what should follow and over what horizon.
Says to count EVERY occurrence, not only remembered ones.
Says what to compare it with (what usually follows any candle).
Says what result would make you reject the hypothesis.
steps.modelAnswer: Hammer: a candle whose lower wick is at least twice its body, with a body ratio under 35% and almost no upper wick. Hypothesis: the close of the fifth bar after a hammer is higher than the hammer's close more often than after any other candle. Test: find every hammer in a large sample, note whether bar five closed higher, and compare the share with the same share for all candles. If the share is about the same, or the sample is too small to tell, I reject the hypothesis.

points: A candle keeps four numbers and throws the path away.
Named candle patterns are labels for shapes.
What follows a pattern is a hypothesis: define it, count every case and compare with a baseline.

lessons.title: Consolidation And Expansion
lessons.aim: Label stretches of a chart as contraction or expansion by comparing candle ranges, and see why the threshold matters.

blocks.text: Charts alternate between stretches of small candles and stretches of large candles. Traders call the first **consolidation** and the second **expansion**.
Those words are vague until they are measured. Measure them with the candle range you already know.
Compare a stretch's average candle range with the average range over the whole chart. Below 0.7 of it is a **contraction**. Above 1.4 times it is an **expansion**. In between is normal.

blocks.title: A chart whose candles average 10 pips
A stretch averages 7.5 pips on a chart that averages 10
steps: With a 0.8 threshold it is a **contraction**.

blocks.title: Different Definitions, Different Counts
blocks.text: Two people can look at the same chart and count a different number of contractions, and both be right under their own rule. State the rule before you count.

steps.title: Direction Is Not Part Of It

blocks.text: Expansion means large candles, not rising prices. A big fall is an expansion too. The test looks only at the size of the ranges.

steps.title: Label The Stretches
steps.intro: Compare each stretch with the whole chart.

points: Compare a stretch's average candle range with the chart's average.
Below 0.7 is a contraction and above 1.4 is an expansion (in this course).
Change the threshold and the count changes, so state it.

lessons.title: Impulse And Correction
lessons.aim: Mark an impulse and its correction, and measure the retracement as a percentage of the impulse.

blocks.text: Price rarely moves in a straight line. A move in one direction is an **impulse**. The move back against it is a **correction**.
In this course an impulse is the leg between two swings, and a correction is the counter-leg. The words say nothing about strength unless a threshold is stated.
Label three points. **A** is where the impulse starts. **B** is where it ends. **C** is where the correction ends.
Retracement = (B − C) ÷ (B − A), the part of the impulse the correction gave back.
Traders talk about corrections of 38.2%, 50% and 61.8% of the impulse. Those are figures people chose. This course makes no claim that price respects them.
That price tends to turn at certain retracement levels is a hypothesis. It can be tested by counting.

steps.title: Measure The Correction
steps.intro: Read B − C and B − A from the chart.

points: An impulse is a leg between swings, a correction is the counter-leg.
Retracement = (B − C) ÷ (B − A).
Common retracement levels are figures people chose. Whether price respects them is a hypothesis.

lessons.title: Swing Highs And Swing Lows
lessons.aim: Find swing highs and lows under a stated size, and tell a confirmed swing from a provisional one.

blocks.text: Swings are the turning points of a chart. To find them the same way every time, they need a definition.
A **swing high** of size n is a candle whose high is above the highs of the n candles before it. It is also at least as high as the n candles after it.
A **swing low** is the mirror: its low is below the lows of the n candles on each side.
You cannot know that a high is a swing high until n more candles have closed after it. Only then is it **confirmed**. Until then it is the newest extreme, and it is **provisional**.

blocks.title: A swing high of size 3 forms at bar 40
steps: It needs bars 41, 42 and 43 to close without going higher.
It is confirmed at the close of bar **43**.

blocks.title: No Hindsight
blocks.text: If you mark the newest extreme as a swing, you are using knowledge you do not have. A later candle could beat it and it would never have been a swing.

steps.title: Change The Size, Then Step Forward
steps.intro: Compare swing sizes. Then step forward one bar at a time and watch a swing get confirmed.
steps.labIntro: Teal columns are confirmed swings. Blue dotted columns are provisional.

blocks.text: A smaller n finds more swings and finds them sooner, but includes small wiggles. A larger n finds only the bigger turns and confirms them later. Neither is right. Each exercise states its n.

steps.title: When Is It Confirmed?
steps.intro: The bar number is the swing plus n.

steps.title: Latest Confirmed Swing
steps.intro: Tap the candle, then Mark. Use the arrows for a precise pick.

steps.title: Every Swing
steps.intro: Mark all of them. Do not mark the newest extreme.

points: A swing high beats n highs on each side. A swing low mirrors it.
A swing is confirmed n bars after it forms. The newest extreme is provisional.
Marking a provisional swing is hindsight. The size n is stated in every exercise.

lessons.title: Higher Highs, Higher Lows, Lower Highs, Lower Lows
lessons.aim: Label a sequence of swings by comparing each with the previous swing of the same kind.

items: **HH**: a swing high above the previous swing high.
**LH**: a swing high below the previous swing high.
**HL**: a swing low above the previous swing low.
**LL**: a swing low below the previous swing low.

blocks.title: Swing highs 1.1050 then 1.1080. Swing lows 1.1010 then 1.1030
steps: The second high is above the first: **HH**.
The second low is above the first: **HL**.

blocks.title: Same Kind Only
blocks.text: A high is compared with the previous HIGH, never with the low just before it. The most common mistake is comparing a swing with its neighbour.
A run of HH and HL is what the swings did.
That it will continue is a hypothesis.

steps.title: Label The Swings
steps.intro: Tap a letter to see the swing. Compare with the previous swing of the same kind.

points: HH and LH compare highs. HL and LL compare lows.
Always compare a swing with the previous swing of the same kind.
A sequence of labels describes what happened. It does not forecast.

lessons.title: Trends And Ranges
lessons.aim: Classify a chart as bullish, bearish, range or unclear from its last swings, and accept that "unclear" is a real answer.

blocks.text: Take the last two swing highs and the last two swing lows. If both are rising: **bullish**. If both are falling: **bearish**. If both are about level: **range**. Anything else: **unclear**.
"About level" needs a number. In this course two swings are level when they differ by no more than 15% of the size of the recent swing range.

blocks.title: Highs 1.2000 and 1.2010, lows 1.1900 and 1.1895
steps: Swing range: 1.2010 − 1.1895 = 0.0115. Tolerance: 15% of that is 0.0017.
Highs differ by 0.0010 and lows by 0.0005, both inside 0.0017: a **range**.

blocks.text: Sometimes the highs rise while the lows fall (a widening swing), or the highs fall while the lows rise (a narrowing one). The two comparisons disagree, so no structure can be called.

blocks.title: Do Not Force It
blocks.text: Calling every chart bullish or bearish is a habit, not an analysis. Unclear is graded as seriously as any other answer, and it is the right answer when the swings disagree.

steps.title: Read The Structure
steps.intro: Classify, then tap the four swings you used.

steps.title: Read Another
steps.intro: The swings are confirmed swings only.

points: Compare the last two swing highs and the last two swing lows.
Rising: bullish. Falling: bearish. Level: range. Mixed: unclear.
Unclear is a real answer, and forcing a call is a mistake.

lessons.title: Breakouts And Pullbacks
lessons.aim: Find a breakout under a stated convention, and see how the convention changes what you count.

blocks.text: A **breakout** is price going beyond a level it had not gone beyond before. To count breakouts the same way twice, you must say what "beyond" means.
Close convention: a breakout is the FIRST bar that CLOSES beyond the level. Wick convention: the first bar whose high (or low) trades beyond it.

steps.title: A Bar That Only Pokes Through

blocks.title: Resistance at 1.2000. One bar reaches 1.2012 but closes at 1.1994
steps: Wick convention: a breakout. The high traded above.
Close convention: **not** a breakout. The bar closed back under.

blocks.text: A **pullback** is a counter-move against the last move that has not broken the structure it moved against.
A counter-move that DOES break the structure is not a pullback. It is a break of structure, which Level 7 covers.
A breakout under a stated rule is something you can find on the chart.
That breakouts keep going, or that they fail, is a hypothesis. The chart does not settle it.

steps.title: Find The Breakout
steps.intro: Close convention: the first CLOSE beyond the line.

steps.title: Two Conventions
steps.intro: The rule changes from question to question. Read it.

points: A breakout is beyond a stated level under a stated convention.
A close convention and a wick convention can give different bars and different counts.
A pullback does not break structure. A breakout does not predict.

lessons.title: Chart Reading Lab I (Guided)
lessons.aim: Read six charts with the routine from this level, using hints when you need them.

items: Read the definitions on the chart: the swing size, and the convention.
Find the CONFIRMED swings only. The newest extreme is provisional.
Compare each swing with the previous one of the same kind.
Classify the last two of each kind: rising, falling, level, or mixed.
Say what would change your reading.

blocks.text: You do not need to predict anything. You are describing the chart under a stated rule, so that anyone applying the rule would get the same answer.

After a wrong answer you get a **question** to think about, not the answer. If you are still off, the region to look at is shaded and the definition is quoted. After that the answer is shown, and that chart comes back later.

blocks.title: Hints Cost Credit
blocks.text: A hint used still lets you learn, but full credit is for answers that did not need one. Use them when you need them.

steps.title: Six Guided Charts
steps.intro: Work through them in order. Tap a candle, use the arrows for precision, then Mark.

points: Read the definition, use confirmed swings, compare like with like, classify from the last two of each.
Hints ask questions before they give answers.
Describing a chart under a rule is different from predicting it.

lessons.title: Chart Reading Lab II (Unguided)
lessons.aim: Read eight charts with no hints and no feedback until you finish.

blocks.text: This set is like the exam: no hints and no answers until you have finished. Every chart states its own swing size and convention. Read them first.

blocks.title: Before you begin
steps: What is the swing size, and is it stated on the chart?
Am I marking anything that is not yet confirmed?

steps.title: Eight Unguided Charts
steps.intro: Answer each one, then see how you did.

points: Read the stated definition first, on every chart.
Mark only confirmed swings.
Unclear is a valid answer when the swings disagree.

lessons.title: Why Structure?
lessons.aim: Describe a chart in three separate layers, so that two people would agree on the first layer.

blocks.text: Ask two traders to describe the same chart and you may hear "strong uptrend" and "choppy". Both are looking at the same prices. They are describing different things.
Structure is a way to describe a chart so that two people would agree.

items: **Observation**: the confirmed swings and their order. Anyone can check it.
**Interpretation**: what you say the observation means now, such as "bullish".
**Hypothesis**: what you think will happen next, such as "it will continue".

blocks.text: The last two swing highs were 1.2050 and 1.2080.
The structure is bullish.
The structure will stay bullish.
The observation is the only layer the chart proves. The interpretation depends on a rule you stated. The hypothesis depends on things the chart cannot show.

blocks.title: Blurring The Layers
blocks.text: When a hypothesis is stated as if it were an observation ("price is going up"), a wrong guess feels like being betrayed by the market. Stating the layer keeps you honest.

points: A reading has three layers: observation, interpretation, hypothesis.
Only the observation is proved by the chart.
Say which layer each statement belongs to.

lessons.title: Swing Points And Structural Points
lessons.aim: Tell an order-1 swing from a structural one, and see why the scale is a convention.

blocks.text: At swing size 2 a chart can have a dozen swings. Some are small wiggles inside a bigger move. You often want the bigger turns only.
A second pass gives you those.
**Order-1 swings** are the swings of size n from Level 6. **Structural (order-2) swings** are the order-1 swings that stand beyond their neighbours of the same kind.

blocks.title: Order-1 highs: 1.2000, 1.2040, 1.2020
steps: The middle one (1.2040) is above both neighbours: it is a **structural high**.
The first and the last are not above both neighbours: they are not.

steps.title: Order 1 And Order 2
steps.intro: Switch between the two. Watch how many swings remain.
steps.labIntro: Teal columns are confirmed swings. Order 2 keeps only the larger turns.

blocks.text: Order 2 is not a law. It is the scale this course uses to say "structural". A different trader might use a bigger n, or a third pass. What matters is that the exercise states which.

blocks.title: State The Scale
blocks.text: The same chart has different structural swings at 5 minutes than at 1 hour. Always name the timeframe and the rule.

steps.title: The Latest Structural Swing
steps.intro: Tap the candle, then Mark.

steps.title: Every Structural Swing
steps.intro: Use the order-2 rule.

points: Order-1 swings are the size-n swings. Structural swings stand beyond their neighbours of the same kind.
Order 2 keeps the bigger turns.
The scale is a convention. Always name it.

lessons.title: Confirmed And Unconfirmed Highs And Lows
lessons.aim: Separate what is confirmed from what is provisional at the live edge, and see how labels change as new candles arrive.

blocks.text: The newest high on a chart looks like a swing high. But a swing needs candles after it. Until they arrive, that high is **provisional**.
The newest extreme is always provisional at the live edge.

Suppose you look at an old chart and mark every peak as a swing. You did that with the whole chart in front of you. At the time, the peak was only the newest high, and it might not have become a swing at all.

blocks.title: Hindsight Flatters
blocks.text: An analysis that uses later candles looks better than one you could have made at the time. In this course, every reference answer is computed as of the decision bar, and yours should be too.

steps.title: Step To The Live Edge
steps.intro: Move one bar at a time. Watch swings appear and change.
steps.labIntro: Teal columns are confirmed. Blue dotted columns are provisional.

blocks.text: As you stepped forward, provisional columns became confirmed, and some disappeared because a higher candle took their place. That is what "provisional" means. It is a candidate that the next candles can promote or discard.

steps.title: The Latest Confirmed Swing
steps.intro: Do not tap the newest extreme.

points: The newest extreme is provisional until n more candles have closed.
Labelling with later candles is look-ahead bias.
Every reading is made as of a bar, never with the future in view.

lessons.title: Bullish Structure
lessons.aim: Recognise a bullish structure from confirmed structural swings, and name the low that holds it up.

blocks.text: A structure is **bullish** when the last two confirmed structural highs are rising AND the last two confirmed structural lows are rising.
Both must rise. If only the highs rise, the structure is unclear.
In a bullish structure the latest confirmed structural low is the swing that "holds" the sequence up. If price closes below it, the sequence of higher lows has ended.
That low is the level that would invalidate the bullish description.
The structural highs and lows are rising.
The structure is bullish.
It will make another higher high. This course makes no claim that it will.

steps.title: Bullish Or Not?
steps.intro: Classify, then tap the four swings you used.

steps.title: Where Is The Low That Holds?
steps.intro: The invalidation is the latest structural low.

points: Bullish: the last two structural highs AND lows are rising.
The latest structural low is the level that holds it.
Bullish is a description. It is not a promise.

lessons.title: Bearish Structure
lessons.aim: Recognise a bearish structure from confirmed structural swings, and name the high that holds it down.

blocks.text: A structure is **bearish** when the last two confirmed structural highs are falling AND the last two confirmed structural lows are falling.
It is the mirror of the bullish case. The same rules apply, including "unclear" when the two comparisons disagree.
In a bearish structure the latest confirmed structural high is the swing that holds the sequence down. A close above it ends the sequence of lower highs.
That high is the level that would invalidate the bearish description.
Nothing about bearish structure is special. The same definition, run in reverse. A trader who reads bullish charts well but stumbles on bearish ones is reading by feel, not by the rule.

items: Find the confirmed structural swings.
Compare the last two highs and the last two lows.
Both falling: bearish.
Name the high that holds it.

steps.title: Bearish Or Not?
steps.intro: Classify, then tap the four swings you used.

steps.title: Where Is The High That Holds?
steps.intro: The invalidation is the latest structural high.

points: Bearish: the last two structural highs AND lows are falling.
The latest structural high is the level that holds it down.
Bullish and bearish follow one rule, mirrored.

lessons.title: Range Structure
lessons.aim: Recognise a range with a stated tolerance, tell it from an early trend, and say "unclear" when it is borderline.

blocks.text: A structure is a **range** when the last two structural highs are about level AND the last two structural lows are about level. The highs form the top boundary and the lows the bottom.

blocks.title: Highs 1.2000 and 1.2008. Lows 1.1900 and 1.1902
steps: The highs differ by 0.0008 and the lows by 0.0002, both inside 0.0016: a **range**.

blocks.text: A range and the start of a trend can look alike. The rule decides, not the feeling. When one comparison sits close to the tolerance, the case is **borderline**, and "unclear" is an accepted answer.

blocks.title: The Edge Cases
blocks.text: A difference just inside the tolerance and one just outside can look the same on a chart. That is why the rule, and not your eye, decides.

steps.title: Range Or Not?
steps.intro: Classify, then tap the four swings you used.

points: A range: the last two structural highs and lows are each about level.
"About level" means within a stated tolerance: 15% of the swing range here.
A borderline case is unclear.

lessons.title: Break Of Structure
lessons.aim: Find breaks of structure under a close convention and a wick convention, and tell a continuation from a shift.

blocks.text: A **break of structure** (BOS) is the first bar that CLOSES beyond the latest confirmed structural swing.
Only the swings that were confirmed before that bar count. The rule is applied one bar at a time.

items: A break in the direction of the structure is a **continuation**: in a bullish structure, a close above the latest structural high.
A break against it is a **shift**: in a bullish structure, a close below the latest structural low.

blocks.title: The latest structural high is 1.2100
steps: A bar closes at 1.2104: a break by **close**.
Another bar reaches 1.2103 but closes at 1.2096: a break by **wick** only.

blocks.title: Both Conventions Are Shown
blocks.text: Under the wick convention the count is higher or equal. Say which convention you use before you count.
A bar closed beyond the latest structural high.
That it will keep going, or that it will fail, is a hypothesis.

steps.title: Find The Breaks
steps.intro: The convention is on the chart.

steps.title: Two Conventions
steps.intro: Read which convention this one uses.

points: A BOS is the first close beyond the latest confirmed structural swing.
With the structure it is a continuation. Against it, a shift.
The wick convention can find more breaks. State the convention.

lessons.title: Structural Shifts And Invalidation
lessons.aim: Name the level that invalidates a structure, and keep a shift (a description) apart from a reversal (a hypothesis).

blocks.text: **Invalidation** is the level whose break ends the current description. In a bullish structure it is the latest confirmed structural low. In a bearish one it is the latest structural high. In a range it is either boundary.
A bar closed below the latest structural low of a bullish structure. That is a **shift**.
The market has reversed and will fall. That is a **reversal**, and it is a hypothesis.
The shift is a fact about the record. The reversal is a guess about the future.

Before you know what happens, write two: one in which the invalidation level holds, and one in which it breaks. Say what each would look like on the chart. You are not choosing one. You are stating what would tell you which one is happening.

steps.title: Find The Invalidation
steps.intro: Tap the candle that holds the structure.

steps.title: Two Scenarios
steps.prompt: A chart is bullish. Its latest confirmed structural low is at 1.2000 and its latest structural high is at 1.2100. Write two scenarios: one where the structure holds and one where it is invalidated. Say what would show you which one is happening.
rubric: Names 1.2000, the latest structural low, as the invalidation level.
Uses a close (or states the convention) rather than a touch.
Describes a scenario where higher lows continue.
Describes a scenario where a close below 1.2000 ends the bullish description.
Keeps the shift (a fact) apart from a reversal (a guess).
steps.modelAnswer: Scenario one: price pulls back but holds above 1.2000, a new structural low forms above it, and the structure stays bullish. Scenario two: a bar closes below 1.2000. Under the close convention the bullish description ends. That would be a shift, and it would tell me the higher-low sequence is over. It would not tell me that price will keep falling, so I would re-read the structure from the new swings rather than assume a reversal.

points: Invalidation is the level whose break ends the current description.
A shift is a fact about the record. A reversal is a guess.
Write both scenarios before you know which one is happening.

lessons.title: Multi-Timeframe Structure
lessons.aim: Read the structure on two timeframes, and state a conflict without turning it into a signal.

steps.title: Each Timeframe Has Its Own Structure

blocks.text: The 1-hour chart is built from 15-minute candles. Each chart has its own swings and its own structure. They can agree or disagree.

steps.title: The Same Candles, Two Scales
steps.intro: Compare the readings on the three charts.

items: Name each timeframe.
State the structure on each, with the swings you used.
Say whether they agree.
Do not average them, and do not pick the one you prefer.

blocks.title: Example
steps: 1 hour: bullish (the last two structural highs and lows are rising).
15 minute: bearish (the last two are falling).
**They conflict**: the smaller scale is moving against the larger.

blocks.title: Not A Signal
blocks.text: A difference between timeframes is information about the two time scales. It says nothing about which one price will follow.

points: Each timeframe has its own structure.
State each reading with its timeframe and say whether they agree.
A conflict is a description, not a signal.

lessons.title: Structure Lab I: Identify Swings
lessons.aim: Find the most recent confirmed swings, and every structural swing, on six charts.

blocks.text: "Identify the most recent confirmed swing high or low." Every chart states its own swing size and order. Read them.

items: Find the order-1 swings.
Keep only the ones beyond their neighbours (order 2).
Ignore the newest extreme: it is provisional.
Tap the latest one that is left.

steps.title: Six Charts With Hints
steps.intro: Hints ask a question first. The region is shaded only if you need it.

points: Order 1 first, then order 2, ignoring the provisional extreme.
The latest structural swing is the one to tap.
Read the stated size and order on every chart.
