lessons.title: Structure Lab II: Classify With Evidence
lessons.aim: Classify six charts as bullish, bearish, range or unclear, and show the swings that support the answer.

blocks.text: "Is this market structurally bullish, bearish, ranging or unclear?" An answer without evidence is not an answer. Tap the four swings you used.

items: Two rising highs and lows: bullish.
Two falling: bearish.
Both level within the tolerance: range.
Anything else: unclear.

blocks.title: Unclear Is Graded Seriously
blocks.text: If the swings disagree, "unclear" is the right answer, and it scores exactly like any other right answer.

steps.title: Six Charts With Evidence
steps.intro: Classify, then tap the last two highs and the last two lows.

points: Classify from the last two confirmed structural highs and lows.
Show the four swings you used.
Unclear is a real answer.

lessons.title: Structure Lab III: Invalidation And Shifts
lessons.aim: Name the level that ends a structure, and find breaks under a stated convention, on six charts.

blocks.text: "Which price movement invalidates the current structure?" First classify the structure. Then name the level that holds it. Then find where, if anywhere, it was broken.

blocks.title: The routine
steps: Bullish: the latest structural low holds it.
Bearish: the latest structural high holds it.
A close beyond that level ends the description (under the close convention).

steps.title: Six Charts On Breaks
steps.intro: Invalidation, breaks and full structure sets.

points: Classify, name the holding level, then look for the break.
A close beyond the level ends the description.
What comes after a shift is a separate question.

lessons.title: Structure Lab IV: Analysis At The Live Edge
lessons.aim: Analyse a chart with the future hidden, commit, and only then look at what came next.

items: The future is hidden. You will not see it until you commit.
State the structure. Mark the latest confirmed structural high and low. Mark what would invalidate the structure.
Write what would change your view.
Commit. Then the next bars are revealed, six at a time.

blocks.text: Your score is for the reading. It does not depend on what price did after.
If you look at the answer before you decide, you learn nothing about whether your method works. Deciding first, then looking, is how you find out.

blocks.title: Outcomes Are Neutral
blocks.text: A good reading can be followed by a break. A poor one can be followed by a continuation. One result does not grade the reading.

steps.title: Read The Live Edge
steps.intro: Analyse, write, commit, then reveal.

points: At the live edge: state, mark, write what would change your view, then commit.
The reveal is neutral. Judge the reading, not the result.
A break of your invalidation level is what you said you would watch for.

lessons.title: Technical Analysis As A Descriptive Framework
lessons.aim: Use price, time and levels to describe a market, and sort what you say into observation, interpretation, hypothesis and evidence.

blocks.text: This course uses three inputs: **price**, **time** and **levels**. It uses no indicators. The only chart tool it adds is the Session Levels overlay, which draws reference lines and never signals.

items: **Price**: what traded.
**Time**: when it traded, and on whose clock.
**Levels**: prices that matter to people, such as previous highs and lows.

steps.title: What It Can And Cannot Do

blocks.text: Analysis can describe what price did at a level or in a session.
Analysis can state a claim about the future in a form that can be tested.

blocks.title: It Cannot Promise
blocks.text: No description of the past tells you what the next candle will do. If it seems to, a hypothesis has been stated as if it were a fact.

items: **Observation**: something checked directly against the recorded prices.
**Interpretation**: a judgement about what the observation means, using a rule you can state.
**Hypothesis**: a claim about what will happen, or about a general pattern, that has not been tested.
**Evidence**: a result from a stated test with a stated sample.

blocks.title: And two more
steps: Hypothesis: "Closes above previous highs are followed by further rises."
Evidence: "In 80 such cases, 47 were followed by a higher close 10 bars later. After any bar, the figure was 51 of 80."

blocks.text: The last one is only evidence that this test found nothing special. It is about a sample, not about tomorrow.

steps.title: Name The Label
steps.intro: One statement at a time.

points: This course uses price, time and levels, and no indicators.
Sort what you say into observation, interpretation, hypothesis or evidence.
Description is the job. Promising the future is not.

lessons.title: Observation, Hypothesis, Test, Result, Conclusion
lessons.aim: Follow a belief through the five steps, and write vague beliefs as testable hypotheses.

items: **Observation**: what you noticed.
**Hypothesis**: a claim written so that a count could refute it.
**Test**: exactly what you will count, over what sample, against what baseline.
**Result**: the numbers.
**Conclusion**: what the result does and does not support.

blocks.text: Belief: "Price reverses at the previous day's high." The figures below are INVENTED to show the shape of a conclusion. They are not real results.

blocks.title: The first three steps
steps: Observation: on 3 of the 4 days I looked at, price turned near the previous day's high.
Hypothesis: within 12 bars of a visit, price moves 10 pips away before any close beyond the high, more often than at a random level.
Test: every day in a 90-day sample, every visit counted, compared with 300 random levels.

blocks.title: The last two steps (invented figures)
steps: Result: 39 of 63 visits reacted (62%). Random levels: median 58%, top 10% at 71%.
Conclusion: 62% sits inside the range random levels produce, so the test does **not** support the hypothesis. The honest conclusion is "insufficient evidence".

blocks.text: A conclusion of "no support" or "not enough data" is a real, useful result. It tells you not to trade on the belief yet. Nothing was wasted.

blocks.title: The Flip Side
blocks.text: Finding support in one sample is not proof either. The next sample can disagree. Each conclusion is about the sample tested.

steps.title: Hypothesis Writer
steps.prompt: Turn each vague belief into a testable hypothesis: (1) "London breakouts are strong." (2) "Support holds." (3) "Price gets pulled to obvious highs." For each, say what you would count, over what sample, and what you would compare it with.
rubric: Defines each key word with a number or a rule (for example, "strong" as a move of a stated size within a stated time).
Says what is counted, and that EVERY occurrence is counted.
Names a baseline to compare with (random levels, other sessions, any bar).
States a sample size or time period.
Says what result would make the hypothesis fail.
steps.modelAnswer: (1) Hypothesis: after a close beyond the Asian session high during the London session, price moves at least 15 pips further within 12 bars more often than after a close beyond a random level at other times. Count every such close over 90 days and compare the two rates; if they are within the noise of random levels, the hypothesis fails. (2) Hypothesis: after price comes within 2 pips of the previous day's low, it moves 10 pips away within 12 bars before closing beyond the low more often than at random levels. Count all visits in 90 days and compare with 300 random levels. (3) Hypothesis: after price trades within 5 pips of the previous day's high or low, its next 12 bars' range is larger than after an ordinary bar. Count every visit in 90 days; if the average is not larger than the baseline by more than chance would give, it fails.

points: The chain: observation, hypothesis, test, result, conclusion.
A testable hypothesis names what is counted, over what sample and against what baseline.
"Insufficient evidence" is an honest, useful conclusion.

lessons.title: Support And Resistance As Reaction Zones
lessons.aim: Treat a level as a zone where price has reacted before, and compare it with random levels before believing it holds.

blocks.text: Price rarely turns at exactly one price. A level is better drawn as a **zone**: a band a few pips wide where price has turned or stalled before.
Price turned in this zone twice last week.
Price will turn here again.

blocks.title: Levels Drawn Afterwards
blocks.text: Draw enough lines on a finished chart and price will seem to have "respected" some of them. The lines were chosen with the answer in view. A level only counts if it was marked BEFORE the price it is meant to explain.

To test whether a level "holds", count how often price reacts there, and count how often it reacts at levels picked at random. If your level does no better than a random one, the belief has no support in that sample.
A level that beats random levels over a large sample has some support. One that does not, has none.

steps.title: Does The Level Hold?
steps.intro: Predict first. The chart has no levels built in.

points: A level is a zone where price reacted before. That is an observation.
That it will react again is a hypothesis. Levels drawn after the fact prove nothing.
Compare a level with random levels over a large sample.

lessons.title: Previous Highs And Lows
lessons.aim: Find the previous day's high and low under a stated day start, and see why the day start changes the answer.

blocks.text: Traders watch the previous day's high and low, and the previous week's. They are easy to find, so many people look at them. That is why they are useful as **references**. It is not evidence that price reacts there.
A day's high and low depend on where the day starts. Two common conventions: **midnight UTC**, and **5 p.m. New York time** (when the FX week rolls over for many traders).

blocks.title: The same market, two conventions
steps: With a 5 p.m. New York start, the previous day's high may have been made in the New York afternoon.
With a midnight UTC start, the same candle may belong to a different day.
The previous day's high and low can be **different candles**.

blocks.title: Ambiguous Without It
blocks.text: A level quoted without its day start is ambiguous. Two people can name different "previous day highs" for the same chart and both be right.

steps.title: Find The Level
steps.intro: The day shading is shown. The day start is stated.

steps.title: Find It Yourself
steps.intro: No shading this time. Work out where the day starts.

points: The previous day's high and low are reference levels.
Where the day starts changes which candles they come from.
They are references. That price reacts there is a hypothesis.

lessons.title: Liquidity: Three Meanings
lessons.aim: Separate the three things people mean by "liquidity", and spot the claim that is not supported.

items: **Market liquidity**: how easily you can trade without moving the price. It shows up in the spread and, where available, in volume. It is OBSERVABLE.
**Resting orders**: the idea that orders sit near obvious highs and lows, such as stop orders. In an over-the-counter market you cannot see them. It is an INTERPRETATION.
**Price is drawn to it**: the idea that price moves towards those orders. It is a HYPOTHESIS, and it can be tested by counting.

blocks.text: When someone says "price went to take liquidity", they are stating meaning two and meaning three as if they were meaning one. A move to a previous high is an observation. The reason given for it is an interpretation. That price will keep going to such highs is a hypothesis.

blocks.title: A Story After The Fact
blocks.text: It is easy to explain any move by saying orders were resting there. Explanations that fit every outcome cannot be tested, so they tell you nothing.

points: Liquidity has three meanings: depth (observable), resting orders (interpretation), price drawn to them (hypothesis).
Explanations that fit every outcome cannot be tested.
Say which meaning you are using.

lessons.title: Volatility, Compression And Expansion
lessons.aim: Measure volatility with plain range comparisons, and label stretches as compression or expansion.

blocks.text: **Volatility** is how big and how fast price changes. The plainest measure is the candle range you already know: high minus low.
There is no indicator here. You compare ranges with each other.
Compare a stretch's average range with the average of the recent past. Below 0.7 of it is a **compression**. Above 1.4 times it is an **expansion**.

blocks.title: The last five daily ranges: 50, 46, 55, 52, 47 pips. Today's range so far: 90 pips
Recent Compared With What?
blocks.text: A five-day average and a twenty-day average give different ratios. Say which you used, just as you say which swing size you used.

steps.title: Range Ratio
steps.intro: Today over the five-day average.

steps.title: Label The Stretches
steps.intro: Compare each stretch with the whole chart.

points: Volatility is the size and speed of price change, measured with candle ranges.
Compression: below 0.7 of the recent average. Expansion: above 1.4 times it.
State the yardstick you compare with.

lessons.title: Momentum As Price Speed
lessons.aim: Measure the speed of a move, count runs of closes in one direction, and describe momentum without forecasting.

blocks.text: Momentum, in this course, is **speed**: the price displacement divided by the time it took.
A **run** is a number of consecutive candles that close in the same direction. A run of 5 closes up is an observation about the last five candles.
Price rose 40 pips in 8 bars.
A fast move is likely to continue. This course makes no claim that it is.

blocks.title: Speed Is Not A Signal
blocks.text: Fast moves stop and reverse as often as they continue, as far as anyone has shown here. A fast move tells you it was fast.

steps.title: Pips Per Bar
steps.intro: Distance over time.

points: Momentum here is speed: displacement per unit of time.
A run is consecutive closes in one direction.
Both describe the past. Neither forecasts.

lessons.title: Breakouts, Failed Breakouts, Continuation And Reversal
lessons.aim: Classify an event under a stated price rule and time rule, and see how the definition changes the count.

blocks.text: "Breakout", "failed breakout", "continuation" and "reversal" are used loosely. To count them the same way twice, each needs a **price rule** and a **time rule**.

items: **Breakout**: the first bar that CLOSES beyond a stated level.
**Failed breakout**: a breakout followed, within k bars, by a close back on the other side of the level.
**Continuation**: the structure's sequence extended after a pullback, such as a new higher high after a higher low.
**Reversal**: an invalidation breach followed by a confirmed opposite structure.

blocks.title: The same chart under two failure limits
steps: A bar closes above the level. Four bars later a bar closes back below it.
With k = 3: a breakout that **held**, because the failure came too late.

blocks.title: Different Definitions, Different Counts
blocks.text: A failed-breakout rate depends on k. Quote it together with the rule, or the number means nothing.

steps.title: Classify The Event
steps.intro: Apply the stated rule bar by bar.

steps.title: One More
steps.intro: The rule is on the chart.

points: Each event needs a price rule and a time rule.
"Failed" needs a stated failure condition, such as a close back within k bars.
A different definition can classify the same event differently.

lessons.title: Forex Sessions: Asian, Frankfurt, London, New York
lessons.aim: Name the sessions and their overlaps, and see why "activity differs by session" is a measured claim that needs a sample.

blocks.text: FX trades around the clock, but activity is not spread evenly. Traders talk about four **sessions**, each defined on its own market's clock.

items: **Asian (Tokyo)**: 09:00–18:00 Tokyo time.
**Frankfurt**: 08:00–17:00 Frankfurt time.
**London**: 08:00–17:00 London time.
**New York**: 08:00–17:00 New York time.

blocks.text: Sessions overlap. London and New York are both open for a few hours each day. Those hours are called an overlap.

blocks.title: A Convention
blocks.text: These hours are typical FX-desk hours, used as a convention. Every value is editable. They are not a law of the market.
Activity (range) is larger in the London and New York sessions than in the Asian session.
That can be measured: take many days of data, average the candle range for each hour, and compare. The result depends on the sample and the market.

steps.title: Activity By Hour
steps.intro: Made-up data. Change the number of days, and switch the pattern off.

points: Sessions are windows on each market's own clock: Asian, Frankfurt, London, New York.
The hours are a convention. Activity differing across them is a tested regularity, not a law.
A pattern needs a large sample to be seen, and may not exist in your data.

lessons.title: Session Time Versus Your Time
lessons.aim: Convert a session's open and close into Guyana time on any date, including the weeks when the US and UK clocks are out of step.

steps.title: Each Session Keeps Its Own Clock

blocks.text: London 08:00 is 08:00 on London's clock, whatever time it is in Guyana. When London changes its clocks, the session moves against every other clock.
Guyana is on UTC−4 all year and never changes. So the gap between Guyana and a market changes when the MARKET changes.
The US changes its clocks on the second Sunday of March and the first Sunday of November. The UK and Europe change on the last Sunday of March and the last Sunday of October.

blocks.title: The Transition Weeks
blocks.text: For a few weeks each spring and autumn the two are out of step. In those weeks the London-to-New York gap is **4 hours**, not the usual 5.

blocks.title: On six dates in 2026
steps: 10 Feb: 04:00. 10 Mar: 04:00 (the US has changed, London has not).
27 Oct: 04:00 (London has changed back, the US has not yet). 10 Nov: 04:00.

steps.title: The Session Clock
steps.intro: Seven dates. Watch which sessions move, and which do not.

steps.title: Time Trap: When Does It Open?
steps.intro: Convert to Guyana time. Watch the date.

steps.title: Time Trap: The Gap
steps.intro: How far ahead is one clock of another on that date?

steps.title: Time Trap: Who Is Open?
steps.intro: Count the sessions open at an hour in Guyana.

blocks.text: Some traders define a window on one fixed clock, such as 20:00–02:00 New York time. That window does not follow London's or Tokyo's daylight saving. It stays fixed on New York's clock.
Which style you use changes when your windows sit against other markets' clocks. State which one.

points: Each session sits on its own market's clock, and follows that market's daylight saving.
Guyana does not change its clock, so the gap changes when the market changes.
In the weeks when the US and UK are out of step, the London-to-New York gap is 4 hours.

lessons.title: Session Highs And Lows
lessons.aim: Find a session's high and low from its window, and see how the definition of the window and the day changes the levels.

blocks.text: A session's **high and low** are the highest and lowest prices of the candles whose open time falls inside its window. They are **final** only after the window closes. Before that they are **developing**.
This is the one chart tool in the course. It draws each chosen session's high and low, and the previous day's high and low, as labelled horizontal lines.

items: It is a **reference**, not a signal.
It never labels anything "buy" or "sell".
A developing level is drawn dashed.

steps.title: Move The Definitions
steps.intro: Change the week, the chart clock, the day start and the sessions. Watch the lines.

blocks.text: Widen or shift a window and the high and low can be made by a different candle. Move the day start and the previous day's high can change. Neither is wrong. Each level is only meaningful together with its definition.

steps.title: Find The Session High
steps.intro: The window is shaded and stated.

steps.title: Find It Without The Shading
steps.intro: Work out where the window sits on the chart's clock.

points: A session's high and low come from the candles inside its window, and are final after it closes.
The Session Levels overlay draws references, never signals.
A different window or day start gives different levels, so quote the definition.

lessons.title: Reaction Zones Lab: The Observation Log
lessons.aim: Record what price did at reference levels, using observations only, with the counts and the sample size.

blocks.text: In this lab you log what price DID at the previous day's high. You do not say what it means, and you do not say what it will do.

items: Say what a visit is.
Count every visit, not just the memorable ones.
Say how many reacted, broke, or did neither.
Say how many days you looked at.

steps.title: The Log
steps.intro: Ten days of random price moves, tallied for you.

steps.title: Observation Log
steps.prompt: Write your log entry for this table. State what a visit was, the counts, the number of days, what a random level gave, and what you can and cannot say from it.
rubric: Says what a visit, a reaction and a break were.
Gives the counts and the number of days.
Compares with what random levels gave.
Does not claim the level is strong or weak.
Says what would be needed to call it a result (more days, a stated test).
steps.modelAnswer: Visit: a bar reaching within 2 pips of the previous day's high. Reacted: price moved 10 pips away within 12 bars before any close beyond it. Over nine days there were a small number of visits, and some reacted and some broke. Random levels on the same chart had a median rate that was similar. I can say what happened at this level on these days. I cannot say the level is strong or that it will hold, because the sample is small and the rate sits within what random levels produce. To call it a result I would need many more days and a stated test.

points: An observation log counts every visit and states the rule for a visit.
Give the counts, the sample size and a random comparison.
A log is not a result until it is a stated test on a large enough sample.

lessons.title: Price Behavior Lab
lessons.aim: Classify events under stated rules on charts, and write a short Price Behavior Report that says what the counts do and do not show.

items: Classify events and find levels under **stated rules**, on several charts.
Write a short **report**: the counts, the sample size, and what they do and do not show.

blocks.text: A report states its rules, its numbers and its limits. It does not tell a story about why.

steps.title: Six Charts
steps.intro: Events, session highs and lows, and previous-day levels. Hints on request.

steps.title: Price Behavior Report
steps.prompt: These figures are MADE UP for this exercise. Over 40 days, price visited the previous day's high 52 times. 31 visits reacted (moved 10 pips away within 12 bars before a close beyond it), 15 broke, and 6 did neither. Random levels on the same charts had a median reaction rate of 55% and a top-decile rate of 68%. Write a short Price Behavior Report: the rules, the counts, the sample, and what this does and does not show.
rubric: States the rules for a visit, a reaction and a break.
Gives the counts and the sample size (52 visits over 40 days).
Works out the rate: 31 of 46 decided visits, about 67%.
Compares it with the random median (55%) and top decile (68%): it is high but not clearly above the random range.
Says what it does NOT show: no proof the level is special, nothing about the future.
Ends with a conclusion such as "suggestive but not enough evidence".
steps.modelAnswer: Rules: a visit is a bar reaching within 2 pips of the previous day's high. A reaction is a move of 10 pips away within 12 bars before any close beyond the high. A break is a close beyond it first. Sample: 52 visits over 40 days. 31 reacted, 15 broke, 6 did neither. Of the 46 that were decided, 31 is about 67%. Random levels reacted at a median of 55% with a top decile of 68%, so 67% is above the median but inside the range that random levels reach. This does not show that the previous day's high is special, and it says nothing about what price will do next. It is suggestive at most. More days, and the same rule applied to a separate sample, would be needed before calling it evidence.

points: Classify events under stated rules, bar by bar.
A report gives the rules, the counts, the sample, the comparison and the limits.
A conclusion of "suggestive, not enough evidence" is honest and useful.

lessons.title: Why Currencies Move: A Map Of Drivers
lessons.aim: Name the main drivers of a currency, match each to its mechanism, and say why several act at once.

blocks.text: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Like any price, it moves when the balance of buying and selling moves.
This level is about the reasons people give for that balance shifting. It is a map. You do not need to become an economist.

items: **Interest rates**: higher returns can attract money.
**Inflation**: it erodes a currency's buying power, and central banks respond to it.
**Growth**: a strong economy can draw investment.
**Policy and communication**: what central banks do and say.
**Risk sentiment**: whether investors are seeking or avoiding risk.
**Flows**: trade, investment and the needs of large buyers and sellers.

blocks.text: Each driver is a reason why a currency MIGHT move. Several act at the same time, sometimes in opposite directions.

blocks.title: A Story After The Fact
blocks.text: After any move it is easy to point at a driver and say that caused it. The same driver can be pointed at for a move in either direction. A driver is an expectation, not a certainty.

points: A currency is a price. Its drivers are rates, inflation, growth, policy, risk sentiment and flows.
Several act at once, and each is an expectation, not a certainty.
A cause named after the move is an interpretation.

lessons.title: Interest Rates And Central Banks
lessons.aim: Explain what a policy rate is, work out a rate differential, and say why expectations matter as much as the level.

blocks.text: A central bank sets a **policy rate**. Other interest rates in the economy are built around it. Raising it makes borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding. Lowering it does the opposite.
The **rate differential** is one economy's policy rate minus another's.
Markets look forward. If everyone already expects a rise, the price may have moved before it happens. What matters is the change compared with what was expected.

blocks.title: A Toy, Not A Model
blocks.text: A rising rate differential does not mean the currency will rise. Many things act at once. The toy below adds up one driver only, and is labelled illustrative.

steps.title: The Differential Toy
steps.intro: Change the rates, then the expectations.

steps.title: Work Out A Differential
steps.intro: A minus B.

points: The policy rate is set by a central bank. The differential is A's rate minus B's.
Expectations matter as much as the level.
A differential is an expectation input, never a promise.

lessons.title: Inflation
lessons.aim: Say what CPI measures, work out a yearly inflation rate from an index, and explain why central banks respond to it.

blocks.text: The **consumer price index** follows the cost of a basket of goods and services over time. It is given as an index number, such as 112.4, that only means something compared with an earlier one.
Inflation = (new index − old index) ÷ old index × 100.

blocks.title: An index of 108.5 a year ago and 112.4 now

blocks.text: Many central banks aim to keep inflation near a target. When it runs above, they may lift rates to cool spending. When it runs below, they may cut. Markets watch the release for what it implies about the path of rates.
A higher-than-expected inflation figure is often read as making a rate rise more likely. That is an interpretation, and markets do not always react that way.

steps.title: Yearly Inflation
steps.intro: Change over the old index, times 100.

points: CPI follows the cost of a basket. Its yearly percent change is inflation.
Central banks respond to inflation, and markets watch what a release implies for rates.
A higher-than-expected figure being read as "rates will rise" is an interpretation.

lessons.title: Employment
lessons.aim: Say what payrolls, unemployment and wages describe, and why policy makers watch them.

items: **Payrolls** count how many jobs were added in a month.
**Unemployment** is the share of people looking for work who cannot find it.
**Wages** show how fast pay is rising.

blocks.text: Strong hiring and rising wages can add to spending and prices. Weak hiring can slow the economy. Central banks weigh both when they set rates, so the market reads each report for what it implies about policy.

blocks.title: The First Number Is Not The Last
blocks.text: Employment figures are often revised in later months. A reaction to the first figure may have been to a number that no longer stands.
"Strong jobs mean a strong currency" is a common reading. It is not a rule.

points: Payrolls, unemployment and wages describe the labour market.
Policy makers watch them for what they imply about growth and prices.
Figures are revised, and readings like "strong jobs, strong currency" are not rules.

lessons.title: GDP And Economic Growth
lessons.aim: Say what GDP measures, and why it is a lagging measure that is often revised.

blocks.text: **GDP** is the value of everything an economy produces in a period. Its growth rate says how fast the economy is expanding or shrinking.
GDP is reported well after the period it covers, and is often revised. By the time it is released, other data has already told markets a lot about that period.

blocks.title: Old News
blocks.text: A GDP release can matter because it differs from expectations, but it describes the past. It is not a forecast.
Faster growth is often read as supportive of a currency, because it can bring higher rates and investment. That is an interpretation. Other drivers can outweigh it.

points: GDP is the output of an economy. Growth is how fast it changes.
It is a lagging measure and is often revised.
A link between growth and a currency is an interpretation.

lessons.title: Monetary Policy And Communication
lessons.aim: Tell tightening from easing, and label the tone of a statement as hawkish or dovish, as a description only.

items: **Tightening**: raising rates or reducing support, to slow spending and prices.
**Easing**: lowering rates or adding support, to encourage spending.

blocks.text: Central banks say what they may do next. That is **forward guidance**, and it moves expectations.
A statement is **hawkish** in tone if it leans towards higher rates or tighter policy. It is **dovish** if it leans towards lower rates or easier policy.

blocks.title: Not A Forecast
blocks.text: Hawkish and dovish describe how a statement reads. They do not say what the bank will do, nor what the currency will do. A statement can be more hawkish than the market expected and the currency can still fall.

points: Tightening raises rates or reduces support. Easing lowers them or adds support.
Hawkish and dovish describe the tone of a statement.
Tone is a description. It forecasts neither policy nor price.

lessons.title: Risk Sentiment And Currency Strength
lessons.aim: Describe risk-on and risk-off, and see that relationships between currencies change across eras.

blocks.text: When investors are willing to take risk, money tends to move towards riskier assets. That is called **risk-on**. When they pull back, it is **risk-off**.
Calling a day "risk-off" is an interpretation of many moves at once. It is a story that fits the data, not a measured fact.

Traders often say that two currencies "move together" or "move opposite". How closely they moved in the past is something you can measure. But the relationship in one period is not the relationship in the next.

blocks.title: One Window, One Description
blocks.text: A relationship measured over a window describes that window. Change the window, or the era, and it can look very different.

steps.title: A Relationship That Shifts
steps.intro: Predict first. The data is made up, with three eras built in.

points: Risk-on and risk-off describe investor mood. They are interpretations.
Relationships between currencies change across eras.
A measured relationship describes the window it was measured in.

lessons.title: The Big US Events: CPI, NFP, FOMC
lessons.aim: Say what each of the three most-watched US events is, who publishes it and why it is watched.

blocks.text: The US **CPI** report gives the change in consumer prices. It is published by a US government statistics agency, monthly. It is watched because it bears on the path of US interest rates.

The **non-farm payrolls** report gives the number of jobs added, and also unemployment and wages. It is published monthly, usually on the first Friday. It is watched for what it implies about growth and policy.
The **FOMC** is the committee that sets US interest-rate policy. It meets on a published schedule, about eight times a year. The decision, the statement and the press conference are all watched.
Each bears on the future path of US interest rates, and the dollar is on one side of most currency pairs. They are watched by many people, which is why prices can move sharply around them.

blocks.title: Watched Does Not Mean Predictable
blocks.text: That many people watch a release tells you it may move prices. It does not tell you which way.

points: CPI gives consumer prices. The employment report gives jobs, unemployment and wages. The FOMC sets US rate policy.
They are watched because they bear on the path of US rates.
Being widely watched does not make them predictable.

lessons.title: ECB, BoE And Other Releases
lessons.aim: Name the main non-US central banks and releases, and see that each keeps its own schedule and clock.

items: The **European Central Bank** decides euro-area policy through its Governing Council.
The **Bank of England** sets UK policy through its Monetary Policy Committee.
Other economies have their own central banks, with their own schedules.

blocks.text: A rate decision is usually followed by a statement, and in some cases a press conference. The words can move prices as much as the decision, because they shape expectations of the next one.

A release is timed on its own market's clock. A UK release at 12:00 is 12:00 London time, whatever time it is in Guyana. Daylight saving applies to that clock, so the time in Guyana changes when London changes its clocks.

blocks.title: Do Not Reuse Last Month's Conversion
blocks.text: A time worked out in January may be an hour out in July. Always convert for the date of the release.

points: The ECB and the Bank of England each set policy through a committee.
The words after a decision can move prices as much as the decision.
Each release keeps its own clock, so convert for the date.

lessons.title: Reading An Economic Calendar
lessons.aim: Read the columns of a calendar row, and convert a release time to your own time on the date.

blocks.text: A calendar row gives the time, the currency, the event, its **impact** rating, and three figures.

items: **Forecast**: what analysts expected.
**Previous**: the last figure.
**Actual**: the released figure.
**Revision**: a change to the previous figure.

blocks.title: Using the teaching row
steps: The previous figure was revised down: 3.3% to 3.2%.
Impact "High" means many people expect a large reaction. It is a rating, not a forecast of direction.

blocks.text: The time on a calendar is on a stated clock: the market's own, your platform's, or UTC. Check which. Then convert for the DATE.

blocks.title: The Same Releases, Two Dates (Teaching Example)
head: Release
Its own clock
Guyana, 20 Jan 2026
Guyana, 10 Mar 2026

blocks.title: The March Trap
blocks.text: On 10 March 2026 the US has moved to daylight time and the UK and Europe have not. The New York releases shift an hour earlier on Guyana's clock. The UK and Europe ones do not.

steps.title: Convert A Release
steps.intro: Convert to Guyana time on the date.

steps.title: Hours After The London Open
steps.intro: Watch the date.

points: A calendar row has impact, forecast, previous, actual and any revision.
Convert a release time for the date, on the stated clock.
Around the March and October transition weeks the London-to-New York gap changes.

lessons.title: Expectations, Surprise And Reaction
lessons.aim: Explain why price reacts to the surprise, why the first move can reverse, and why direction cannot be read from the number alone.

blocks.text: The **surprise** is the actual figure minus the forecast. Price tends to react to that gap, because the forecast is already in the price.
A high figure that was fully expected is no surprise.
Even so, the first move may go the other way from what the number suggests. It may then reverse within minutes. The move an hour later may be unrelated to the first one.
Price moved up 25 pips, then fell 40 pips within ten minutes.
A figure above forecast will lift the currency. Reactions like this show that it is not reliable.

steps.title: Rise Or Fall?
steps.intro: Eight made-up releases. Guess the first five minutes.

steps.title: Work Out The Surprise
steps.intro: Actual minus forecast.

points: Price reacts to the surprise, actual minus forecast.
The first move can reverse, and the hour after can go the other way.
The direction cannot be read from the number alone. Decide your rule beforehand.

lessons.title: News And Execution Conditions
lessons.aim: Explain what news does to spread, slippage and stops, and write a rule for trading around events.

items: The **spread** can widen sharply.
**Slippage** grows: fills can be far from the price you clicked.
A **stop** can fill far beyond its price, or a price can gap.
Quotes can pause for a moment.

blocks.text: Spreads on many pairs widen around major releases. How much depends on the pair, the release and the broker.

steps.title: Spread Around A Release
steps.intro: Watch how the spread and the fill change.

blocks.text: The moment a number lands is the worst time to decide what to do. So decide in advance. There are three choices.

items: **Stand aside**: no new trades, and no open ones, in a stated window.
**Reduce**: trade smaller, or widen the stop and cut the size to keep the risk the same.
**Trade**: only under written rules, knowing the spread and slippage may cost more than planned.

blocks.title: Open Trades Count Too
blocks.text: A rule that only covers new trades leaves an open trade exposed to a jump or a gap. Say what you do with trades already open.

blocks.title: A news rule has parts
steps: Which events (impact rating, the currencies in your pair).
The window: how long before and after.
The action: stand aside, reduce, or trade.
A spread limit above which you do not trade.

steps.title: My News Rule
steps.prompt: Write a news rule for the trades you might take. Name which events it covers, the window before and after, the action, what happens to open trades, and a spread limit.
rubric: Names which events are covered (for example high-impact releases for the currencies in the pair).
States the window before and after in minutes.
Chooses an action: stand aside, reduce or trade, and says what size if reduced.
Says what happens to trades already open.
Sets a spread limit or another condition that stops trading.
steps.modelAnswer: I stand aside from 15 minutes before to 30 minutes after any high-impact release for either currency in the pair. I place no new orders in that window. If I have a trade open, I close it or move the stop to reduce the risk before the window starts, since a stop can fill beyond its price. After the window, I trade only if the spread is back below 1.5 pips. If I ever choose to trade a release, I halve my usual size and treat slippage as part of the planned risk.

points: Around a release, spreads widen, slippage grows and stops can fill far from their price.
Stand aside, reduce or trade is a rule decided in advance.
A news rule covers open trades as well as new ones.

lessons.title: News Event Lab
lessons.aim: Compare price ranges around release times with ordinary periods, on made-up data, and say what the counts do and do not show.

blocks.text: An **event study** asks: what did price do around every event, compared with ordinary times? It counts ALL the events, states its sample and its rule, and reports what it found.

blocks.title: Unverified Data
blocks.text: This lab uses made-up data and made-up release times. A real event study needs a **verified list of release timestamps**. Until one has been checked, the app marks the dataset "unverified", and so should you.

steps.title: The Event Study
steps.intro: Compare the release half-hour with the same half-hour on ordinary days.

steps.title: Event Study Report
steps.prompt: Write a short report on what the event study shows. State the rule, the sample sizes, the averages with their uncertainty, and what it does NOT show.
rubric: States what was compared: the range in the same 30 minutes on release days and on ordinary days.
Gives the sample sizes and the averages, with the standard error.
Says the data is made up and the timestamps are unverified.
Says it measures size, not direction.
Does not claim a way to trade it.
steps.modelAnswer: Rule: I compared the range of the 13:30 UTC half-hour on 20 made-up release days with the same half-hour on the other 40 days. Release days averaged a much larger range than ordinary days, and with 20 and 40 days the standard errors were small compared with the gap. The data and the release times are made up and unverified, so this is a demonstration of the method, not a finding about a real market. It measures the size of the range, not the direction, so it does not say which way to trade. It supports only the idea that ranges are larger at releases.

points: An event study counts every event and compares with ordinary periods.
Data and timestamps must be verified, or marked unverified.
It can show the size of a range. It says nothing about direction or profit.

lessons.title: Risk Per Trade
lessons.aim: See what a chosen risk per trade does to an account over a losing streak, and choose it from survivability.

blocks.text: This is the most important level of the course. The size of your risk on each trade decides how bad a losing streak can get, whatever your method is.
This course does NOT tell you what percentage to risk. It shows what each choice does, and you write your own limits.
One common approach risks the same **percent of the current balance** on each trade.

blocks.title: An account of $10,000 risking 1%
steps: After a loss the balance is $9,900, so the next risks $99.
After a win to $10,100, the next risks $101.

blocks.text: Do not choose a risk by what you hope to make. Choose it by what you could sit through. A run of losses in a row will happen. The question is how deep it takes the account, and whether you would keep following your rules.

blocks.title: Gains Are Not A Reason
blocks.text: "I want to make 20% a year, so I must risk 5%" is choosing from hope. It ignores that the same 5% takes a 22.6% bite out of the account after five losses in a row.

steps.title: The Streak Ladder
steps.intro: State your answer first. Then run it.

points: Fixed-fraction risk uses the same percent of the current balance each trade.
Choose the risk by what a losing streak would do, not by the gains you hope for.
This course shows consequences. You write your own limits.

lessons.title: Position Sizing In Practice
lessons.aim: Size positions correctly on any listed pair, including yen pairs and non-dollar accounts, and report the realized risk after rounding.

items: Work out the **risk budget**: balance × risk percent.
Measure the **stop distance** in pips.
Find the **pip value** per lot in YOUR account currency.
Lots = risk budget ÷ (stop pips × pip value per lot). Round DOWN to the lot step.
On a yen pair a pip is **0.01**, and the pip value is in yen, so convert it: 1,000 ÷ the USD/JPY rate.
If your account is in **euros**, a pip worth $10 is worth 10 ÷ EUR/USD in euros.
On a cross such as EUR/GBP, the pip is worth £10, so in dollars multiply by GBP/USD.

steps.title: The Position-Size Calculator
steps.intro: Try a yen pair and a euro account.

steps.title: Step By Step
steps.intro: Each step is marked against your own number.

steps.title: A Yen Pair
steps.intro: Convert the pip value to dollars.

steps.title: A Cross Pair
steps.intro: The pip is in pounds.

points: Lots = risk budget ÷ (stop pips × pip value per lot). Round DOWN.
Convert the pip value into your account currency.
Report the realized risk after rounding.

lessons.title: The Stop Is Invalidation
lessons.aim: Place a stop where the idea is wrong, and only then size the position to fit it.

blocks.text: A stop belongs just beyond the level that shows the idea was WRONG. The position size is then worked out to fit it.
Level 7 gave you the level: in a bullish structure it is the latest confirmed structural low. A close beyond it ends the description.

blocks.title: A long idea: entry 1.2010, latest structural low 1.1980, buffer 3 pips for the spread and noise
A Warning Sign
blocks.text: If you choose the stop from a dollar amount ("I will risk $50, so the stop goes here"), or use the same distance every time, the stop is not tied to the idea. It can be hit while the idea is still right, or sit far beyond the point where it failed.

steps.title: Where Does The Stop Go?
steps.intro: Choose the stop that fits the idea.

steps.title: The Level On A Chart
steps.intro: Tap the candle whose extreme holds the structure.

points: Place the stop just beyond the level that ends the idea, with a buffer for spread.
Size the position to fit the stop, never the reverse.
A stop from a dollar amount, or a fixed distance, is a warning sign.

lessons.title: Maximum Daily And Weekly Loss
lessons.aim: Set circuit breakers, say how a limit is measured, and say what you do when one is hit.

blocks.text: A **maximum daily loss** stops you for the day once you have lost a stated amount. A **maximum weekly loss** does the same for the week. They limit how much a bad stretch, or a bad decision made in the heat of a loss, can cost.

items: **Closed trades only**: the limit counts losses you have taken.
**Open losses too**: the limit also counts what an open trade is losing right now.

blocks.title: Say Which
blocks.text: If open losses are not counted, a trade can sit far below its stop in your head and never trip the limit. State which one your rule uses.
Decide in advance what happens: you stop for the day, you close everything, you review the trades. A limit with no action is only a number.

steps.title: How Many Losses?
steps.intro: Round up to the first count that reaches the limit.

points: Circuit breakers stop you after a stated daily or weekly loss.
Say whether the limit counts closed trades only, or open losses too.
Decide in advance what you do when a limit is hit.

lessons.title: Drawdown Rules
lessons.aim: Write what changes after a drawdown, and see why the answer is never to risk more.

blocks.text: A **drawdown** is a fall from the highest balance. Write two lines in your plan: the drawdown at which you **cut your risk**, and the drawdown at which you **stop and review**.

blocks.title: A peak of $12,000 and a balance of $10,800

blocks.text: After a loss there is a pull to risk more to get it back. That makes the next loss bigger, and the gain needed to recover grows faster than the fall.

blocks.title: The Wrong Rule
blocks.text: "I lost 10%, so I will risk double until I am even" makes a bad stretch deeper. Your rule should cut risk inside a drawdown, not raise it.

blocks.title: A rule: at 8% drawdown, trade at half the normal risk
steps: Normal risk 1%: after the cut, 0.5% per trade.
The same run of losses now takes half as much from the account.

points: A drawdown is measured from the highest balance.
Write the drawdown that cuts your risk and the one that stops you.
Risk goes down inside a drawdown, never up.

lessons.title: Account Exposure And Open Risk
lessons.aim: Add up the risk across open trades and hold it to a limit written in advance.

blocks.text: Each open trade has its own risk: the money lost if its stop is hit. **Open risk** is the total across every open trade.
If several stops are hit together, you lose the whole total at once. Trades that seem separate can all turn against you on the same news.

blocks.title: A Limit Written In Advance
blocks.text: Write a maximum open risk in your plan. A sensible check is that it does not exceed your daily loss limit, so open trades alone cannot break the limit.

steps.title: Add The Risk
steps.intro: Sum the three.

points: Open risk is the sum of the risk on every open trade.
Write a maximum open risk in advance, no more than your daily limit.
Separate-looking trades can all turn against you at once.

lessons.title: Correlation
lessons.aim: Count exposure by currency across all positions, and find the hidden common exposure.

blocks.text: Long EUR/USD and long GBP/USD are largely one bet: that the dollar will fall. Both positions are short the dollar. If the dollar rises, both may lose together.
Positions in different pairs can share a currency. Your real exposure is counted BY CURRENCY, across every position.
For each position, one currency is bought and the other sold. Add them up across all positions, keeping the direction.

blocks.title: Long 1 lot EUR/USD, long 1 lot GBP/USD, short 1 lot USD/JPY
steps: Every one of them is short the dollar.
The dollar is the largest net exposure, though there are three different pairs.

blocks.title: Not A Constant
blocks.text: How closely two pairs move together changes across eras (Level 9). Counting exposure by currency tells you what you HOLD. It does not tell you that pairs will keep moving together.

steps.title: Find The Hidden Exposure
steps.intro: Three sets of positions. Guess, then see.

steps.title: Net Exposure In Lots
steps.intro: Keep the signs.

points: Count exposure by currency across all positions, keeping direction.
Different pairs can be one bet on a single currency.
Relationships change, so this counts what you hold and does not forecast.

lessons.title: Concentration Risk And Leverage
lessons.aim: Tell notional from risk, and say why available leverage is not leverage to use.

blocks.text: The **notional** of a position is its full value. The **risk** is what you lose if the stop is hit. They are different.

blocks.title: A $5,000 account, 2 lots of EUR/USD at 1.175, stop 20 pips
steps: Risk at the stop: 2 × 20 × $10 = **$400**, which is **8%** of the account.

steps.title: The Leverage Lens
steps.intro: Change the size and the stop. Watch the risk as a percent.

blocks.text: A broker may offer 500 : 1. That is what is AVAILABLE. How much you USE is decided by your position size and your stop. With a proper stop and a risk cap, a large notional can still keep the risk small.

blocks.title: But Gaps And Slippage
blocks.text: A large position makes a gap or slippage cost more, in money. The stop is not a guarantee. The bigger the size, the bigger the surprise.

points: Notional is the full value. Risk is what the stop puts at stake.
Leverage available is not leverage to use.
Large positions make gaps and slippage costly, whatever the stop.

lessons.title: Risk Of Ruin Revisited
lessons.aim: Read simulated ruin curves across risk levels, win rates and payoffs, and say what they do and do not tell you.

steps.title: The Same Idea, With Your Own Numbers

blocks.text: In Level 5 you defined ruin as a drawdown of a size you choose. Here you see how that chance changes with the risk per trade, the win rate and the payoff.

steps.title: The Ruin Explorer
steps.intro: Predict first, then run it.

blocks.text: A simulated chance of ruin assumes the win rate and payoff are TRUE. They are estimates from your data, with a standard error. Use the table to compare risk settings, not to forecast.

blocks.title: The Lever You Control
blocks.text: The win rate and payoff come from the method. The risk per trade is the one you set yourself, and it moves the chance of ruin a great deal.

points: The chance of ruin changes a lot with risk per trade, win rate and payoff.
The output assumes your inputs are true. They are estimates.
Use it to compare risk settings, not to forecast.

lessons.title: The Losing-Streak Simulator
lessons.aim: Apply runs of losses to an account at several risk settings, and compare the result with what you said you could survive.

blocks.text: Pick an account and a risk. Apply 1, 3, 5, 8 and 10 losses in a row. Repeat at other risk levels, and switch between risking a percent of the current balance and a fixed dollar amount.
State first how many losses in a row you could survive before you would stop trading. Then run it.

steps.title: The Streak Ladder
steps.intro: Try at least three risk settings.

steps.title: What The Ladder Showed Me
steps.prompt: Look at the ladder for two different risk settings. Write what surprised you, and how many losses in a row you could really sit through at the risk you are thinking of, and why.
rubric: Names the risk settings compared and the drawdown after a stated number of losses.
Compares the answer given BEFORE the run with the result.
Says what recovery would require.
Ties the answer to surviving and following the rules, not to profit.
Does not claim the losing streak cannot happen.
steps.modelAnswer: At 1% risk, ten losses in a row leaves the account about 9.6% down and needs about 10.6% to recover. At 5% the same ten losses leave it about 40% down and need a gain of about 67%. I had said I could sit through eight losses at 5%, but the ladder shows that is 33.7% down, and I do not think I would keep following my rules there. So the risk I can really live with is nearer 1%. I am picking it by what I could survive, not by what I hope to make.

points: Apply runs of losses at different risk settings to see what each does.
State what you could survive before the run, then compare.
Choose the risk by what you could follow through, not by the profit you hope for.

lessons.title: Drawdown Distributions
lessons.aim: See the spread of maximum drawdowns and longest losing streaks that the same rules can give, and plan for its unlucky end.

blocks.text: The same rules, run over the same number of trades, give different results each time. Run them thousands of times and you see a **distribution**: the middle, and the unlucky and lucky ends.

steps.title: One Hundred Trades, Many Times
steps.intro: Change the rules and watch the spread.

blocks.text: The middle of the spread is what usually happens. The unlucky 5% is what you must be able to survive. Set your risk so that the unlucky end is a drawdown you could follow your rules through.

blocks.title: It Assumes Your Numbers
blocks.text: The simulation takes the win rate and payoff you give it as true. Yours are estimates from a limited sample, so the real spread may be wider.

points: The same rules give a spread of drawdowns and losing streaks.
Plan for the unlucky end, not the middle.
The simulation assumes your win rate and payoff are true, and they are estimates.

lessons.title: Planned Versus Realized Risk
lessons.aim: Work out the risk you actually take after spread, slippage and rounding, and build a buffer.

blocks.text: The **planned** risk is what your sizing gives. The **realized** risk is what you actually lose when the stop is hit, after the spread, the slippage and any gap.

blocks.title: 0.5 lots of EUR/USD, a 25-pip stop, 1.5 pips of spread and 3 pips of slippage

steps.title: One Trade, Many Fills
steps.intro: Compare fills under looser and stricter assumptions.

blocks.text: Spread and slippage are costs of every trade, and news or gaps make them larger. Two habits help. Keep your planned risk under your cap by a margin. And measure your own realized risk against the plan in the journal.

blocks.title: A Cap Is A Limit On What Is Realized
blocks.text: If your cap is 1%, a trade planned at exactly 1% may realize 1.15%. Plan a little under, and check.

steps.title: Realized Loss
steps.intro: Add the spread and the slippage.

points: Realized risk is the loss you actually take after spread, slippage, gaps and rounding.
It is usually larger than the planned risk.
Keep planned risk a little under your cap, and measure the difference.

lessons.title: Building A Risk Plan
lessons.aim: Write your own Risk Plan, make it consistent, and have your mentor approve it.

blocks.text: You have seen what risk per trade, loss limits, drawdowns, open risk and exposure do. Now you write yours. The course does not choose the numbers.

items: Risk per trade, within the cap in Settings.
Maximum daily loss, weekly loss and the drawdown that stops you.
The drawdown that cuts your risk, and what it cuts to.
Maximum open risk, and maximum risk in one currency.
How a loss limit is measured.
Your news rule.

steps.title: The App Checks It Holds Together

blocks.text: The builder checks that your numbers agree with each other: for example that the weekly limit is not smaller than the daily one. It also shows what they mean in your own dollars. It does not say whether the numbers are wise.

blocks.title: Your Mentor Decides
blocks.text: When the plan is complete you send it to your mentor. They approve it or ask for changes. The Level 10 assessment is not finished until they approve it.

steps.title: Build Your Risk Plan
steps.intro: Fill in every part. The plan is saved as you go.

points: A Risk Plan is your own limits, written down and consistent with each other.
The app checks that they hold together and shows what they mean in dollars.
Your mentor approves it. The journal later enforces it.

lessons.title: Process Quality Against Trade Outcome
lessons.aim: Grade a decision by whether the plan was followed, and keep the result separate.

blocks.text: Every trade asks two separate questions. Was the DECISION good: did it follow the plan? And did the trade make money? They are different questions with different answers.

items: Followed the plan and won: a good decision that paid.
Followed the plan and lost: a good decision that did not pay. This is normal.
Broke the plan and won: a poor decision that got lucky.
Broke the plan and lost: a poor decision that cost you.

blocks.title: The Dangerous Cell
blocks.text: Breaking the plan and winning feels like proof that the plan is unnecessary. It teaches the wrong lesson, and it gets repeated.

steps.title: Judge The Decision
steps.intro: Judge by the plan, not by the result.

steps.title: Judge Another
steps.intro: Same rule.

points: Judge the decision by the plan and the result separately.
A good decision can lose. A poor decision can win.
Breaking the plan and winning is the dangerous cell.

lessons.title: Outcome Bias
lessons.aim: Grade a trade blind to its result, then see the result.

blocks.text: Once you know a trade won, its flaws vanish. Once you know it lost, its strengths do. That is **outcome bias**.

blocks.title: The Fix
blocks.text: Grade the process BEFORE you look at the result. Then reveal it. If your process score tracks the result, you are grading the result.

steps.title: An Audit With The Result Hidden

blocks.text: Next you are given a trade with its result hidden. Judge each rule from the record alone. If a rule cannot be judged from the record, say "Cannot Tell". Then rate the process. Only then is the result shown.

points: Outcome bias judges a decision by its result.
Grade the process first, blind to the result.
Say "Cannot Tell" for a rule the record does not show.

lessons.title: FOMO
lessons.aim: Recognize entering because price has moved, and write the rule that stops it.

blocks.text: **FOMO** is entering because price has already moved and you feel you are missing out, not because a rule fired.

items: An entry price far from the planned entry level.
An entry after a fast move.
No valid setup logged.

blocks.text: A rule of the form "no plan level, no order" is a countermeasure. Whether it works for you is shown by your own journal.

points: FOMO is entering because price has moved, with no rule firing.
Signature: an entry far from the planned level, after a fast move, with no valid setup.
Rule: no plan level, no order.

lessons.title: Revenge Trading And Raising Risk After Losses
lessons.aim: Recognize trading to win a loss back, and write the pause and the risk rule.

blocks.text: After a loss there is a pull to trade at once, bigger, to recover. That is **revenge trading**.

items: A trade opened soon after a loss.
A larger size than the previous trade, or an invalid setup.
Risk on the next trade greater than the last after a loss.
"After a loss, a fixed pause before the next decision."
"Risk never increases inside a drawdown."
"Size depends on the plan, never on the last result."

blocks.title: Written Before, Not During
blocks.text: These are pre-commitments. In the moment after a loss you are the least able to decide them well.

points: Revenge trading is trading to win a loss back.
Signature: a trade soon after a loss, with larger size or no valid setup.
Rules: a fixed pause after a loss, and risk never rises inside a drawdown.

lessons.title: Overtrading
lessons.aim: Recognize taking more trades than the plan allows, and write the limit.

blocks.text: **Overtrading** is taking more trades than the plan allows, or trades with no valid setup. A method has an expectancy per VALID trade. Extra invalid trades dilute it, and every trade pays the spread.

items: Trades per day above the plan's maximum.
Trades with no valid setup logged.

blocks.text: "Maximum trades per day, written in the plan." When you reach it, you are done for the day, whatever the chart shows.

points: Overtrading is more trades than the plan allows, or trades with no valid setup.
Signature: trades per day above the plan's maximum.
Rule: a maximum trades per day, written in the plan.

lessons.title: Moving Stops
lessons.aim: Recognize widening a stop after entry, and write the rule that stops it.

blocks.text: You placed the stop at the level where your idea is wrong. **Moving it** further away after entry means you are letting the trade be wrong for longer.

items: Stop distance increased after entry.
A loss larger than 1R.

blocks.text: "Stops move only toward reducing risk." Once the trade is running, the stop can be tightened or moved to breakeven. It is never pushed back.

blocks.title: The Pull
blocks.text: It always feels reasonable at the time: "it will come back". That is exactly why the rule is written in advance.

points: The stop marks where the idea fails.
Signature: stop distance increased after entry.
Rule: stops move only toward reducing risk.

lessons.title: Cutting Winners And Holding Losers
lessons.aim: Recompute expectancy when winners are cut short and losers are held.

blocks.text: **Cutting winners** is closing a trade early to lock in a gain. **Holding losers** is keeping a losing trade past its stop, hoping it returns. Both feel safe. Together they can turn a positive expectancy negative.

items: Average winner materially below the planned target.
Losses larger than 1R, or a stop removed.

blocks.title: A method wins 45% of trades, +2R planned and −1R planned
steps: The trader cuts winners at +1R and lets losers run to −1.5R.

items: "Management rules written before entry."
"A stop is set with the order, always."

steps.title: The Achieved Expectancy
steps.intro: Use the sizes actually taken.

points: Cutting winners and holding losers lower expectancy in R.
Signature: average winner below target, losses beyond 1R.
Rules: management written before entry, and a stop set with the order.

lessons.title: Fear Of Losing And Loss Aversion
lessons.aim: Recognize skipping valid setups after losses and holding losers, and check for them in the numbers.

blocks.text: For most people a loss feels heavier than a gain of the same size. That is **loss aversion**. It pushes two ways: you skip valid setups after losses, because another loss would hurt, and you hold a loser past its stop, because closing it makes the loss real.
You cannot see loss aversion in one trade. You see it in the average time in trade.

blocks.title: One Month Of Trades
head: Group
Trades
Average Time In Trade
blocks.note: Losers held almost four times as long as winners.

blocks.text: The countermeasure is to measure it: compare the average time in trade of winners and losers every month. If losers last much longer, the stop is not being obeyed.

points: Loss aversion is feeling a loss more than an equal gain.
Signature: losers held longer than winners, or valid setups skipped after losses.
Check: compare the average time in trade of winners and losers.

lessons.title: Recency Bias And The Gambler's Fallacy
lessons.aim: See that trades are independent, and that a losing streak does not make a win due.

blocks.text: **Recency bias** gives the last few trades far more weight than the whole record. Three wins and you are sure the method is great. Three losses and you are sure it is broken. The **gambler's fallacy** is the belief that after a run of losses a win is "due".

steps.title: Independent Sequences
steps.intro: Twenty identical traders with the same win rate. Look at how differently the streaks fall.

blocks.text: Every trader has the same method, and yet the streaks differ wildly. Each trade is independent of the one before. Nothing is "due", and a streak is not a verdict on the method.

blocks.title: The Signature
blocks.text: Size raised after a losing streak. The rule: **size depends on the plan, never on the last result.**

points: Trades are independent. A streak does not make a win due.
Recency bias overweights the last few trades against the whole record.
Rule: size depends on the plan, never on the last result.

lessons.title: Confirmation Bias
lessons.aim: Find the evidence a trader ignored, and use the disconfirming-evidence field.

blocks.text: Once you lean long, you notice the reasons it will go up and discount the ones it will not. That is **confirmation bias**. It does not feel like bias. It feels like research.

blocks.title: The Signature And The Rule
blocks.text: Signature: the "evidence against" field of the journal left empty. Rule: **write the strongest case against the trade before entry.**

points: Confirmation bias is looking for evidence that agrees.
Signature: the evidence-against field left empty.
Rule: write the strongest case against the trade before entry.

lessons.title: Rules, Checklists And Pre-Commitment
lessons.aim: Turn each countermeasure into an if-then rule, and add your behavior rules to your Risk Plan.

blocks.text: The moment of temptation is the worst time to decide. A **pre-commitment** is a rule written in advance, in the form: **if** this happens, **then** I do that.

steps.title: Every Behavior Has A Signature And A Rule

blocks.title: Behavior, Signature, Rule
head: Behavior
Signature
Rule
rows: Entry far from the planned level, after a fast move
A trade soon after a loss, larger or with no setup
A fixed pause after a loss
Risk higher than the last trade after a loss
Risk never increases inside a drawdown
More trades per day than the plan allows
Stops move only toward reducing risk
Average winner below the planned target
Losses beyond 1R, or a stop removed
A stop is set with the order, always
Compare the time in trade of winners and losers
Size raised after a losing streak
Size depends on the plan, never on the last result
Write the strongest case against the trade first
Score the process before viewing the result

items: Is there a valid setup from my plan?
Am I entering at my planned level?
Is the stop at the invalidation level, set with the order?
Is the size from the stop, at or under my risk?
Have I taken fewer trades than my daily maximum, and is my pause after a loss over?
Have I written the strongest case against this trade?

blocks.text: If any answer is no, there is no order.

steps.title: My Three Behavior Rules
steps.prompt: Choose the three behaviors you think are most likely to catch you out. For each, write the signature you would look for in your journal and the if-then rule you will follow.
rubric: Names three specific behaviors.
For each, states a signature that a journal could show (a number or a field), not a feeling.
For each, writes a rule in the form "if ... then ...".
The rules can be followed without judgement in the moment.
Does not promise to "try harder" or "stay disciplined".
steps.modelAnswer: Revenge trading: if a trade closes at a loss, then I take no new order for 30 minutes and I write down what I feel. FOMO: if price is more than 10 pips from my planned level, then I place no order and wait for a retest. Gambler's fallacy: if I have lost three in a row, then the next trade is taken at exactly the normal size, not more. I will see these in my journal as a trade opened within 30 minutes of a loss, an entry far from the level, and a size above normal after losses.

steps.title: Add Behavior Rules To Your Risk Plan
steps.intro: Set a maximum trades per day, a pause after a loss, and write your behavior rules. Your mentor sees them.

points: A pre-commitment is a rule written before: if this, then that.
Every behavior has a signature you can measure and a rule that answers it.
Run a checklist before every order. If any answer is no, there is no order.

lessons.title: Scenario Lab
lessons.aim: From a short story, name the behavior, name the rule, and score the process.

blocks.text: Each story is short and never names the behavior. Read it, name the behavior, then name the rule that answers it. Twelve stories, in a mixed order, come up as you practise.

points: Name the behavior first, then the rule that answers it.
The story never says the name. The signature gives it away.
A valid setup does not cancel a pause, a limit or the planned size.

lessons.title: The Post-Trade Review
lessons.aim: Review a trade in the right order: process, then outcome, then what the trade proves.

items: **Score the process.** Were the rules followed and was risk as planned? Judge from the plan and the record, before you look at the result.
**Note the outcome.** In R, not in dollars.
**Decide what evidence the trade adds.** One trade rarely changes what you believe about the method. Say what it does and does not prove.

blocks.title: The Order Matters
blocks.text: If you look at the result first, the process score follows it. That is outcome bias.

blocks.title: The Record
head: Item
Value
rows: Risk 1%. Enter at a retest of a broken level, in the direction of the higher-timeframe trend. Stop just beyond the level. Maximum 2 trades a day. 30-minute pause after a loss.
Break of the 1.0950 resistance level, retest planned at 1.0950
1.0983, market order, 7 minutes after the previous trade closed at a loss
0.40 lots on a $10,000 account, after the previous trade at 0.20 lots

blocks.text: The result is hidden until you have decided the process.

steps.title: My Review Of This Trade
steps.prompt: Write a post-trade review of the trade above, in the right order: the process score and which rules were or were not followed, then the outcome in R, then what the trade does and does not prove.
rubric: Scores the process first, before the outcome.
Names which rules were broken and which were followed.
States the outcome in R.
Says what the trade does not prove (for example, that one loss says nothing about the method).
Names the behaviors involved (revenge trading, moving a stop, raised size, overtrading, FOMO) and the rule that answers each.
steps.modelAnswer: Process: poor. Five rules were broken. Entry was 33 pips above the planned retest level (FOMO), 7 minutes after a loss (no 30-minute pause, so revenge trading), at twice the previous size, with the stop moved from 1.0951 to 1.0921, on the third trade of a two-trade day. Only the stop being set was followed. Outcome: −1.9R, worse than a normal 1R loss because the stop moved. Evidence: the trade does not show that the method fails, because the method was not followed. It shows the behavior costing me. Rules that answer it: no plan level, no order; a pause after a loss; stops move only toward reducing risk; size never rises after a loss; a maximum of two trades a day.

points: Review in order: process, outcome, then the evidence.
Score the process from the plan before you look at the result.
One trade adds little evidence about the method. It can show a behavior.

lessons.title: What Is A Strategy?
lessons.aim: State the ten components, and read a strategy to find which are missing.

blocks.text: A **strategy** is a written procedure: for this market, at this time, when these conditions are true, do this, and when they are not, stay out. It does not say where price will go. It says what you will do.

blocks.title: Hypothetical
blocks.text: Everything you write in this level is a hypothetical strategy for practice. The course never tells you which strategy to use, and nothing written here has been tested.

blocks.title: What A Strategy Must Specify
head: Component
Must Specify
rows: A window in a named time zone
The exact trigger and the order type
A fixed R, a structure or a time
The risk and how the size is computed
Every partial exit, stop move or trail

blocks.text: Below, a strategy is shown with some components left blank. Your job is to say which are missing.

points: A strategy is a procedure, not a prediction.
It specifies ten components: market, timeframe, session, setup, entry, stop, target, sizing, management and no-trade conditions.
A missing component is a decision left for the moment of trading.

lessons.title: A Belief Against A Strategy
lessons.aim: Rewrite a belief as a procedure that could be applied, and found wrong.

blocks.text: "I think price will go up" is a belief. "My strategy produces a long setup when A, B and C occur" is a strategy. The first cannot be wrong until price has moved, and then it is explained away. The second can be applied to a chart and found wrong.

blocks.title: Belief: "EUR/USD looks bullish this week."
steps: Strategy: "On the 1-hour chart, when a candle closes above the previous day high between 08:00 and 11:00 New York time, place a buy limit at that high with a stop 4 pips below the pullback low and a fixed 2R target."

steps.title: My Three Rewrites
steps.prompt: Rewrite each belief as a rule that two people could apply to the same chart: (1) "The market is trending, so buy dips." (2) "Gold always reacts to news." (3) "This level is important."
rubric: Replaces "trending" with a measurable condition (for example, a rule on swings or closes).
Says what counts as a dip, and what action is taken and where.
Turns "always reacts" into a testable statement with a window, a size of reaction and a count.
Turns "important" into a level defined by a rule (a previous high, a session low) and what happens when price reaches it.
Avoids words like strong, clear, good, important, always.
steps.modelAnswer: (1) When the 1-hour structure makes higher highs and higher lows by the swing rule, and price closes back above the 20-bar average after touching it, buy at the next candle open with the stop below the pullback low. (2) In the 15 minutes after a high-impact USD release, price moves at least 20 pips in one direction more often than after a random 15-minute window; I count every release for 100 days. (3) A level is the previous day high. If price touches it within the session, I place a buy limit there and stop below the lowest low of the approach.

points: A belief cannot be wrong until it is explained away.
A strategy says: when A, B and C, do this. It can be applied and found wrong.
Replace words like strong, clear or important with a number, a level or a clock time.

lessons.title: Market And Timeframe Choices
lessons.aim: Choose a market and timeframe under constraints, and say why.

items: **Costs.** The spread is a bigger share of a small stop.
**Liquidity.** Thin markets slip.
**Session activity.** Your market must move during the hours you can watch.
**Data.** You need enough history to test.
**Opportunities.** A shorter timeframe gives more trades, and more costs.

blocks.title: Write The Reason
blocks.text: The market component is only complete when a reason is given. "EUR/USD" alone is a name, not a choice.

A strategy states two: the timeframe you **analyse** on, to see the setup, and the one you **execute** on, to place the order. A common choice is one step down to execute, for example 1-hour to analyse and 5-minute to execute.

points: Choose by costs, liquidity, session activity, data and opportunities.
Write the reason down. A name alone is not a choice.
State both the analysis and the execution timeframe.

lessons.title: Session And Time Rules
lessons.aim: Write a trading window with a named time zone that survives the clock changes.

blocks.text: "Trade the London open" means different hours on your clock across the year, because the UK and the US change their clocks on different dates. A rule must say the **zone** and the **hours**.

blocks.title: Ambiguous: "Trade the London open."
steps: Written: "Trade from 07:00 to 10:00 London time, all year. On my Guyana clock that is 03:00 to 06:00 in summer and 04:00 to 07:00 in winter."

blocks.title: Name The Clock
blocks.text: A window is tied to ONE clock. If it follows London, it moves on your clock when London changes, and that is correct for a London-open strategy.

A robust rule gives the window in the market's own time, and in the student's time for the dates it matters. The market's own clock is the rule. The student's clock is a convenience that changes twice a year.

points: Name the zone and the hours. Do not say "the open".
The window follows one clock, and it moves on your clock when that clock changes.
Write the rule in the market's time. Convert it for your own clock when the dates matter.

lessons.title: Setup Against Entry Trigger
lessons.aim: Separate the context that makes a trade possible from the event that fires the order.

blocks.text: A **setup** is a state: the conditions that make a trade possible, which can last for hours. An **entry trigger** is an event: the single moment that fires the order.

blocks.title: Setup: the 1-hour structure is up and price is inside the session window.
steps: Trigger: a 5-minute candle closes back above the broken level.

blocks.text: If the two are mixed, you cannot say when the trade was allowed and when it happened. Separate them and you can count: how often is the setup present, and how often does it produce a trigger.

points: A setup is a state. A trigger is an event.
The trigger fires only when the setup is already in place.
Keep them apart so you can count how often each happens.

lessons.title: Stop And Target Conditions
lessons.aim: Write a stop and a target as rules, and compute expectancy under different target rules.

blocks.text: A stop is a **condition**: "3 pips below the swing low of the pullback." A target is a condition: "a fixed 2R" or "the previous day high." Words like "somewhere below" or "when it looks done" are hopes.

steps.title: A Target Trades Win Rate Against R

blocks.text: A nearer target is hit more often and pays less. A farther target is hit less often and pays more. The product decides.

blocks.title: The Same Entries, Three Target Rules
head: Target Rule
Win Rate
Expectancy
