blocks.note: A made-up example where the three happen to be equal.

blocks.title: No Best Target
blocks.text: No target rule is best in general. Which is better depends on the win rates you measure, and you only learn those by testing.

steps.title: Expectancy Of A Target Rule
steps.intro: Win rate times R, minus the losers.

points: A stop and a target are conditions tied to a level, a number of pips or an R.
A nearer target wins more and pays less. Expectancy decides which is better.
Which target rule is better is learned by testing.

lessons.title: Position Sizing And Trade Management
lessons.aim: Write sizing and management as rules, so every change after entry is testable.

steps.title: Sizing Links To The Risk Plan

blocks.text: The sizing component does not invent a risk. It says: "risk is the percent in my Risk Plan, and lots are computed from the stop distance and rounded down." The Risk Plan holds the number. The strategy holds the method.

steps.title: Management Is Part Of The Strategy

blocks.text: Partial exits, moving a stop to breakeven, trailing: each is a **rule**, written before entry. If you change things by feel during a trade, your results describe you, not the strategy, and cannot be tested.

blocks.title: A rule: "If price reaches 1R, move the stop to breakeven. No other changes."
steps: Not a rule: "Adjust the stop as the trade develops."

blocks.title: No Management Is A Choice
blocks.text: If you do nothing after entry, write "no management". That is complete, and testable.

points: Sizing links to the Risk Plan and is computed from the stop.
Every management action is a rule written before entry.
"No management" is a complete, testable choice.

lessons.title: No-Trade Conditions
lessons.aim: Write at least three testable conditions that mean you stay out.

steps.title: Staying Out Is A Rule Too

blocks.text: A **no-trade condition** says when you do not trade even if the setup is present. Examples: a high-impact release within 30 minutes; a spread above a stated number; the daily loss limit reached; the chart data is missing.

blocks.title: Testable
blocks.text: Each must be something you can check without a feeling. "Avoid news" is not testable. "No order within 30 minutes of a high-impact release for either currency" is.

steps.title: Saying Why There Is No Setup

blocks.text: Sometimes the right answer is "no setup here". Say why: which condition is not met. That is what makes a no-trade decision reviewable.

points: A no-trade condition says when to stay out even with a setup.
Write at least three, each testable from a number or the clock.
When there is no trade, say which condition was not met.

lessons.title: Making Rules Testable: The Two-Person Test
lessons.aim: Rewrite ambiguous rules until two people would reach the same decision.

blocks.text: Could two people apply these rules to the same chart and get the same decision? If not, the rules are not yet testable. The usual culprits are words like **strong, clear, good, nearby, around, enough, significant**.

blocks.title: Ambiguous: "Enter when the trend looks strong."
steps: Testable: "Enter when the 1-hour close is above the close 20 bars earlier."

steps.title: Your Mentor Will Apply Your Rules

blocks.text: When you send your strategy to your mentor, they will apply the written rules to five charts. They may not ask you what you meant. If they cannot decide, you will be asked to rewrite.

steps.title: My Three Rewrites
steps.prompt: Rewrite these ambiguous rules so that two people would agree: (1) "Enter when there is a clear pullback." (2) "Take profit near the next resistance." (3) "Skip the trade if volatility is high."
rubric: Replaces "clear" with a rule on price (for example, a pullback of at least a stated number of pips or candles against the trend).
Replaces "near the next resistance" with a defined level and what happens at it.
Replaces "high" with a measured threshold (for example, a range larger than a stated number of pips over a stated number of bars).
Uses numbers, levels or clock times, not judgement words.
Each rewrite could be applied to a chart by another person.
steps.modelAnswer: (1) Enter when price has pulled back against the 1-hour trend by at least 15 pips and no more than 40 pips from the last swing high, and a 5-minute candle closes back in the trend direction. (2) Take profit at the previous day high if it is at least 1.5R from the entry, otherwise a fixed 2R. (3) Skip the trade if the average true range of the last 14 five-minute bars is above 6 pips.

points: The Two-Person Test: two people, one chart, one decision.
Replace words like strong, clear and good with a number, a level or a clock time.
Your mentor will apply your rules to five charts, without asking what you meant.

lessons.title: Hypotheses And Expectations
lessons.aim: Write what you expect, and what would count as failure, before any test.

blocks.text: A test with no stated failure cannot fail. Before any test, write four things: the **win rate range** you expect, the **average R**, the **smallest sample** you will accept, and **what result would count as failure**.

blocks.title: After The Fact Is Not A Hypothesis
blocks.text: If you write what you expect after you see the result, you will find that you expected what happened. Write it first and keep the date.

blocks.title: Expect a win rate of 35% to 45% at a fixed 2R target, so an expectancy between 0.05R and 0.35R.
steps: Accept no fewer than 100 trades before reading anything.
Failure: an average R at or below zero, with the interval around it entirely below +0.2R, after 100 trades.

steps.title: My Expectations Before Testing
steps.prompt: Write pre-registered expectations for the Training Rule Pack strategy (a fixed 2R target, breakeven move at 1R): the win rate range, the average R, the smallest sample and the failure condition.
rubric: Gives a win rate range, not a single number.
Gives an expected average R that follows from the win rate range and the 2R target.
States a smallest sample before reading any result.
States a failure condition that a result could meet (a number).
Is written before any test, and says so.
steps.modelAnswer: Before any test: I expect a win rate of 35% to 45%. With a fixed 2R target that gives an expectancy of 0.05R to 0.35R, a little lower because the breakeven move turns some winners into zeros. I will read nothing until I have 100 trades. Failure: an average R at or below zero after 100 trades, or a win rate below 30%. I am writing this today, before I have looked at any chart.

points: Write the win rate range, the average R, the smallest sample and the failure condition before any test.
A test that cannot fail cannot prove anything.
Date the page. After the fact is not a hypothesis.

lessons.title: Strategy Builder Lab
lessons.aim: Build a hypothetical strategy in ten parts that passes the Completeness Check.

blocks.text: Write your own hypothetical strategy in the ten parts, or start from the **Training Rule Pack**. The pack is exercise text. It is not a recommendation, it has not been tested, and you are expected to change it.

blocks.title: The Checks
blocks.text: The Completeness Check must show ten out of ten, and no vague words may remain. Then you can send it to your mentor, who applies it to five charts.

steps.title: The Strategy Builder
steps.intro: Write each part. Replace every vague word with a number, a level or a clock time.

points: A strategy is ten written parts that pass the Completeness Check.
The Training Rule Pack is exercise text, not advice.
Your mentor applies the rules to five charts before approving.

lessons.title: Strategy Critique Lab
lessons.aim: Critique three supplied strategies for missing parts, ambiguity and overfitting.

items: **Missing or vague components.** Can two people apply it?
**Discretionary management or exits.** Does a feeling change the trade?
**Overfitting warning signs.** Many very precise numbers, hundreds of variants tried, a single short period, a narrow window that looks fitted.

blocks.title: A Sign, Not A Proof
blocks.text: These are warning signs. They do not prove a strategy is bad, and a clean-looking one is not proven good. Only testing on new data tells.

points: Look for missing or vague components, discretionary management and overfitting signs.
Warning signs are not proof either way.
Only testing on data you have not used can tell.

lessons.title: What Is Backtesting?
lessons.aim: Say what a backtest can show and what it cannot.

blocks.text: A **backtest** applies a written strategy to past data and records what the rule would have done. It needs a precise rule, which is why Level 12 came first.

steps.title: What It Can And Cannot Show

blocks.title: Backtest Claims
head: A Backtest Can Show
A Backtest Cannot Show
rows: How the rule behaved on this data, under stated assumptions
That it will behave the same way on new data
Whether a rule is even unambiguous enough to test
The size of losses, losing streaks and drawdowns it produced
That you would have followed it through them
That there is an edge, from a small sample

blocks.title: As Honest As Its Protocol
blocks.text: Every bias in this level is a way a test can look better than the truth. The protocol you will learn is what keeps a backtest honest.

points: A backtest shows how a precise rule behaved on past data under stated assumptions.
It cannot show that the rule will work.
It is only as honest as the protocol used to run it.

lessons.title: Sample Size And Randomness
lessons.aim: See how a small sample shows an edge that is not there, and how the interval shrinks.

blocks.text: The average R of a set of trades is itself uncertain. The **standard error** is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of trades. To halve the uncertainty you need four times the trades.

steps.title: The Randomness Lab
steps.intro: Guess first. Then run one hundred traders who all flip a fair coin.

blocks.text: Every trader had the same fair rules. About half finish ahead, a few look "significant", and the best looks skilled. Pick the best of many and you will always find one. That is what chance does, and it is why a single good-looking result proves little.

steps.title: The Standard Error
steps.intro: Divide by the square root of the number of trades.

steps.title: Trades Needed
steps.intro: Smaller effects need far more trades.

points: The standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of trades.
Halving the uncertainty takes four times the trades.
Among many traders with no edge, some will look skilled.

lessons.title: Hindsight And Look-Ahead Bias
lessons.aim: Find the information a test used before it could have been known.

blocks.text: **Look-ahead bias** is using information that was not available at the moment of the decision. Two examples: a swing low marked on the bar where it occurred, when it is only confirmed after more bars have closed; and a day's high used to decide an entry before the day has ended.
**Hindsight bias** is its cousin in your own head: on an old chart, the right trades look obvious.

steps.title: Find It In A Supplied Test

blocks.text: Below is a test, step by step. Select the steps that use information not available at that moment.

points: Look-ahead bias uses information that was not available at the decision.
A swing before it is confirmed, or a day's high before the day ends, are the classic cases.
Hindsight makes old charts look easy. Test only on what was known then.

lessons.title: Cherry-Picking And Survivorship Bias
lessons.aim: Spot the results that were chosen, and the ones that were never counted.

blocks.text: **Cherry-picking** is showing the good examples and leaving out the rest. **Survivorship bias** is testing only on what survived, such as companies still listed today, so every failure is missing. The same thing happens in your own journal if you log only the trades you are proud of.

blocks.title: A seller shows twelve winning screenshots of a strategy. Questions to ask: How many trades were taken in total? How many were not shown? Who chose these twelve? What would the whole list look like?

points: Cherry-picking shows the good and hides the rest.
Survivorship bias tests only what survived.
In your own journal, log every valid setup, winners and losers, and explain every skip.

lessons.title: Data Snooping And Overfitting
lessons.aim: See that the best of many rules on random data looks good, and fails on new data.

blocks.text: **Data snooping** is trying many variants on the same data and keeping the best. **Overfitting** is fitting many parameters so closely to one sample that they describe its noise. Both make a past result look much better than anything you should expect from new data.

steps.title: The Noise Mine
steps.intro: Try many rules on random data, keep the best, then test it on new random data.

blocks.text: The data was random, so no rule has a real edge. Yet the best of many looked good in the data it was mined from, and ordinary on new data. The more rules you try, the better the winner looks, and the less it means.

blocks.title: The Warning In Your Own Tools
blocks.text: The Journal counts how many slices you have looked at. After a dozen, a good-looking slice is expected by chance. Treat it as a hypothesis to test on new data.

points: Data snooping keeps the best of many tries. Overfitting fits noise with many parameters.
The best rule on random data looks good in-sample and ordinary out-of-sample.
The fix is data the rule has never seen.

lessons.title: In-Sample And Out-Of-Sample
lessons.aim: Split the data before looking, and keep the out-of-sample part clean.

blocks.text: Divide the data into an **in-sample** part and an **out-of-sample** part BEFORE you look at either. Use the in-sample part to write and test the rule. Freeze it. Then run the out-of-sample part once, with no changes.

blocks.title: A Used Test Is Used Up
blocks.text: If you look at the out-of-sample result, change the rule, and run it again, the out-of-sample data has become in-sample. You can only use it once. The Backtest Lab locks the out-of-sample bars until your in-sample conclusion is saved.

points: Split the data before you look.
Freeze the rule, then run the out-of-sample data once.
Data you looked at and changed the rule for is no longer out-of-sample.

lessons.title: Costs And Realistic Fills In Tests
lessons.aim: See what spread, slippage and the same-candle rule do to a result.

blocks.text: Spread, commission and slippage each take R from every trade. A strategy that averages +0.3R gross with a 10-pip stop and a 1.5-pip spread loses 0.15R per trade to the spread alone.

steps.title: After The Spread
steps.intro: Gross R minus the spread divided by the stop.

steps.title: The Fill Assumptions Lab
steps.intro: One rule, one set of bars, four sets of assumptions.

blocks.text: Chart data cannot say what happened inside a candle. When one candle reaches both the stop and the target, the conservative rule takes the **stop first**. It may sometimes be wrong against you. It is never kinder than the truth could be.

points: Spread, slippage and commission take R from every trade.
When a candle reaches both stop and target, take the stop first.
A result is only as good as its assumptions. State them.

lessons.title: Running A Manual Backtest Properly
lessons.aim: Follow the protocol so the test cannot flatter itself.

items: **Write the hypothesis first:** expected win rate range, average R, smallest sample, and what counts as failure. It is time-stamped.
**Fix the data window and the split** before any trade is logged, and declare the costs.
**Step bar by bar** through the in-sample bars. Log EVERY valid setup, winners and losers, and explain every skip.
**Conclude in-sample**, and lock the conclusion.
**Unlock the out-of-sample bars.** Run them once. No parameter changes.
**State the final conclusion** with the interval, whether it includes zero, and what can and cannot be concluded.
Pre-registered: the hypothesis time-stamp precedes the first trade.
Split declared first.
Out-of-sample untouched until the in-sample conclusion is locked.
In time order.
No silent skips and no look-ahead.
Costs applied.
Conclusion calibrated: an edge cannot be claimed when the interval includes zero.

blocks.title: Graded On Honesty
blocks.text: The lab is graded on how the test was run and how honestly it was concluded. It is not graded on whether the rule made money.

points: Pre-register, split, step bar by bar, log everything, lock, unlock the out-of-sample data once, conclude with the interval.
The checks test how it was run, not the result.
The lab minimums are far too few to establish an edge, and the lab says so.

lessons.title: The Trading Journal
lessons.aim: Keep a complete, accurate journal, and read what its audit tells you.

blocks.title: Journal Fields And Their Jobs
head: Field
Why It Is There
rows: So you can filter and order the record
Suggested from the time and the clocks of the day; you confirm
So results can be split by setup
So R can be recomputed from the prices
So sizing can be checked against your Risk Plan
Entered by you, then compared with the prices
So stops moved or trades cut short can be seen
Empty is itself a signature of confirmation bias
Pre-filled when measurable, such as risk above your cap

blocks.text: Every save runs the audit: R recomputed from the prices must match the recorded R within 0.05R; the stop must be on the right side; the lots, stop distance and money at risk must agree; the session tag must match the time with daylight saving; all required fields must be present. Failures are **notes to fix**, not penalties.

steps.title: Fix The Entry
steps.intro: The journal entry below has four mistakes. Fix the record until every check passes.

points: Every journal field has a job.
The accuracy audit compares prices, R, stop side, sizing and session tag.
Failures are notes to fix, not penalties for trading.

lessons.title: Performance Statistics
lessons.aim: Compute the statistics from a journal, and read each with its uncertainty.

items: **Number of trades**, always shown beside every figure.
**Win rate**, with breakeven trades counted apart.
**Average R** and **expectancy**, net of costs.
**Profit factor**: total winners divided by total losers. Not defined with no losses.
**Average winner** and **average loser**.
**Maximum drawdown** in R, with where it began and whether it recovered.
**Longest winning and losing streaks.**
**Median R**, compared with the mean to show outlier dependence.

steps.title: Profit Factor
steps.intro: Winners over losers.

steps.title: Drawdown From A List
steps.intro: The largest fall from a peak, in R.

blocks.text: Each figure has sampling error. The analytics show an **interval** on the average R, say whether it includes zero, and run a **sign-flip test**: flip the sign of each trade at random many times and see how often the average is at least as good. A result that random outcomes match one time in three is not evidence of much.

steps.title: Analytics On A Sample Journal
steps.intro: A made-up journal of 60 trades. Read the interval first, then use the filters.

points: Every statistic shows how many trades it rests on.
The interval on the average, and whether it includes zero, is the real answer to "how sure am I?".
After many slices, a good one is expected by chance.

lessons.title: Interpreting Results
lessons.aim: Answer the eight evidence questions on a supplied result, and say what can and cannot be concluded.

items: What information do I have?
What are the possible outcomes?
What would invalidate my hypothesis?
What is my risk?
What does the historical evidence say?
Is there actually an edge?
How large is my sample?
Could this be random?

blocks.text: The Analytics page ends with these eight, filled in where the app can answer and blank where you must.
Read the result below. Then write what can and cannot be concluded.

steps.title: What I Can And Cannot Conclude
steps.prompt: Using the eight questions, write what you can and cannot conclude from the supplied result. Say what you would do next.
rubric: Says the interval includes zero, so an edge is not shown.
Notes the sample of 48 trades is small, and gives the interval as the real answer.
Notes that 14% of random sign-flip runs did as well, so it could be random.
Mentions the 11 slices examined and the snooping warning, or the costs that leave out slippage.
Says what would invalidate the hypothesis or what to do next (more data, a clean out-of-sample test), without claiming an edge or no edge.
steps.modelAnswer: Information: 48 backtest trades, spread included but not slippage. Outcomes: the average could plausibly be anywhere from −0.12R to +0.54R. Invalidation: an out-of-sample average at or below zero. Risk: not shown here, so I would check the drawdown against my Risk Plan. Evidence: a positive average of +0.21R, but the interval includes zero, so I cannot say there is an edge. Sample: 48 trades is small. Random: random outcomes of the same sizes did this well in 14% of runs, so chance is a real explanation. The 11 slices I looked at mean one good-looking result is expected anyway. I conclude: not enough to say. Next: a clean out-of-sample run with slippage included, and more trades.

points: Ask the eight questions. Most results on small samples answer "cannot say".
The interval, the sample and the sign-flip test are the real answer.
Say what you would do next: more data, a clean out-of-sample run.

lessons.title: The Ladder Of Evidence
lessons.aim: Order the rungs and say what each one can catch.

blocks.title: From Cheap To Costly
head: Rung
What It Can Catch
rows: Whether a precise rule shows anything on past data
Whether it survives data it was not built on
Whether you can apply the rule live, bar by bar, without hindsight
Real-time fills, spreads, and your own execution, with no money at risk
The psychology of real money, at a size you can lose
Whether larger size changes fills and behaviour

blocks.text: Each rung catches something the one below cannot. You climb only with evidence on each.

steps.title: What This Curriculum Does Not Say

blocks.title: Not A Strategy
blocks.text: Finishing this curriculum does not give you a profitable strategy. It does not encourage funded-account programs, and it does not suggest any amount of capital. If you ever trade live, it is a small amount that you can afford to lose.
Whether any rule in this course has an edge is not claimed. Everything you test here is for learning how to test.

points: The ladder: backtest, out-of-sample, replay, demo forward test, small live, scaling.
Each rung catches a problem the one below cannot.
Completing this curriculum is not a profitable strategy, and nothing here encourages funded accounts or significant capital.

lessons.title: Backtest Lab
lessons.aim: Run the full protocol on the Training Rule Pack, and conclude with the interval.

blocks.text: You will run the Training Rule Pack on synthetic bars, following the protocol: hypothesis, locked window and split, in-sample run, locked in-sample conclusion, out-of-sample run, final conclusion with its interval. Your trades go to the Journal, marked as backtest.

blocks.title: Graded On Honesty
blocks.text: The lab is graded on how you run the test and how honestly you conclude, not on whether the rule paid. The data is synthetic and has no edge in it. The minimums are far too few to establish one, and the lab says so.

steps.title: The Backtest Lab
steps.intro: Follow the six steps in order. Every check must pass.

points: The protocol: hypothesis, split, in-sample, lock, out-of-sample once, final conclusion with the interval.

lessons.title: Hidden-Future Plan Series
lessons.aim: Plan with the future hidden, and see your process scored before the outcome.

blocks.text: You are shown a chart with its future hidden. Decide whether the rule gives a setup, and if so choose the stop, the target and the size. If there is no setup, say why. Submit. Your **process** is scored first. Only then is the future shown and your plan simulated.

blocks.title: Two Numbers, Kept Apart
blocks.text: The process score measures what you control. The outcome is one trade, and six outcomes say almost nothing. Both are kept, separately.

steps.title: The Plan Series
steps.intro: Six charts. Half of them have no setup.

points: Plan with the future hidden, then see the process score, then the outcome.

lessons.title: The Platform Landscape
lessons.aim: Tell a charting platform, a trading platform and a broker apart, and say what each does and does not do.

items: **A charting platform** draws charts from a data feed.
**A trading platform** sends your orders and shows your account.
**A broker** holds your account and fills or routes the orders.

blocks.text: One product can do more than one of these. The jobs stay separate: a chart can be correct while a fill is poor, and an account can be fine while the chart is misleading.

blocks.title: Verify On Your Own Copy
blocks.text: Menu names and options differ between platform versions and change over time. Treat every platform detail in this track as something to verify on your own copy.

steps.title: An Alert Is Not A Signal

blocks.text: A price alert tells you that price reached a level. It does not say whether to trade. It is a notification, nothing more.

blocks.title: No Provider Is Recommended
blocks.text: This track teaches you to operate the tools and to evaluate providers yourself. It does not tell you which to use.

points: A charting platform draws, a trading platform sends orders, a broker holds the account and fills them.
An alert is a notification, not a signal.
This track recommends no provider.

lessons.title: Charting Setup
lessons.aim: Set the time zone, timeframe and sessions on a chart, and know what replay shows.

blocks.text: A chart drawn in the wrong time zone makes every time rule wrong. Set the zone on your charting platform to the one you chose in Level 0, then read the time of the latest candle and check it against your own clock.

blocks.title: Verify On Your Own Copy
blocks.text: Menu names and options differ between platform versions and change over time. Treat every platform detail in this track as something to verify on your own copy.

items: A timeframe is how much time each candle summarises (Level 6).
A session display shades the hours of a market. Check that it follows that market's own clock through daylight saving.
**Replay** steps through past bars one at a time. It is useful for practice and for the forward-only stepping of a manual backtest. It does not show the spread or the slippage you would have met.

points: Set the time zone first, and read the latest candle against your own clock.
Sessions follow each market's own clock.
Replay is practice. It leaves out the spread and the slippage.

lessons.title: Trading Platform Orientation
lessons.aim: Find the main panels, read a symbol specification and find the server time.

items: A list of symbols with their quotes (often called Market Watch).
A list of tools and accounts (often called the Navigator).
A panel for open trades, history and the account (often called the Terminal).
A specification for each symbol: contract size, smallest lot, lot step, spread and more.

blocks.title: Verify On Your Own Copy
blocks.text: Menu names and options differ between platform versions and change over time. Treat every platform detail in this track as something to verify on your own copy.

Your trading platform has a **server time**. Market time and your own time are two others. The server clock is usually offset from UTC by a whole number of hours, and the offset can change twice a year. Find it by comparing the platform clock with UTC, write it down, and recheck it after a clock change.

steps.title: Read The Offset
steps.intro: Server time minus UTC.

points: Find the main panels and the symbol specification.
The server clock is a third clock. Find its offset from UTC and write it down.
Recheck the offset after a clock change.

lessons.title: Accounts And Specifications
lessons.aim: Read the account currency, leverage setting, lot limits and contract specification.

items: **Account currency.** Profit and loss are shown in it, and conversion applies to pairs that do not include it.
**Leverage setting.** It sets how much margin a position needs. It is a limit, not an aim.
**Smallest lot and lot step.** They set how finely you can size a trade, and why sizes are rounded down.
**Contract specification.** The contract size, pip size and spread of each symbol.

blocks.title: Verify On Your Own Copy
blocks.text: Menu names and options differ between platform versions and change over time. Treat every platform detail in this track as something to verify on your own copy.
A demo and a live account can differ in fills, spreads, execution speed and the conditions attached to them. Do not assume they match: measure.

points: Know the account currency, the leverage setting, the lot limits and the symbol specification.
Leverage is a limit, not an aim.
Demo and live may differ. Measure.

lessons.title: Opening A Demo Account
lessons.aim: Open a demo on your own device, record what it shows, and know what a demo cannot teach.

items: Choose a platform to practise on. The choice is yours. Your mentor does not need it to be any particular one.
Open a demo account with pretend money.
Write down the platform and version, the account currency, the leverage setting and the starting balance.

blocks.title: Personal Details
blocks.text: A demo may ask for contact details. Think before giving any, and never give passwords, bank or card details to anyone who asks for them while you practise.

blocks.title: Verify On Your Own Copy
blocks.text: Menu names and options differ between platform versions and change over time. Treat every platform detail in this track as something to verify on your own copy.

steps.title: What A Demo Does Not Show

blocks.text: A demo teaches the **mechanics**: how to place, modify and close a trade, and how to read the account. It may not reproduce real fills, spreads or execution speed, and it cannot reproduce the feeling of real money. Do not judge a strategy by a demo's fills.

points: Open a demo and record the platform, currency, leverage and balance.
A demo teaches mechanics. It may fill more kindly than live, and it cannot reproduce real money.
Never share passwords or payment details while practising.

lessons.title: Placing, Modifying And Closing Trades
lessons.aim: Place a demo trade with a stop and target, check the ticket, modify it and close part of it.

blocks.text: Before you press the button, the ticket should match your plan: the direction, the lots from your size calculation, the stop at the invalidation level, and the target. Attach the stop and target to the order. A trade without a stop is a choice to be wrong without limit.

steps.title: Check The Ticket Against Your R

blocks.text: From the prices on the ticket you can recompute your planned R: reward distance divided by risk distance. If it does not match the R you planned, something on the ticket is wrong. Fix the ticket before you send it.

steps.title: R From The Ticket Prices
steps.intro: Reward over risk, from the prices.

blocks.text: Move a stop only to reduce risk (Level 11). To close part of a position, close a number of lots you can choose, and note the price. Write each action in your journal with its reason.

points: Make the ticket match the plan before you send it.
Recompute R from the prices on the ticket.
Move a stop only to reduce risk. Write every action in the journal.

lessons.title: Reading The Account
lessons.aim: Read balance, equity, margin, free margin and margin level on a real panel.

items: **Balance:** your money without the open trades.
**Floating profit or loss:** what the open trades show now.
**Equity:** balance plus floating profit or loss.
**Margin:** what the open positions need as a deposit.
**Free margin:** equity minus margin used.

blocks.text: **Margin level** is equity divided by margin, as a percent. Check the panel on your own demo: the numbers should agree with each other.

steps.title: Free Margin
steps.intro: Equity minus the margin used.

points: Equity is balance plus floating profit or loss.
Free margin is equity minus margin used.
Margin level is equity divided by margin.

lessons.title: Exporting Trade History
lessons.aim: Export a platform statement and check it before it goes anywhere near your journal.

blocks.text: Every platform can produce a history or a statement of the trades you took. It is the platform's own record, so it is the best check on your journal. Export one from your demo, and open it.

blocks.title: Verify On Your Own Copy
blocks.text: Menu names and options differ between platform versions and change over time. Treat every platform detail in this track as something to verify on your own copy.

items: Is every trade there, including the ones you would rather forget?
Which clock do the times use: server time, UTC or your own?
Are costs shown: spread, commission, swap?
Does each trade's result match the prices, in R?

blocks.title: Not Built Yet
blocks.text: This version of the app cannot import a platform file into the Journal. It can export the Journal as a file. Copy trades by hand, and let the audit check them.

points: The exported statement is the platform's own record.
Check that every trade is there, which clock the times use, and that costs are shown.
This version cannot import a platform file. Copy trades by hand.

lessons.title: Evaluating Providers I: Regulation
lessons.aim: Verify a provider's regulation at the regulator's own register, and say what regulation does and does not guarantee.

blocks.text: A provider's website may say it is licensed. So may an advert, a review or a friend. None of those is the source. The source is the **regulator's own register**, which you reach yourself, by typing its address or searching for it, not by following a link the provider gave you.

items: Write down the provider's exact legal name and the license number it claims.
Find the regulator's own register yourself.
Look up the name and number. Do they match exactly? Is the license current, and does it cover the service offered?
Note the date you checked, and the source.

blocks.text: Regulation can mean the firm must follow rules and may be inspected. It does not promise profit, good fills or that nothing can go wrong. Jurisdictions differ in what they require, and a firm may be licensed in one place and not another. If you cannot find the firm on the register, record that as a finding.

blocks.title: No Provider Is Recommended
blocks.text: This track will never name a provider. A regulation check tells you whether a claim is true. It does not tell you whether the provider is right for you.

points: Verify regulation at the regulator's own register, which you reach yourself.
Regulation does not promise profit or good fills, and jurisdictions differ.
Record the source and the date you checked. This track recommends no provider.

lessons.title: Evaluating Providers II: Costs And Execution
lessons.aim: Read the costs from the terms, and measure spread and slippage yourself on a demo.

items: **Spread, commission and swap** are in the provider's terms. Read them for the pairs you trade, and note where you read them.
**Spread in practice** varies through the day and around news. Record it on a demo at the hours you trade.
**Slippage** is the gap between the price you asked for and the fill. Record it over many orders, not one.

blocks.title: A Demo May Be Kind
blocks.text: A demo may fill more kindly than live. Measured slippage on a demo is a floor, not a ceiling.

steps.title: Slippage In Dollars
steps.intro: Pips times lots times the pip value.

steps.title: Total Cost In R
steps.intro: Spread, commission and swap against the stop.

points: Read the costs from the terms and note the source.
Measure spread and slippage on a demo, at your hours, over many orders.
Measured demo slippage is a floor. Live may be worse.

lessons.title: Evaluating Providers III: Funds And Restrictions
lessons.aim: Read the conditions for deposits, withdrawals and restrictions, and complete the Broker Worksheet.

items: Which methods are accepted for deposits and withdrawals, and in which currencies?
What do they cost, and what are the limits?
How long does a withdrawal take, in the terms and in practice?
Are there conditions on withdrawing, such as a required trading volume, inactivity fees or account closure rules?

blocks.text: Read the terms and keep a copy with its date. Terms change. Test a **small withdrawal** before you rely on the provider, and time it.

Some providers limit styles (for example scalping or news trading), set maximum leverage by account type, or charge when an account is idle. None of this is good or bad in itself. It is a condition that must fit how you trade, and it must be written down, with its source.

steps.title: The Broker Worksheet
steps.intro: A blank grid. Name two providers yourself, and fill every cell with a value, a source and a status.

points: Read the conditions for deposits, withdrawals and restrictions, and keep the source and date.
Test a small withdrawal before relying on a provider.
In the Broker Worksheet, unverified is an honest status.

lessons.title: Funded-Account Programs: Rules And Expected Value
lessons.aim: Read a program's rules and compute the expected value of its fee from your own honest inputs.

blocks.text: A **funded-account program** charges a fee and offers access to someone else's capital if you meet its rules, such as a profit target, a daily loss limit and a maximum drawdown. The fee is paid whether or not you pass.

blocks.title: Read The Terms Yourself
blocks.text: Rules, fees and payout terms differ between programs and change. Read the current terms of any program yourself. This course does not describe a particular one.

**Expected value** = (chance of passing × what you expect to receive) − fee. The chance of passing is YOUR honest estimate, built from evidence like a backtest interval, not from hope. A rule set with a tight daily loss limit and a small drawdown allowance makes a pass harder for a method with streaks (Level 10).

blocks.title: Fee $150. Payout if you pass $2,000. Honest chance of passing 5%: 0.05 × 2,000 − 150 = −$50.
steps: The same program with a 10% honest chance: 0.10 × 2,000 − 150 = +$50.

blocks.title: Not Encouraged
blocks.text: This course does not encourage funded programs. It shows the arithmetic so you can see what a fee is. If your honest estimate of passing is a guess, the expected value is a guess too.

steps.title: Expected Value Of A Fee
steps.intro: Chance times payout, minus the fee.

points: Expected value = chance of passing × payout − fee.
The chance must be your honest estimate from evidence.
The fee is paid whether or not you pass. This course does not encourage funded programs.

lessons.title: The Path To Live
lessons.aim: Write your own Path-To-Live Plan, with readiness in numbers, a capital rule and scaling last.

blocks.text: Level 13 gave the ladder: backtest, out-of-sample test, replay, demo forward test, small live, and only then any scaling. A Path-To-Live Plan turns it into your own written rules, **before** you are tempted.

items: **Readiness criteria in numbers:** for example how many demo forward-test trades, what the interval must show, how many days you followed your Risk Plan.
**The capital rule:** only money you can lose completely without changing how you live.
**Small live rules:** the size, the loss that stops the test, and how long it runs.
**Going back:** the exact conditions that send you back down the ladder.
**Scaling last:** what evidence must exist before size ever rises.

steps.title: What This Course Does Not Say

blocks.title: Not A Strategy, Not A Promise
blocks.text: Completing this curriculum is not a profitable strategy. Nothing in it encourages funded accounts or any amount of capital. If you ever trade live, it is a small amount you can lose completely, and only after the rungs below it.

steps.title: Your Path-To-Live Plan
steps.intro: Write each part in your own words, with numbers. Your mentor reads it.

points: A Path-To-Live Plan: readiness in numbers, a capital rule, small live rules, a way back, and scaling last.
Only money you can lose completely.
Completing this course is not a profitable strategy.

options.text: The name of the market's owner

questions.modelAnswer: Each trade is only one draw from a range of possible results. Say a method wins 40% of the time, makes $30 on a winner and loses $10 on a loser. On average it earns 0.4 × $30 − 0.6 × $10 = +$6 per trade. But on any one trade it is more likely to lose than win, and it will have runs of several losses in a row. So one loss does not show that the method is broken, and one win does not show that it is good. I should judge the method over many trades, and judge each decision by whether it followed the plan. With only a few trades, luck can make a good method look bad or a poor one look good.

rubric.text: Defines the terms with rules or numbers: which session and window, what counts as "taking" or "reaching" a high or low.

questions.modelAnswer: Hypothesis: after the London session closes (08:00–17:00 London time), the next New York session's first two hours trade beyond the London high or low within 12 bars more often than they trade beyond a level chosen at random within the same range. Test: over 120 trading days, note the London high and low each day, then count every day on which price trades beyond either one in the first two hours of the New York session, and compare with the same count for 300 random levels each day. The hypothesis fails if the London-level rate is not clearly above the range of the random levels. I count every day, not just the memorable ones, and I use the sessions' own clocks so daylight saving does not shift the windows.

templates.explain: Equity = {{balance|money}} + ({{pnl|money}}) = {{equity|money}}. Free margin = equity − used margin = {{answer|money}}.

templates.prompt: Your account equity is {{equity|money}} and your open position is worth {{value|money}}. How many times larger than the account is the position? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: You divided the account by the position. Divide the position by the account.

templates.explain: {{value|money}} ÷ {{equity|money}} = {{answer|dec:1}} times the account.

templates.prompt: The spread on {{pair|pair}} is {{sp}} pips and you trade {{lots|lots}}. Your account is in US dollars. What does the spread cost you, in dollars?

errorDetectors.message: You forgot the pip value. One pip on one lot is $10.
That is the cost for ONE lot. Multiply by your {{lots|lots}}.

templates.explain: {{sp}} pips × $10 per pip per lot × {{lots}} = {{answer|money}}.

templates.prompt: Your broker's swap for this position is {{rate|money}} per lot per night (a negative number is a charge). You hold {{lots|lots}} for {{nights}} nights. What is the total swap? Use the − key for a charge.

errorDetectors.message: That is one night only. Multiply by the number of nights.
That is for one lot. Multiply by your {{lots|lots}}.

templates.explain: {{lots}} lots × {{nights}} nights × ({{rate|money}}) = {{answer|money}}.

templates.prompt: A broker charges {{side|money}} per lot each way (once to open, once to close). You trade {{lots|lots}}. What is the commission for the full round trip?

errorDetectors.message: That is one way only. A round trip is opening AND closing, so it is charged twice.

templates.explain: {{lots}} lots × {{side|money}} × 2 = {{answer|money}}.

steps.label: Swap charge (a credit counts as negative)

templates.prompt: A EUR/USD trade of {{lots|lots}}: spread {{sp}} pips, commission {{comm|money}} per lot round trip, held {{nights}} nights at {{swap|money}} per lot per night, slippage {{slip}} pips. A pip is $10 per lot. What is the total cost? (A swap credit reduces it.)

errorDetectors.message: You left out the swap. Holding overnight adds a charge (or a credit).
You left out the commission.
You left out slippage.

templates.explain: Spread {{spreadC|money}} + commission {{commC|money}} + swap {{swapC|money}} + slippage {{slipC|money}} = {{answer|money}}.

templates.prompt: A trade's total cost is {{cost|money}} and its risk is {{risk|money}}. How much of 1R do the costs take, in percent? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the decimal. Multiply by 100 to make it a percent.
You divided the risk by the cost. Divide the cost by the risk.

templates.explain: {{cost|money}} ÷ {{risk|money}} = {{answer|dec:3}}, which is {{answer|fixed:1}}% of 1R.

templates.prompt: A trade makes {{gross|r}} before costs. Costs take {{costR}}R. What is the result after costs, in R?

errorDetectors.message: You forgot the costs. They reduce every result, winners included.
Costs are a subtraction, not an addition.

templates.explain: {{gross}}R − {{costR}}R = {{answer|dec:2}}R.

lv.expr: if(combo == 0, bid - d * ps, if(combo == 1, ask + d * ps, if(combo == 2, ask + d * ps, bid - d * ps)))

values.0: You expect the price to pull back to the level and then rise again, so you want to BUY if it falls to the level.
values.1: You expect that once the price rises through the level it will keep going, so you want to BUY when it reaches the level.
values.2: You expect the price to rally to the level and then fall back, so you want to SELL if it rises to the level.
values.3: You expect that once the price falls through the level it will keep falling, so you want to SELL when it reaches the level.

options.why: That is the right direction but the wrong type. A LIMIT waits for a better price (a pullback). A STOP waits for the price to move through the level (a breakout).
That trades in the wrong direction for your idea.
That trades in the wrong direction for your idea.

templates.explain: The level is {{lvT}}, and the market is {{bidT}} / {{askT}}. To {{name|up}}: a limit waits for the price to come back to a better level. A stop waits for the price to go through a level. So the order is a {{name}}.

values.0: it waits for the price to fall to a better buying price
values.1: it waits for the price to rise through the level
values.2: it waits for the price to rise to a better selling price
values.3: it waits for the price to fall through the level

templates.prompt: You place a {{name}} order on {{pair|pair}}. On which side of the current price must it sit?

options.why: That is the opposite side. Check whether the order is a limit (waits for a better price) or a stop (waits for a move through a level).
An order at the current price would just be a market order.

options.text: On either side, whichever you like.
options.why: Each pending order type has one valid side. The platform rejects the other.

templates.explain: A {{name}} sits {{where}} the current price: {{why}}.

templates.prompt: {{pair|pair}} is quoted {{bidT}} / {{askT}}. Tap a price where the platform would accept a {{name}}.
templates.explain: A {{name}} must sit on the correct side of the market, or the platform rejects it. Buy limits and sell stops go below the price. Buy stops and sell limits go above it.

templates.prompt: You have a {{name}} at {{lvT}}. Over a weekend the price {{moves}} straight past your level, and the market reopens with the ask at {{fillT}}. At what price is your order filled?

options.text: About {{fillT}}, the first price available. That is {{better}} than your level.
Exactly {{lvT}}, because that is the price you chose.
options.why: A pending order fills at the first available price once it is triggered. If the market jumped past your level, that is not your level.

options.text: It is cancelled, because the price never traded at {{lvT}}.
options.why: The order is triggered as soon as the price is at or beyond your level.

options.text: About {{fillT}}, which is {{wrongBetter}} than your level.
options.why: Check the direction: a limit gives you your level or better. A stop gives you your level or worse.

templates.explain: A limit order gives you your price or better, and a stop order gives you your price or worse. The market jumped from one side of {{lvT}} to {{fillT}}, so the fill is at {{fillT}}, {{better}} than the level.

values.0: It fills at about {{jumpT}}, within your limit.
values.1: It triggers but does not fill, because the ask is beyond your limit.

values.0: It triggers but does not fill.
It is rejected, because the price moved too fast.

templates.prompt: You place a buy stop-limit: trigger {{trigT}}, limit {{limT}}. The price rises and the ask jumps to {{jumpT}}. What happens?

options.why: Once triggered, a stop-limit fills only at your limit or better. Check where the ask is compared with the limit.
A stop-limit fills at your limit or better, and only if the market offers that price.

templates.explain: After the trigger, a stop-limit becomes a limit order. It fills only at {{limT}} or better. The ask is {{jumpT}}, so the outcome depends on whether that is within the limit.

templates.prompt: You {{go}} {{pair|pair}} at market. The price on screen when you clicked was {{shownT}}, and you were filled at {{fillT}}. How many pips of slippage against you? (Use the − key if the fill was BETTER than the screen. One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: You counted the fifth decimal as a whole pip. It is a tenth of a pip.
Check the sign. Slippage is measured against you: a worse fill is positive, a better fill is negative.

templates.explain: The screen showed {{shownT}} and you were filled at {{fillT}}. That is a gap of {{s|dec:1}} pips against you. A negative number would mean the fill was better than the screen.

templates.prompt: You are long with a stop-loss {{stop}} pips below your entry. Over the weekend the price gaps down and the market reopens {{total}} pips below your entry. The stop fills at the first available price. What is your result in R? Use the − key. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: A stop-loss does not guarantee the price. When the market gaps, it fills at the first available price, so the loss is bigger than 1R.
That is the loss in pips. R is the loss divided by the risk of {{stop}} pips.

templates.explain: You planned to lose {{stop}} pips (1R). The fill was {{total}} pips away, so the loss is {{total}} ÷ {{stop}} = {{answer|dec:2}}R. Gaps make some losses larger than planned.

templates.prompt: The spread on a pair is normally {{normal}} pips. Around a news release it widens to {{wide}} pips. Your stop is {{stop}} pips from your entry. How much EXTRA cost is that, in R? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the extra spread in pips. Divide by the stop distance to state it in R.
You used the whole wide spread. The normal spread is a cost you would pay anyway. Only the EXTRA counts.

templates.explain: The spread grew by {{wide}} − {{normal}} pips. Divided by the {{stop}}-pip stop, that is {{answer|dec:2}}R of extra cost.

templates.prompt: You place a buy stop on {{pair|pair}} at {{entryT}} with a stop-loss at {{stopT}} and a take-profit at {{targetT}}. What is the reward-to-risk of this bracket? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: You divided risk by reward. Reward-to-risk is the reward divided by the risk.

templates.explain: Risk: {{stopPips}} pips. Reward: {{targetT}} − {{entryT}} = {{answer|dec:2}} × {{stopPips}} pips. Reward-to-risk is {{answer|dec:2}}.

templates.prompt: An account goes from {{old|money}} to {{nw|money}}. What is the percent change? Use the − key for a fall. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: You divided by the NEW value. A percent change is measured against the STARTING value.
That is the new value as a percent of the old. The CHANGE is that minus 100.

templates.explain: ({{nw|money}} − {{old|money}}) ÷ {{old|money}} × 100 = {{answer|fixed:2}}%.

templates.prompt: What is {{p}}% of {{x|money}}?

errorDetectors.message: You used {{p}} instead of {{p}}%. Divide the percent by 100 first.

templates.explain: {{p}}% = {{p}} ÷ 100. So {{p}}% of {{x|money}} = {{answer|money}}.

templates.prompt: The ratio of risk to reward on a trade is {{a}} : {{b}}. What percent of the total is the risk? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the share of the REWARD. The question asks for the risk.
You divided one part by the other part. A share divides a part by the WHOLE ({{a}} + {{b}}).

templates.explain: The whole is {{a}} + {{b}} parts. The risk is {{a}} of them: {{a}} ÷ ({{a}} + {{b}}) = {{answer|fixed:1}}%.

templates.prompt: Your account falls {{d}}%, then rises {{d}}%. What is the net change over the two moves, in percent? Use the − key. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: A fall of {{d}}% and a rise of {{d}}% do NOT cancel. The rise is measured on a smaller balance.

templates.explain: After the fall you hold {{d}}% less, so 1 − {{d}}%. Then × (1 + {{d}}%). Together that is {{answer|fixed:2}}%, not zero.

templates.prompt: Trade A risked {{riskA|money}} and finished with {{pa|money}}. Trade B risked {{riskB|money}} and finished with {{pb|money}}. Which trade did better, measured in R?

options.why: Compare each result with the risk taken. A bigger dollar result on a bigger risk is not necessarily a better result in R.
Work out each result in R: divide the money result by the money risked.

templates.explain: Trade A: {{pa|money}} ÷ {{riskA|money}} = {{ra|r}}. Trade B: {{pb|money}} ÷ {{riskB|money}} = {{rb|r}}. {{best}} did better in R.

templates.prompt: You close {{f|dec:2}} of a position at +{{r1}}R. You leave the rest to run, and it finishes at {{r2|r}}. What is the result of the whole trade, in R? Use the − key for a loss. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: You averaged the two exits equally. Each part counts in proportion to how much of the position it was.
You counted only the first exit. The rest of the position also has a result.

templates.prompt: You risked {{risk|money}}. You moved your stop to breakeven and were stopped out at your entry price. Costs on the trade were {{cost|money}}. What is the result in R? Use the − key. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: A breakeven stop is not free. Costs still come off, so the result is slightly negative.

templates.explain: The price result was zero, and costs were {{cost|money}}. {{cost|money}} ÷ {{risk|money}} = {{answer|dec:3}}R: a small loss.

templates.prompt: Each trade wins with a {{p}}% chance, independently of the others. What is the chance of at least one win in {{k}} trades, as a percent? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: You added the chances. Instead find the chance of losing every time, then subtract it from 100%.
That is the chance for one trade. Over {{k}} trades the chance of at least one win is higher.

templates.explain: The chance of losing every time is (100% − {{p}}%) multiplied {{k}} times. Subtract that from 100%: {{answer|fixed:1}}%.

templates.prompt: A method wins {{p}}% of the time and each trade is independent. It has just lost {{k}} in a row. What is the chance the NEXT trade wins?

options.text: More than {{p}}%, because a win is due
options.why: Independent trades have no memory. A run of losses does not make a win more likely.

options.text: Less than {{p}}%, because the method has gone cold
options.why: A run of losses does not change the odds of the next independent trade either.

templates.explain: The trades are independent, so the chance on the next one is still {{p}}%.

templates.prompt: Results of {{n}} trades: {{rs|rlist}}. What is the mean (average) result, in R? (Two decimal places. Use the − key if negative.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the median, the middle value. The mean is the total divided by the number of trades.
That is the total. Divide it by the number of trades to get the mean.

templates.explain: Add the {{n}} results and divide by {{n}}: the mean is {{answer|r}}.

templates.prompt: Results of a set of trades: {{rs|rlist}}. What is the median, in R? (Sort them first. Use the − key if negative.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the mean. The median is the MIDDLE value once the results are in order.

templates.explain: In order, the middle result is {{answer|r}}.

templates.prompt: {{n}} trades each make +1R, and one more makes +{{big}}R. What is the mean result of all {{count}} trades, in R? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the median (and the typical trade). The mean is pulled up by the one big winner.
That is the total. Divide by the number of trades.

templates.explain: Total = {{n}} + {{big}} = {{total}}R over {{count}} trades: {{answer|r}}. The median stays at +1R, so one big winner moves the mean much more than the median.

templates.prompt: Results of {{n}} trades, in R: {{rs|nlist}}. What is the sample standard deviation? (Two decimal places. Divide by n − 1.)

errorDetectors.message: You divided by n. For a SAMPLE of trades, divide the sum of squared gaps by n − 1.
That is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.

templates.explain: Find the mean, then each result's gap from it. Square the gaps, add them, divide by n − 1, and take the square root: {{answer|fixed:2}}.

templates.prompt: The results of a strategy have a standard deviation of {{sd}}R. You have {{n}} trades. What is the standard error of the average result, in R? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: You divided by n. The standard error divides by the SQUARE ROOT of n.
The average gets MORE certain with more trades, so divide by √n, do not multiply.

templates.explain: Standard error = SD ÷ √n = {{sd}} ÷ √{{n}} = {{answer|dec:3}}R. Four times as many trades halves it.

templates.prompt: A method wins {{w}}% of its trades, averaging +{{wr}}R on a winner and −{{lr}}R on a loser. What is its expectancy per trade, in R? Use the − key if negative. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the win rate as a decimal. Expectancy weighs the size of the wins and losses too.
You counted only the winners. The losers take away from the average.
You averaged the win size and the loss size equally. Weight each by how often it happens.

templates.explain: {{w}}% × {{wr|r}} − {{lose}}% × {{lr|r}} = {{answer|r}} per trade.

templates.prompt: A strategy risks 1R to make {{rr}}R on every winner. What win rate does it need to break even, in percent? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the share of reward, not the win rate needed. Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + reward-to-risk).
You divided by the ratio alone. The break-even win rate is 1 ÷ (1 + ratio).

templates.explain: Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + {{rr}}) × 100 = {{answer|fixed:1}}%.

templates.prompt: A method wins {{w}}% of the time and loses {{lr}}R on a loser. What average win, in R, makes its expectancy exactly zero? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is upside down. The rarer the wins, the LARGER each win must be.
A win the same size as the loss only breaks even at a 50% win rate.

templates.explain: For zero expectancy: {{w}}% × win = {{lose}}% × {{lr}}R, so win = {{answer|r}}.

templates.prompt: Results of {{n}} trades: {{rs|rlist}}. What is the profit factor? (Gross profit ÷ gross loss. Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the average result, not the profit factor. Profit factor is total winnings divided by total losses.
You compared the NUMBER of winners with the number of losers. Compare the total R won with the total R lost.

templates.explain: Add the winners and add the losers (without the sign). Divide: {{answer|fixed:2}}.

templates.prompt: A method wins {{w}}% of its trades at +{{wr}}R and loses the other {{lose}}% at −1R. What is its profit factor? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the reward-to-risk ratio. Profit factor also weighs how often each happens.
That is the expectancy. Profit factor divides winnings by losses instead of subtracting.

templates.explain: Gross profit per 100 trades: {{w}} × {{wr}}R. Gross loss: {{lose}} × 1R. Divide: {{answer|fixed:2}}.

templates.prompt: An account falls {{d}}% from its peak. What gain, in percent, is needed to get back to the peak? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: A gain of {{d}}% is NOT enough. The gain is measured on a smaller balance, so it must be bigger than the fall.

templates.explain: After a {{d}}% fall you hold (100% − {{d}}%) of the peak. To get back you need 1 ÷ (1 − {{d}}%) − 1 = {{answer|fixed:1}}%.

templates.prompt: A run of {{n}} trades gave these results, in order: {{rs|rlist}}. Adding them up as you go, what is the maximum drawdown, in R? (The biggest fall from a high point of the running total. Start the total at 0.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the worst single trade. A drawdown is the biggest fall from a HIGH POINT of the running total, over several trades.

templates.explain: Track the running total and its highest point so far. The biggest fall below a high point is {{answer|dec:2}}R.

templates.prompt: An account's highest balance was {{peak|money}}. Later it fell to {{low|money}}. What is the drawdown, in percent? (One decimal place.)

errorDetectors.message: A drawdown is measured against the PEAK, not against the low.

templates.explain: ({{peak|money}} − {{low|money}}) ÷ {{peak|money}} × 100 = {{answer|fixed:1}}%.

templates.prompt: You start with {{x|money}} and lose {{r}}% of your CURRENT balance on each of {{n}} trades in a row. What is the balance now, to the nearest dollar?

errorDetectors.message: You took the same dollar amount each time. Each loss is a percent of the balance AT THAT TIME, which is smaller after each loss.

templates.explain: Each loss multiplies the balance by {{r|dec:0}}% less than 1. After {{n}} of them: {{x|money}} × (1 − {{r}}%)^{{n}} = {{answer|money:0}}.

templates.prompt: An account of {{x|money}} grows {{g}}% each month, and each month's growth is added to the balance. What is it worth after {{n}} months, to the nearest dollar?

errorDetectors.message: That adds the same amount each month. When growth is added to the balance, next month's growth is on a bigger balance.

templates.prompt: You risk {{r}}% of your CURRENT balance on every trade and every trade loses. How many losses in a row does it take to reach a {{d}}% drawdown? (A whole number: the first count that gets there.)

errorDetectors.message: That takes the same amount off the STARTING balance each time. Each loss is a percent of what is left, which is smaller, so it takes MORE losses.
That count does not quite reach the drawdown yet. Round UP to the first count that gets there.

templates.explain: After n losses you hold (1 − {{r}}%)^n of the balance. You need that to fall to {{keep}}%. Solving gives {{raw|dec:2}}, so {{answer|fixed:0}} losses.

templates.prompt: You close {{f|dec:2}} of a position at +{{r1}}R and leave the rest, which finishes at {{r2|r}}. Work out the whole trade in steps.

steps.label: The first part: its share × its R
steps.hint: the share closed first, times its result

steps.label: The rest: its share × its R
steps.hint: what is left of the position, times its result

templates.explain: The first part adds {{f|dec:2}} × {{r1|r}}. The rest adds {{rest|dec:2}} × {{r2|r}}. Together: {{answer|r}}.

templates.prompt: During one candle, these six prices arrived in order: {{s1}}, {{s2}}, {{s3}}, {{s4}}, {{s5}}, {{s6}}. What is the candle's {{askName}}? (Five decimal places.)

answer.expr: if(ask == 0, p1, if(ask == 1, max(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6), if(ask == 2, min(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6), p6)))

errorDetectors.message: The close is the LAST price of the candle, not the highest one.
The open is the FIRST price of the candle.
That is the last price. The high is the highest price reached and the low the lowest, wherever they came in the candle.

templates.explain: Open = first price ({{s1}}). Close = last price ({{s6}}). High = the biggest of the six. Low = the smallest.

templates.prompt: A candle, in pips above 1.10000: open {{o}}, high {{hi}}, low {{lo}}, close {{c}}. How long is its {{askName}}, in pips?

answer.expr: if(ask == 0, rng, if(ask == 1, bd, if(ask == 2, uw, lw)))

errorDetectors.message: The body runs only from the open to the close. The range runs from the low to the high, wicks included.
You measured the other wick. The upper wick sits above the body, the lower wick below it.
That is the whole range. A wick is only the part of the range outside the body, on one side.

templates.explain: Range = high − low = {{hi}} − {{lo}} = {{rng}}. Body = |close − open| = {{bd}}. Upper wick = high − the higher of open and close = {{uw}}. Lower wick = the lower of open and close − low = {{lw}}.

templates.prompt: A candle's range is {{r}} pips and its body is {{bd}} pips. What percent of the range is body? (Whole number.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the share of the range in the wicks. The body ratio is body ÷ range.
Divide by the whole RANGE, not by the wicks alone.

templates.explain: Body ratio = body ÷ range = {{bd}} ÷ {{r}} = {{answer|fixed:0}}%.

templates.prompt: Three 5-minute candles in a row (prices in pips above 1.10000). First: O {{o1}} H {{h1}} L {{l1}} C {{c1}}. Second: O {{o2}} H {{h2}} L {{l2}} C {{c2}}. Third: O {{o3}} H {{h3}} L {{l3}} C {{c3}}. Together they make one 15-minute candle. What is its {{askName}}?

answer.expr: if(ask == 0, o1, if(ask == 1, max(h1, h2, h3), if(ask == 2, min(l1, l2, l3), c3)))

errorDetectors.message: The open of the combined candle is the open of the FIRST small candle.
The close of the combined candle is the close of the LAST small candle.

templates.explain: Open = first open ({{o1}}). Close = last close ({{c3}}). High = the highest of the three highs. Low = the lowest of the three lows.

templates.prompt: How many {{small}}-minute candles fit inside one {{bigName}} candle?

errorDetectors.message: That is upside down. Divide the LONGER period by the shorter one.

templates.explain: {{big}} minutes ÷ {{small}} minutes = {{answer|fixed:0}} candles.

errorDetectors.message: A swing is not confirmed when it forms. It needs {{n}} more bars to close after it.

templates.prompt: The last five daily ranges were {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}}, {{d}} and {{e}} pips. Today's range so far is {{today}} pips. What is today's range as a ratio of the five-day average? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the average divided by today. Put today's range on top.
You divided by the total of the five ranges. Divide by their average.

templates.prompt: A backtest averages +{{g|dec:2}}R per trade before costs. Every trade pays a spread of {{c|dec:1}} pips and the stop is {{s}} pips. What is the average R per trade after the spread? Use the − key if negative. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the figure before costs. The spread takes away spread ÷ stop in R on every trade.

templates.explain: The spread costs {{c|dec:1}} ÷ {{s}} R per trade. {{g|dec:2}}R − that = {{answer|r}}.

templates.prompt: Your trading platform's server clock shows the hour {{s}} when the UTC hour is {{u}}. What is the server time minus UTC, in hours? Use the − key if the server is behind UTC.

errorDetectors.message: You subtracted the wrong way. Server time minus UTC is positive when the server is ahead.

templates.explain: Server {{s}}:00 minus UTC {{u}}:00 = {{answer|sign}} hours.

templates.prompt: You buy EUR/USD with a market order on a demo. You clicked at {{req|dec:4}} and the fill was {{fill|dec:5}}. You trade {{lots|lots}} and one pip of one lot is $10. What did the slippage cost on this trade, in dollars? (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the slippage in pips. Multiply by the lots and the $10 per pip per lot.

templates.explain: Slippage = {{pips|dec:1}} pips × {{lots|lots}} × $10 = {{answer|money}}.

templates.prompt: A funded-account program charges a fee of {{fee|money}}. If you pass, you expect payouts worth {{payout|money}}. Your honest estimate of the chance of passing is {{p}}%. What is the expected value of paying the fee? Use the − key if negative. (Two decimal places.)

errorDetectors.message: That is the expected payout before the fee. The fee is paid whether or not you pass.
That assumes you pass every time. Multiply the payout by the chance of passing.

templates.explain: {{p}}% × {{payout|money}} − {{fee|money}} = {{answer|money}}. The fee is paid every time. The payout only comes when you pass.

values.0: A provider says it is licensed by a regulator and gives a license number.
values.1: A review site says a provider has "the tightest spreads".
values.2: A provider's advert says withdrawals are "instant".
values.3: A friend says a provider "never slips".

values.0: Look up the exact legal name and number on the regulator's own register, which you reach yourself
values.1: Measure the spread yourself on a demo at the hours you trade, and compare
values.2: Read the withdrawal terms, then test a small withdrawal and time it
values.3: Measure slippage yourself on a demo, many orders, and record them

templates.prompt: {{claim}} What is the best way to check it?

options.text: Trust it if it appears on several websites
options.why: Several sites can repeat one claim. Verify at the source, or measure it yourself.

options.text: Trust it if the provider looks professional
options.why: Appearance is not evidence. Verify at the source, or measure it yourself.

options.text: Trust it if it is a well-known name
options.why: A name is not evidence. Verify at the source, or measure it yourself.

templates.explain: Verify rather than believe: {{how}}.
